Overview

Standard operating procedures for a wealth-management practice serving families with $30M to several hundred million, delivered as the family's personal chief financial officer. The library is a Bowen/CEG consultative-process spine with a Hughes family-systems layer and a Palaveev team-building section. Everything here is original procedural writing informed by those sources; nothing is reproduced from them (see SOURCES.md).

How to use this library

  1. Start with Foundations. 01 gives the model and operating principles, 02 the two engagement modes, 03 who does what, 04 client psychology, 05 the protocol every client meeting follows.
  2. Run the sequence. New client: 10 → 12 → 14 → 15 → 16 → 20. Existing client: 10 (Rediscovery variant) → 20. Whole family (Mode A): 10 → 41 → 12 … → 43.
  3. Use the templates. Every procedure names the template it consumes or produces (T01–T28).
  4. Follow the callouts. Mode B boxes say what changes when the Advisor serves an individual inside a larger family team. Beyond Bowen boxes mark content from Hughes, Palaveev, Bonner, or our own extension.
  5. Keep it alive. 60 explains how the library is reviewed; build/build.py --check validates it; build/build.py renders dist/sop-library.html for sharing.

The model in one screen

  • Wealth management = investment consulting + advanced planning + relationship management (Bowen). Advanced planning = wealth enhancement + wealth transfer + wealth protection + charitable planning. Relationship management = client relationships + expert-network relationships.
  • Complete wealth = five capitals — human, intellectual, social, spiritual, financial — with financial capital as the tool that grows the other four (Hughes). Time is measured in generations: 20 / 50 / 100 years.
  • The consultative sequence: Discovery → +2 weeks Investment Plan → +1 week Mutual Commitment → +45 days Follow-up → +90 days first Regular Progress Meeting → recurring at the cadence the client chose in Discovery.
  • Two engagement modes. Mode A — the whole family is under the Advisor's umbrella. Mode B — the Advisor serves one or more individuals inside a family that has its own central team; the mandate is scoped at intake (B-full / B-partial / B-narrow) and every procedure branches on it.
  • Default confidentiality rule. An adult's personal information is never shared upward, sideways, or with a family's central team without that person's written consent recorded on T05 / T14.

Roles at a glance

LA Lead Advisor · SA Service Advisor · AA Associate Advisor / Analyst · CSA Client Service Associate · ISB Internal Specialist Bench (sister-company experts) · EEN External Expert Network · COA Client's Other Advisors (Mode A) · FCT Family Central Team (Mode B). Where a role is unfilled, the Lead Advisor performs it — see 03.

Scope boundary

These SOPs cover client service delivery, advanced planning, the family layer, and team building. They do not cover business development (handled elsewhere), portfolio construction, trading, rebalancing, or manager selection (the firm's investment platform), or the firm's compliance manual. Where a step touches those, it says so and hands off.

01 The wealth management model and operating principles

01 — The wealth management model and operating principles

One page that every other document assumes. The model says what the practice delivers; the principles say how the Advisor behaves while delivering it.

Purpose

  • State the service model in a form the whole team can recite.
  • Fix the positioning the practice sells, so it never markets one service and delivers another.
  • List the operating principles that resolve most judgment calls without a meeting.

The model

Wealth management = investment consulting + advanced planning + relationship management.

Component What it means here Where it lives in the library
Investment consulting (IC) Competence in the basics of managing the family's investable assets, sufficient to oversee every other professional's work; delivered through the investment plan and the firm's platform SOP 12, 13, 24
Advanced planning (AP) = wealth enhancement + wealth transfer + wealth protection + charitable planning The family's financial house in order beyond the portfolio: taxes on returns; passing assets between generations the way the family intends; protection from creditors, litigants, and catastrophe; giving that serves the family's aims SOP 30, 31, 32, 46–48
Relationship management (RM) = client relationships + expert-network relationships Deep, consultative relationships with the family; a managed network of specialists; coordination with the advisors the family already has SOP 05, 10, 20, 21, 31, 33

Positioning: the family's personal chief financial officer — the one professional who keeps the whole picture in mind, thinks through challenges with the family, and coordinates every specialist, inside [Firm] and outside it, to carry out the decisions.

Why this model: advisors who actually practice it serve fewer, larger families more deeply and earn several times what investment generalists earn; the families get one accountable professional instead of a dozen unconnected ones.

Beyond Bowen

Complete wealth. At $30M and above, the family's wealth is five capitals — human (the members themselves), intellectual (what they know), social (their relationships and their capacity to decide together), spiritual (a shared intention larger than any one member), and financial. Financial capital is the tool that grows the other four. Time is measured in generations: 20, 50, and 100 years. A family flourishes when its individual members flourish inside a culture that supports it. Every recommendation in this library is tested against that, not only against tax and return.

What "comprehensive" means at this level

  • Entities and trusts, not accounts. The unit of planning is the family's structure chart: households, operating companies, holding entities, trusts, foundations — and the decision-maker for each.
  • Multiple advisors are the norm. No family at this level has one advisor; the practice coordinates rather than competes (SOP 33).
  • Governance is part of the plan. How the family decides together determines whether any structure survives a generation (SOP 45).
  • The rising generation is a client of the plan even when it is not a client of the practice — someone must advocate for it (SOP 40, 42).
  • Transitions, not transactions. A sale, a death, a marriage, a succession is a multi-year transition; no single transaction matters unless it improves the transition it sits inside.

The positioning choice

Two legitimate kinds of professional serve wealthy families. A personne d'affaires supplies knowledge and products for the stewardship of financial capital. A personne de confiance supplies, in addition, the courage the family needs to act on what it already knows, and works to grow the family's human and intellectual capital. Both are honorable; the failure is to market one and deliver the other. This practice sells the second. Its procedures — the family layer, the advanced-planning loop, the do-no-harm gate — are the proof, and its fee conversation (SOP 14) says so plainly.

Operating principles

  1. Do no harm. Before any long-term structure, ask what unintended consequences it could have for the people it is meant to serve — and put the answer to the client (SOP 20, 30).
  2. Eighty percent of the time, do nothing. Most apparent problems resolve with time and new information. When a client insists on something they would not want done if calm, be tardy: give it the weekend.
  3. Small early joint successes. Engineer a small decision the family can make together and win at before asking it to make a hard one (SOP 16, 43).
  4. Transitions, not transactions. Frame every event by the transition it belongs to; rename "succession" to "transition" in the family's vocabulary.
  5. Serve as if this were the only family you will ever serve. Capacity is protected by the roles and triggers in SOP 03 and 70 so that this can be true.
  6. Never mediate a marriage. Serve the couple; refer the relationship.
  7. Who pays, who is the client, who advocates for the rising generation. Answer all three on T05; if the third answer is "no one," act (SOP 40).
  8. The client is always yours to be responsible for. Borrowed and external experts do the work; the Advisor answers for it.
  9. No surprises. Anything material is told before the meeting, never in it; the family's central team hears about a recommendation before the family does.
  10. Whoever has the ball is the quarterback. The person who receives a request owns it to completion.
  11. Say which service you sell. Knowledge and products, or courage and complete wealth — and deliver the one you named.
  12. Confidentiality is structural. An adult's information moves only with that adult's written consent (SOP 02).

02 Engagement modes — Mode A / Mode B and the scoping rules

referenceOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — relationship management includes working with the professional advisors the client already has · Hughes: Compact — family council as the family's voice to outside professionals; confidentiality for hyperagent families; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 9 — who pays / who is the client / who advocates for the rising generation · Other: Extension — the scope ladder, the default confidentiality rule and the master matrix are ours

02 — Engagement modes

The practice serves families in two fundamentally different configurations. Every procedure in this library branches on which one applies, so the mode — and, for Mode B, the scope rung — is decided at intake, written on T05, confirmed in the engagement letter, and revisited whenever the family's situation changes.

Purpose

  • Define Mode A and Mode B and the three Mode B scope rungs.
  • Fix the rules for who the client is and what may be shared with whom.
  • Hold the master matrix of what changes in each SOP under Mode B, so the Advisor can see every delta in one place.

The two modes

Mode A — whole family under the Advisor's umbrella

The Advisor is the family's personal chief financial officer. The family (one or several households, their entities and trusts) has no other central advisory team; the Advisor's expert network, the firm's internal bench, and the family's incumbent CPA/attorney are coordinated by the Advisor. The family layer (SOPs 40–48) applies in full.

Mode B — individuals inside a family that has its own central team

A large family ($100M+) has a family office, trust company, counsel, or lead advisor of its own — the Family Central Team (FCT). The Advisor serves one or more individuals or branches of that family. The FCT quarterbacks family-level structures; the Advisor's role is scoped by mandate.

Scope rung What the Advisor owns What the FCT owns Typical use
B-full Full wealth management for the individual/branch: investment consulting, advanced planning for that person's own assets, relationship management Family-level structures (dynasty trusts, family entities, family-wide investment policy, governance) A G2 sibling with her own household, business interest, and personal assets
B-partial Investment consulting for the individual's assets plus liaison into the FCT's planning process; contributes into their advanced planning rather than running his own Advanced planning, tax, estate for the whole family including this individual A family member whose family office does all planning centrally
B-narrow A defined mandate only — one trust's portfolio, one member's personal accounts Everything else A trustee appoints the Advisor to manage one trust

Who is the client — rules

  1. Name the client(s) in writing on T05 and in the engagement letter: the individuals and, in Mode A, the households and entities. "The family" is never the client without a named decision-maker for each entity.
  2. Answer the three questions at intake and annually: who pays the fee; who is the client; who advocates for the rising generation. Record the answers on T05.
  3. Mode A with governance in place: when a family council or equivalent exists, it is the Advisor's institutional counterparty for family-level matters; individual households remain clients in their own right.
  4. Mode B: the individual is the client. The FCT is a counterparty to coordinate with under SOP 33, never a party that can instruct the Advisor about that individual's affairs unless the individual has authorized it on T05.
  5. A couple is one client unit with two people who may each speak directly with the Advisor (SOP 21); either spouse may hold information in confidence from the other only where the engagement letter says so and [Firm Compliance] has approved.

Default confidentiality rule (both modes)

An adult's personal information is not shared upward (to parents), sideways (to siblings or spouses of siblings), or with a family's central team without that adult's written consent recorded on T05 (Mode B) or T14 (Mode A). Consent is specific — what may be shared, with whom, for what purpose — and is reviewed annually. Where a sister company of [Firm] also sits on the family's central team, the same wall applies inside the firm.

Engagement scoping — the procedure in brief

  1. At handoff from business development the CSA opens T05 with the known facts (source, relationship, family context, known advisors, conflicts check).
  2. During and after CCM1 the LA completes the mode determination and, for Mode B, proposes the scope rung and the information-sharing consent.
  3. Before CCM2 the LA confirms the mandate with the client (and, in Mode B, whether the FCT needs a courtesy notice) so the investment plan is scoped correctly.
  4. At CCM3 the engagement letter states the client, the mode, the scope, the fee basis, and the consent; T05 is signed alongside it.
  5. Annually (at the first progress meeting of the year) and on any trigger in SOP 22, the LA reviews T05 and re-scopes.

When modes change

  • A Mode B individual's family later asks the Advisor to serve the whole family → re-scope to Mode A; run SOP 41 (family discovery) before expanding the plan.
  • A Mode A family sets up its own family office or engages a central advisor → decide, family by family, whether the Advisor becomes the FCT or moves to Mode B for the households he continues to serve; update T05 for every affected client.
  • A member of a Mode A family asks for confidential advice the rest of the family must not see → serve that member under the confidentiality rule; if the member's interests conflict with the family's, disclose the conflict and, if necessary, arrange a separate advisor for that member (SOP 40).

SOP Mode B delta

03 Roles and RACI

03 — Roles and RACI

Every procedure in this library names roles, never people. This reference defines the roles, records who covers each one today, states the trigger for filling it, and fixes the delegation rules that keep the client experience intact as the team grows.

Purpose

  • Give every SOP a stable vocabulary for "who does this step."
  • Let the practice run today (solo plus borrowed specialists) and tomorrow (a full team) without rewriting the client-facing procedures — only this table changes.
  • Make the boundary between the Advisor's own team, borrowed sister-company experts, external experts, and the family's other advisors explicit.

The role set

Role Abbr. Owns Track Today Target / trigger to fill
Lead Advisor LA Every client relationship and every decision about what is best for the client; all consultative and family meetings; the asks; drop/defer/do coaching; quarterback of the expert network; the service-failure call; sign-off on plans and proposals Professional (owner) [Advisor] [Advisor]
Client Service Associate CSA Scheduling, correspondence (T01), meeting logistics and packets, sign-here paperwork, the implementation tracker (T07), the client notebook / [Document vault], [CRM] hygiene, reporting assembly, service-failure intake, red-flag monitoring Support [Advisor] with [Firm shared services] First hire. Trigger: recurring administrative errors, or the LA spends > 25% of client-facing hours on CSA work
Service Advisor SA Can serve existing clients independently from day one: plan and portfolio production, periodic reviews, routine progress meetings (co-attended, then independent), watching for held-away assets and advanced-planning openings; attends every client meeting with a named role Professional [Advisor]; borrowed from a sister RIA per engagement Second hire, first professional. Trigger: ~$500–700K revenue in the profit center, or ~40 relationships, whichever first (see SOP 70)
Associate Advisor / Analyst AA Investment plan and IPS drafts, reporting analysis, meeting packets, advanced-planning tracker (T10) upkeep, expert-meeting case briefs, executive-summary drafting support; second chair on large relationships Professional (entry) [Advisor]; borrowed from a sister RIA Third hire, when relationship size justifies a third professional level
Internal Specialist Bench ISB Sister-company specialists engaged per matter: [Trust Co.] (trust administration, fiduciary services), [ESOP Co.] (business succession and liquidity), tax, insurance, lending, sister RIAs Borrowed Named per engagement under SOP 71 Standing roster maintained in SOP 31
External Expert Network EEN Private-client attorney (the client hires directly), independent insurance specialist, and as needed valuation, corporate tax, credit, concentrated-stock, actuary, charitable-planning, family-governance facilitator, counselor External To be built Core two (attorney + insurance) in place before advanced planning is promised
Client's Other Advisors COA The client's incumbent CPA, attorney, other managers (Mode A) Not ours to direct Mapped per client on T05 Coordinated under SOP 33
Family Central Team FCT The family office, trust company, counsel, and other advisors of a large family in which the Advisor serves individuals (Mode B) Not ours to direct Mapped per client on T05 Coordinated under SOP 33
Firm Compliance — Recording consent, fee-sharing and disclosure, engagement letters, gifts, licensing Firm [Firm Compliance] —
Family roles (Mode A) — Principal, household lead, decision-maker, trustee, beneficiary, elder, council member, rising-generation member Client side Defined per family on T14 See SOP 40

Rule: where a role is unfilled, the LA performs it — the procedures do not change.

Support track vs professional track

  • The support track (CSA, operations) makes administrative decisions and is not expected to pursue a professional career. The professional track (AA → SA → LA) makes professional judgments about a client's plan and portfolio.
  • Moving from support to professional is a change of track, not a promotion; it requires the hiring process in SOP 72.
  • Whoever owns operations today is named here: <span class="ph">[Advisor]</span> until the CSA is hired. The path from CSA to an operations lead is a stated career option, so operations does not become a second-class job as the team grows.

Delegation ladder

Never delegate (LA only): the Discovery and family-executive-summary interviews; presentation of the investment plan and the wealth management plan; the additional-assets and introductions asks; drop/defer/do coaching; the service-failure apology call; facilitation of the expert-network meeting; facilitation of family meetings unless an external facilitator is engaged.

Delegate first (in this order as hires arrive):

  1. Routine execution — scheduling, confirmations, paperwork, notebook, [CRM] logging, reporting assembly → CSA.
  2. Plan and portfolio production, periodic reviews, supporting analysis → SA / AA.
  3. Routine progress meetings — first co-attended, then led by the SA with the LA present, then independent → SA.
  4. Relationship management (the client calls the SA first) → SA, when the relationship-manager test in SOP 73 is met.
  5. Relationship ownership (all meetings including strategy) → SA, when the relationship-owner test in SOP 73 is met.
  6. Business development — last; it needs a decade of experience and is out of scope here.

Lean RACI convention

Every procedure's ## Roles line uses three verbs only:

  • Owner — accountable for the outcome; there is exactly one.
  • Does — performs named steps.
  • Consulted — supplies input or review before a step completes.

"Informed" is deliberately omitted; who gets told what is governed by the contact plan (SOP 21) and the coordination protocol (SOP 33).

Operating rules that protect the relationship

  • Whoever has the ball is the quarterback. The person who receives a client request owns it to completion. "Let me put you through to someone" is not an acceptable answer inside this practice.
  • The relationship stays with the LA. Borrowed and external experts are introduced by name, role, and what they will do for this client; they never become the client's primary contact unless the LA and the client agree (SOP 71).
  • Language. The team says "our clients" and "the family we serve," never "my clients." Possessive language is corrected on the spot.
  • Independent-action scope. The LA acts alone on anything within the profit center's authority. Matters with more than a stated materiality threshold of impact on the firm, on a sister company, or on a future partner (default: the equivalent of one quarter of a professional salary) are discussed with the relevant firm leader first.
  • Three questions the LA asks about every engagement: who pays the fee; who is the client; who is advocating for the rising generation. If the first two answers are "the senior generation" and the third is "no one," the engagement is at risk and SOP 40 applies.

04 High-net-worth psychology — the nine personalities and how to serve each

referenceOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 3 — the nine high-net-worth personalities (after Prince), which to be cautious with; Ch. 4 — determine the personality at Discovery and reinforce it at every greeting; Ch. 6 — incorporate psychology into every contact · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 4 — rising-generation patterns as awareness cues; The Compact — assessment batteries are specialist work · Other: Extension — the family-mix note and the meeting-design guidance are ours

04 — High-net-worth psychology

Wealthy clients are not alike, and treating them alike is the commonest service error. This reference gives the team one table of the dominant client personalities, what to listen for at Discovery, and how to present, pace, and contact each — plus the awareness cues that matter when the client is a family rather than a person.

Purpose

  • Identify each client's dominant personality at Discovery (SOP 10) and record it in [CRM].
  • Reinforce it at every greeting and in every presentation choice (SOP 05).
  • Design family meetings for the mix of personalities in the room (SOP 43).

The nine personalities

Shares are approximate proportions of the affluent population in the underlying research; use them to calibrate expectations, not to label a client.

Personality Share What they want from the Advisor Discovery cues — listen for Presenting the plan Contact style Risk flag
Family Steward about one in three The family taken care of; conservative; not investment-minded "my children," "security," "what happens to them," questions about the next generation before the portfolio Lead with what the plan does for the family; keep investment detail short; show the protection and transfer pieces Warm, regular, family news welcome; the couple together —
Independent about one in six The freedom money buys; investing is a means, not an interest "so I don't have to think about it," travel, second careers, "make work optional" Show the goal (freedom date, income) and that the plan gets there; minimal process talk Efficient; fewer, purposeful contacts; honor their stated cadence exactly —
Phobic about one in nine Relief from a responsibility they dislike; trust in the person Discomfort with numbers, "I just want someone I can trust," avoidance of technical questions Plain language, no jargon, one page; emphasize who is looking after them and how Reassuring, personal, proactive in downturns; never a data dump —
Anonymous about one in twelve Privacy above all; will concentrate assets with an advisor who protects it Questions about who sees what, reluctance to share, few other advisors Confidentiality first; consolidated reporting as a privacy benefit; explain the consent rules (SOP 02) Discreet; single point of contact; nothing by open channels —
Mogul about one in thirteen Control; investing as an extension of power; decisive "I decide," wants options not recommendations, impatience with process Present choices with clear trade-offs and let them choose; be crisp; do not over-explain Direct, fast, respectful of time; agenda-driven —
VIP about one in fifteen Prestige; affiliation with leading institutions and advisors Names of firms and people, status of the arrangement, how others see them Emphasize the calibre of the network and the firm's standing; polished materials Formal; the LA personally; recognition matters —
Accumulator about one in sixteen A bigger portfolio; performance-focused; frugal Return figures, comparisons, fee questions ahead of goals Numbers-forward, benchmark-aware; keep the goal frame visible Frequent performance information; expect scrutiny caution — demanding, transactional
Gambler about one in twenty The excitement of investing; high risk tolerance; involved Stories of trades, appetite for ideas, wants to discuss markets Contain the appetite inside the plan; a small self-directed sleeve if the firm allows Will want frequent market talk; set boundaries caution — time-consuming, plan-eroding
Innovator about one in twenty-five Leading-edge and complex products; technically sophisticated Asks about structures, new vehicles, complexity for its own sake Explain the investment policy in depth once; then hold the line on simplicity Technical, detailed, expects the IPS to be read caution — complexity for its own sake

The last three are the ones most interested in investing itself and, in the research, the most demanding and least loyal. The practice does not refuse them, but it accepts them knowingly, prices the service accordingly, and holds the plan.

Rules of use

  1. Determine the dominant personality at Discovery. Everyone shows traits of several; almost everyone has one dominant type. Record it in [CRM] with the cues you heard.
  2. Reinforce it at every greeting. The first minute of every meeting speaks to what this client values — the family, the freedom, the privacy, the standing — before any business (SOP 05).
  3. Match the presentation, not the advice. The plan is the plan; the length, order, and vocabulary of its presentation change by personality. A Phobic gets one page and a person; an Innovator gets the investment policy statement.
  4. Match the contact plan. The stated process preference from Discovery governs (SOP 21); the personality suggests the tone and what non-portfolio contact will be welcome.
  5. Re-check after transitions. A liquidity event, a death, or retirement can shift a client from Independent to Family Steward, or from Mogul to Phobic. Re-read the cues at the next progress meeting.

The family mix

A family is several personalities across two or three generations — often a Family Steward founder, an Independent in the second generation, and an Innovator or Gambler among the rising generation. Design family meetings (SOP 43) for the mix: an agenda with something for the steward (protection, continuity), the independent (what this frees them to do), and the technically minded (the investment policy, in an appendix); ground rules that stop the Mogul from deciding for everyone; and a facilitator when the mix is combustible.

Beyond Bowen

Rising-generation cues, not diagnoses. Hughes describes patterns a large founder's shadow can produce in heirs. Use these only to notice and ask, never to label: the dutiful steward whose own dreams are crowded out; the member who learned the size of the wealth by accident; the one slowly made comfortable into passivity; the one raised as if the money did not exist and now unsure what is real; the anxious heir measuring up; the one who constrains every choice to protect the family name; the one who wants to give it all away to be free. The Advisor's job is individuation — helping each member find work, relationships, and a voice of their own — and that is done through the family layer (SOP 40, 42, 44), not through the investment plan.

Formal assessments

Learning-style, values, work-style, and personality instruments are useful to families and are referred to qualified specialists through the expert network (SOP 31). The practice does not administer or interpret them; it records the client's stated preferences and honors them.

05 Client meeting protocol — the wrapper for every meeting

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the recurring steps of every CCM meeting: greet by name, reinforce personality, agenda, schedule next meeting in the room, send confirmation; office-experience rules; recording consent · Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 11 and 13 — define success at the top of the meeting; one-week follow-up call; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 16 — agenda in advance, listening time after weighty disclosures · Other: Palaveev — introduce every team member by name, role and what they will do; a named role for any junior in the room

05 — Client meeting protocol

Every client meeting in this practice — the five consultative meetings, family meetings, trustee meetings, and ad hoc reviews — runs inside this wrapper. The meeting-specific SOP supplies the body; this procedure supplies the preparation, the opening, the close, and the follow-up so that the client has the same experience every time, whoever is in the room.

Purpose

  • Deliver a consistent, prepared, agenda-driven experience that signals the practice is a refined process, not an individual's improvisation.
  • Make sure every meeting ends with the next one scheduled and every decision recorded within 24 hours.
  • Let team members and borrowed specialists take part without the client ever feeling "passed down."

Trigger

Any client-facing meeting is scheduled — in person, video, or phone — with a client, a prospective client, a family group, or a trustee/beneficiary.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (letter, confirmation, logistics, packet assembly, [CRM] entries), AA (analysis in the packet; a named role in the room) · Consulted: ISB / EEN specialists when they attend.

Timing

When What
T−10 business days Meeting scheduled in [CRM]; agenda drafted from T02
T−7 Pre-meeting letter or email sent (T01) with the agenda and anything the client should bring
T−3 Packet assembled; team briefing held; any change since the last meeting the client should hear before the meeting is communicated now
T−1 Confirmation call or message
T+0 Meeting
T+1 (≤ 24 hours) Written recap, confirmation of the next meeting, [CRM] log, tasks assigned
T+7 One-week call after a first meeting or any meeting with heavy disclosures or decisions

Inputs

  • The meeting-specific agenda (T02) and the SOP for that meeting.
  • The client's Total Client Profile (SOP 11) and the recap of the last meeting.
  • Open items: implementation tracker (T07), advanced-planning tracker (T10), service-failure log.
  • The most recent quarter-end statements or reporting package (SOP 24).
  • The client's stated process preference (how they want to be contacted and how often) and personality notes (SOP 04).
  • T05 for who may attend and what may be discussed in front of whom.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Agenda adapted from T02; client invited to add items in the pre-meeting letter.
  • [ ] Packet: agenda, prior-quarter figures, tracker extracts, any documents to sign with "sign here" flags.
  • [ ] Attendee list checked against T05 (consent) and the client's wishes; every team member or specialist attending has a named role for this meeting.
  • [ ] Anything material that changed since the last contact has already been told to the client — no surprises in the room.
  • [ ] Room or video link tested; beverages; no financial television or market commentary visible in the waiting area.
  • [ ] Recording plan decided (Discovery and family-executive-summary interviews are recorded with consent; otherwise notes by the AA/CSA).
  • [ ] Personality note reviewed: how this client likes to be greeted, paced, and presented to.

Procedure

  1. Send the pre-meeting letter (T01). Confirm date, time, place, purpose, attendees, and what to bring. Attach the agenda and invite additions.
  2. Brief the team. Two minutes per attendee: what they will do in the room, what they may and may not discuss, who takes notes.
  3. Greet. Every team member greets the client by name, formally. The LA reinforces something the client values (a recent event, an interest) before any business.
  4. Introduce anyone new — by name, role in the practice, and what they will do for this client today. Promote their skills; never sound uncertain about them.

  5. Open with purpose and success. State why we are meeting. Ask what needs to happen for the client to leave feeling this was time well spent. Walk the agenda and ask for additions.

    Say something like

    "Before we start: what would make this a genuinely useful hour for you? I'll make sure we get there."

  6. Ask what has changed. "What has happened since we last met?" — then, if needed, "Anything in your life or the family's that affects your finances and that I should know about?" Listen for marriages, births, deaths, health, job or business changes, sales, disputes.

  7. Run the body per the meeting-specific SOP. Present, then pause for questions; do not answer everything immediately if the packet will answer it in sequence.
  8. Coach decisions, don't push. For each recommendation, the client chooses drop / defer / do (Mode B adds refer to family team). Record the choice.
  9. Close. Summarize decisions and next steps by owner and date. Ask whether the meeting achieved what the client wanted and what to do differently next time.
  10. Schedule the next meeting in the room according to the client's stated cadence. Never leave with "we'll be in touch."
  11. Confirm in writing within 24 hours (T01). Date and time of the next meeting, decisions, tasks with owners, and any documents outstanding.
  12. Log in [CRM] within 24 hours. Life changes, decisions, asks made and outcomes, the personality note, and the next-meeting date.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours: recap and confirmation sent; tasks created; documents filed to the [Document vault]; tracker(s) updated.
  • Within one week: after a first meeting or any meeting with weighty disclosures, the LA calls to answer questions that surfaced on reflection.
  • Any promise made in the room has a date and an owner before the day ends.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Agenda and pre-meeting letter [CRM] activity; client's [Document vault] CSA
Meeting notes and recap [CRM]; recap sent to the client AA / CSA
Decisions and tasks [CRM] tasks; T07 / T10 trackers CSA
Next-meeting confirmation [CRM] calendar; written confirmation CSA
Updated personality and process notes [CRM] client record LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Prepare an agenda for every meeting, including the "quick" ones.
  • Tell the client bad news before the meeting, never in it.
  • Keep Discovery to ninety minutes; keep every other meeting inside the time promised.
  • Give every junior in the room something substantive to do — the notes and follow-through, one analysis to present, one project to own.

Don't

  • Don't take the check at the investment-plan meeting; commitment has its own meeting.
  • Don't let a specialist become the client's point of contact by default.
  • Don't answer the first question with a lecture; the packet and the sequence usually answer it.
  • Don't "pass the puck" — whoever receives a request in the meeting owns it to completion.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Attendance follows the family map and communication map (T14); confidentiality between members is checked before anyone joins.
  • Family meetings add the ground rules and facilitation protocol in SOP 43 on top of this wrapper.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Recap distribution follows the consent on T05: the individual only, unless the FCT is authorized.
  • Recording consent explicitly covers privacy from the family and the FCT, not only from third parties.
  • If an FCT representative attends, the LA states at the opening what will and will not be covered in their presence.

Metrics

  • Share of meetings with a written confirmation sent within 24 hours (target 100%).
  • Share of meetings that ended with the next meeting scheduled (target 100%).
  • Service-failure log entries traceable to a meeting promise (target zero).

Onboarding — CCM1 to CCM4

10 CCM1 — Discovery Meeting (and the Rediscovery variant)

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — Discovery Meeting objectives, steps, critical success factors, opening script, Total Client Profile interview and mind map; Ch. 5 — rediscovery meetings for existing clients before any new business development · Hughes: Family Wealth Ch. 17 — the two opening questions (passion, mentor); Complete Family Wealth Ch. 1 — qualitative-vs-financial budget comparison; Compact — generational position; essential questions as a discovery vocabulary · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes — the seven-pitfalls probe (used lightly); Extension — Mode B mandate qualification and the handoff minimum are ours

10 — CCM1 Discovery Meeting

The Discovery Meeting is where the practice decides, with the prospective client, whether it can add substantial value — and, if so, builds the Total Client Profile that every later document is drawn from. It is a qualification and a listening exercise, never a sales presentation. The same procedure, run as a Rediscovery meeting, refreshes the profile of an existing client.

Purpose

  • Establish trust by positioning the Advisor as an expert with a disciplined process, not a product to sell.
  • Uncover what is genuinely important to the client — values first, money fourth — and determine the client's dominant wealth personality (SOP 04).
  • Collect everything needed to assess fit, scope the engagement (T05), and draft the investment plan (SOP 13).
  • Leave with a precommitment and CCM2 in the calendar.

Trigger

  • Business development hands off a prospective client with T05 Part 1 completed, or
  • An existing client is due for a Rediscovery meeting (annually, at a mode change, at a major life event, or when the profile is more than 18 months old), or
  • A member of a Mode A family is being onboarded (SOP 42 calls this procedure).

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (pre-meeting letter T01, logistics, photocopying/scanning of documents during the meeting, confirmation), AA (mind-map capture if the LA prefers to stay fully engaged; packet) · Consulted: [Firm Compliance] on recording consent.

Timing

  • Day 0. Ninety minutes maximum; sixty is often enough for a single household.
  • CCM2 is scheduled in the room for +2 weeks.
  • T05 Parts 2–5 completed by the LA within two business days; confirmation and recap within 24 hours.

Inputs

  • T05 Part 1 (handoff minimum): source of the relationship, family context, known advisors, known family office / central team, conflicts check cleared with [Firm Compliance], asset estimate.
  • Documents requested in the pre-meeting letter: recent statements for all accounts, last two years of tax returns, trust and entity documents, insurance schedules, any existing investment policy.
  • T03 interview guide; blank unlined sheet or T04 outline for the mind map; digital recorder.
  • SOP 04 personality cues.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Pre-meeting letter sent at T−7 with the document list and a two-line description of what the meeting is for (T01).
  • [ ] Agenda drafted from T02 and attached.
  • [ ] Waiting area free of market television and financial magazines; beverages ready; every team member briefed to greet the client by name.
  • [ ] Recording consent wording approved by [Firm Compliance]; recorder tested.
  • [ ] LA has read T05 Part 1 and any public information about the family's enterprise; no assumptions written into the profile in advance.
  • [ ] For a couple: both partners invited and both names will go at the centre of the mind map.

Procedure

  1. Greet and settle. Formal greeting by name from everyone the client meets. Two minutes of genuine interest in the person before any business.

  2. State the purpose — qualify, don't sell. Explain that the meeting exists to find out whether the practice is the right fit, that it works with a limited number of families for whom it can make a substantial difference, and that if the fit is wrong the Advisor will gladly point them to a better one.

    Say something like

    "Our purpose today is to understand what matters most to you and to be honest with each other about whether we're the right firm for your family. If we're not, I'll say so and help you find who is."

  3. Walk the agenda and ask for additions (SOP 05 opening). Ask what would make this a valuable meeting for them.

  4. Explain the process and ask consent to record. Say why: so the Advisor can listen without scribbling. Assure confidentiality whether or not they become a client. If they decline, the AA takes notes.
  5. Conduct the profile interview in Bowen's order — Values → Goals → Relationships → Assets → Advisors → Process → Interests — using T03. Draw the mind map on unlined paper with the client's name (both names for a couple) in the centre, one branch per area, connecting lines where answers relate. Rules:
    • Ask second-order questions: when an answer is general ("security"), ask what specifically about it matters most.
    • Ask about assets fourth, never first; hand statements to the CSA to scan while the conversation continues.
    • Under Advisors, capture every professional and what has and has not worked with each; under Process, capture exactly how and how often they want to be contacted — this preference is honoured for the life of the relationship.
    • Listen for the dominant wealth personality and note it on the map (SOP 04).

  6. Add the family overlay where the household is part of a larger family or wealth spans generations.

    Beyond Bowen

    Ask each person present what they are passionate about and who they learn from — the two questions that reveal a calling and whether the person has the means to pursue it. Ask, without judgment, roughly what the family spends each year to preserve and grow its money and what it spends, on purpose, to develop its people; the ratio is a planning conversation in itself. Establish where the family sits in the generational arc (founder generation, siblings, cousins) and which transitions are under way. Choose two or three essential-question topics from T03 that fit this family — shared values, how decisions get made together, how the rising generation is being prepared — and ask them in your own words. Treat the answers as the seed of the family-level profile (SOP 11).

  7. Ask the Mode B mandate questions when the client belongs to a family that has its own central team: what that team already does for them; what they want from the Advisor that they are not getting; who else will need to know about this relationship; what information they cannot access themselves. Record the family position and the central team by name and function on the Advisors branch.

  8. Assess fit — silently, then aloud. Fit means: the ideal-client criteria (asset level, complexity the practice is built for, personality compatibility, mandate workability in Mode B), and evidence that the Advisor can make a substantial difference. Avoid the three most demanding personalities as primary clients unless the mandate is narrow and the economics are sound.
  9. If the fit is poor, say so graciously. Thank them for their candour, explain that another firm would serve them better, name one or two if possible, and offer an introduction. Send a short note the same day. Log the outcome and inform the referring party in a confidentiality-safe way (T01).

  10. If the fit is good, describe the next steps — the investment plan meeting in two weeks, the commitment meeting a week after that, the follow-up at forty-five days, and the regular progress meetings at the cadence they chose. Ask for a precommitment to move forward.

    Say something like

    "In two weeks I'll bring you a written plan that shows what I would do and why. If it makes sense to you then, we'll meet once more to commit to each other and put it in motion."

  11. Schedule CCM2 in the room. Confirm the cadence preference they stated under Process.

  12. Close (SOP 05): summarise what you heard back to them in one minute; ask if anything was missed; thank them for their openness.
  13. Within 24 hours: written confirmation of CCM2 (T01); mind map scanned to the [Document vault]; T05 Parts 2–5 drafted; [CRM] updated with the profile, personality note, process preference, and advisor map.
  14. Within one week: the one-week call (SOP 05) to answer questions that surfaced on reflection and to request any documents still outstanding.

Variant — Rediscovery meeting

Run steps 1–14 for an existing client with these differences only:

  • No qualifying script. Open by explaining that the practice has deepened how it understands the families it serves and wants to make sure it knows everything that matters now.
  • Compare to the prior profile. Bring the old mind map; draw a fresh one; mark what changed. Ask specifically about assets held elsewhere and with whom, about advisors added or dropped, and about the rising generation.
  • Outputs: refreshed profile; a list of held-away asset targets for SOP 50; advanced-planning hooks for the next expert-network case brief (SOP 32); any change to mode or scope on T05.
  • Sequencing rule: with a sufficient base of existing ideal clients, complete at least ten Rediscovery meetings before any new-client effort — they surface the most value with the least acquisition cost.
  • Next step is not CCM2 but a refreshed investment plan presented at the next regular progress meeting (SOP 20), or CCM2 if the scope has changed materially.

Follow-up

  • ≤ 24 hours: confirmation of CCM2, recap, [CRM] and [Document vault] updated, T05 drafted.
  • ≤ 2 business days: LA completes T05 Parts 2–5; conflicts or consent questions raised with [Firm Compliance].
  • ≤ 1 week: one-week call; outstanding documents chased by the CSA.
  • Before CCM2: profile reviewed by the LA; investment-plan drafting begins (SOP 13).

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Total Client Profile mind map (photo/scan + T04 outline) [Document vault]; [CRM] profile fields LA (AA transcribes)
Personality note and process preference [CRM] client record LA
Advisor map (and FCT table in Mode B) T05 Part 5; [CRM] LA
T05 Parts 2–5 (draft) [CRM]; [Document vault] LA
Scanned documents [Document vault] CSA
Recording (with consent) [Document vault], restricted folder CSA
CCM2 date and confirmation [CRM] calendar; T01 CSA
Fit decision and referral note (if declined) [CRM] LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Keep it to ninety minutes; the affluent have enough friends and not enough time.
  • Listen far more than you talk; the map should be in the client's words.
  • Record the process preference exactly and honour it forever.
  • Practise the mind map on colleagues before running it with a $30M family.

Don't

  • Don't present products, portfolios, or your firm's history — that is what the investment plan is for.
  • Don't ask about money before you have asked about values, goals, and people.
  • Don't promise advanced-planning services the expert network cannot yet deliver.
  • Don't accept a client whose mandate you cannot actually execute (no information access, no authority to act).

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Discovery with the principal household is the first step; it does not substitute for the family-wide discovery. Hand off to SOP 41 for the confidential member interviews and the family balance sheet before drafting a family-level plan.
  • Ask who else in the family should be interviewed and who would object; record the answers on T14.
  • Both names of a couple sit at the centre of the map; each household in a family gets its own map (SOP 11).

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Qualification becomes "is the mandate workable?": can the Advisor get the information, does the client have authority to act on the assets in question, and is there a conflict with a sister company already serving the family?
  • The Relationships and Advisors branches must capture the family-tree position and every member of the family central team by name and function.
  • Output adds the advisor map and a proposed scope rung on T05; a courtesy notice to the family team is sent only if the client agrees (T01).
  • The fee conversation and information-sharing consent are previewed here and settled at CCM3.

Metrics

  • Share of Discovery meetings with T05 Parts 2–5 completed within two business days (target 100%).
  • Share of Discovery meetings ending with CCM2 scheduled in the room (target ≥ 90%).
  • Rediscovery meetings completed per year against the existing-client base (target: every ideal client every 12–18 months).

11 Total Client Profile — the data model every meeting feeds

specOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the seven areas of the Total Client Profile, second-order questions, mind-map mechanics and advantages, downstream uses · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 1–2 — five capitals; family of affinity; transitions; Family Trusts Ch. 2 — the trustscape as a map of everyone touched by the family's trusts; Compact — generational position (founders, siblings, cousins) · Other: Extension — two-level profile, confidentiality flags, FCT table are ours

11 — Total Client Profile

The Total Client Profile is the practice's single picture of a client: seven areas captured in Discovery, extended with what a $30M+ family adds (entities, trusts, liquidity events, philanthropy, governance), and kept current at every meeting. The investment plan, the wealth management plan, the expert-network case brief, and the contact plan are all drawn from it.

Purpose

  • Define what a complete profile contains, in what order it is gathered, and how it is recorded.
  • Fix the two-level structure used for whole families (Mode A) and the family-context additions used for individuals inside a larger family (Mode B).
  • State who may see which parts (confidentiality flags) and when the profile is refreshed.

Contents

The seven areas (in this order)

# Area What it captures Second-order pattern
1 Values What is truly important to the client about money and life; the "why" behind every goal Ask what specifically about a stated value matters most, and what that would look like in practice
2 Goals What they want to achieve over the long run — lifestyle, family, enterprise, legacy — with rough timing For each goal: when, for whom, what "done" looks like
3 Relationships Who counts: spouse/partner, children and their partners, parents, siblings, close non-family, pets; the family tree as the client describes it Who depends on whom; who influences decisions; who is not on speaking terms
4 Assets Everything and where it is held: accounts and custodians, entities, trusts, real estate, operating businesses, concentrated positions, deferred compensation, insurance, debt; income sources Asked fourth. Who controls each asset; what is held away and with whom
5 Advisors Every professional relied on — CPA, attorney(s), trustees, other managers, insurance agent, family office — and what has and has not worked with each What would make them change an advisor; who they trust most
6 Process How they want to work with the Advisor: channel, frequency, meeting style, who should be present, level of detail, decision style Honoured for the life of the relationship; recorded verbatim
7 Interests Hobbies, sports, travel, philanthropy, faith, children's activities — the material of relationship depth Shared interests noted for future contact (SOP 21)

The mind map

  • One unlined sheet (or T04 in digital form), the client's name — both names for a couple — at the centre, a branch per area, lines between related items.
  • Drawn live, in the client's words, using symbols and short phrases; it is a stimulus for deeper questions, not a form.
  • Scanned to the [Document vault] the same day; transcribed into [CRM] fields by the AA within 24 hours.
  • Advantages the practice relies on: faster drill-down to what matters, cross-references between areas, client involvement, a one-page review document, and a ready case brief for the expert network.

UHNW overlay (every profile)

Beyond Bowen

Add these nodes under the relevant areas; at $30M+ they are where the planning work lives.

  • Entity and trust map ("trustscape") — every trust, partnership, LLC, foundation, and company; for each: purpose, trustee/manager, beneficiaries/owners, protector, situs, key terms known, statements received. Who is touched by each and how they feel about it.
  • Concentrated positions and closely held businesses — size relative to net worth, restrictions, succession intentions, whether [ESOP Co.] or a sale is under consideration.
  • Liquidity events — past, pending, and possible (sale, inheritance, distribution, vesting), with dates and rough amounts.
  • Philanthropy — vehicles (DAF, foundation), causes, who is involved, giving history and appetite.
  • Family office / central team — existence, who leads it, what it does, how the client experiences it.
  • Existing governance — family meetings, council, constitution, mission statement, family bank; rituals the family keeps.
  • Rising generation — each member's stage, work, individuation, exposure to the wealth, who is advocating for them.
  • Transitions under way — family (generation to generation), ownership, board, management; health changes; marriages and divorces.

Two-level profile (Mode A)

Family level (one per family, built through SOP 41):

  • Family map — households, members with stage of life, roles (principal, household lead, decision-maker, trustee, beneficiary, elder, council member), affinity members (spouses, in-laws, long-serving advisors).
  • Entity and trust map for the whole family.
  • Five-capitals summary — human, intellectual, social, spiritual, financial — from the family balance sheet (SOP 44).
  • Shared values and goals; what the family says makes it different.
  • Transitions under way and the next two expected.
  • Full advisor map across all households; existing governance.

Household level (one per household): the seven areas plus the UHNW overlay, exactly as for a single client.

Family context (Mode B)

  • Family-context node — the client's position in the tree, entities in which they have an interest but no control, information they cannot access, the family's rules they must live within.
  • FCT table — every member of the family central team by name, function, what they do for this client, contact protocol, and whether they may receive anything from the Advisor (T05 Part 4).

Confidentiality flags

Every node carries one of three flags: Shared (may appear in family-level documents), Household (visible to the household only), Private (visible to the individual and the Advisor only). Default is Household for a couple and Private for anything told to the Advisor by one adult alone. Flags are set from T05/T14 consent and reviewed at every Rediscovery.

Downstream uses

Consumer What it takes from the profile
Investment plan and IPS (SOP 13) Values, goals, assets, process; entity/trust constraints; scope
CCM3 preparation (SOP 14) Whole profile re-read; open questions from CCM2
Wealth management plan (SOP 30) All seven areas plus the overlay; the four advanced-planning areas map onto Assets, Relationships, Values, Interests
Expert-network case brief (T09) Anonymised summary of the profile with the overlay; qualitative capitals
Contact plan (SOP 21) Process and Interests; life-event triggers
Family discovery (SOP 41) Household profiles roll up into the family level
Asks (SOP 50) Held-away assets from the Assets area; relationships for introductions

Standards

  • Captured in the client's words; no advisor interpretation on the map itself (interpretation goes in the [CRM] note).
  • Complete: every area has at least one entry before CCM2; "not discussed" is recorded explicitly.
  • Dated: every node shows when it was last confirmed.
  • Traceable: the source of each asset figure (statement, client estimate, tax return).
  • Confidential: flags set before the profile is shared with anyone, including sister-company specialists.

Refresh cadence

  • Every progress meeting: changes captured from the "what has happened since we last met" question (SOP 20) and logged within 24 hours.
  • Every Rediscovery meeting (SOP 10 variant): full redraw with the prior map alongside; at least annually for ideal clients, and always at a mode or scope change.
  • On any trigger in SOP 22 (marriage, birth, death, sale, dispute, health change): the affected nodes are updated within one week.
  • Family level: refreshed with the family balance sheet every one to three years (SOP 44) and before each annual family meeting.

Owner

LA owns the profile; AA transcribes and maintains it in [CRM]; CSA files scans and documents. Sister-company specialists receive extracts only, per the confidentiality flags and the scope memo (SOP 71).

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Build the family level through SOP 41 before drafting any family-level plan; household profiles are drawn in each household's own Discovery.
  • Consent for what rolls up from a household to the family level is recorded on T14; anything not consented stays at Household or Private.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Add the family-context node and the FCT table; note explicitly what the client cannot access so the investment plan's scope banner (SOP 13) is accurate.
  • Nothing from the profile is shared with the family central team without the consent recorded on T05 Part 4, and never with a sister company that sits on that team unless the same consent covers it.

12 CCM2 — Investment Plan Meeting

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — Investment Plan Meeting: timing, purposes of a written plan, the nine steps, no check at this meeting, investment plan is not a financial plan, the IPS is not walked through in detail · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 20 — the investment policy statement as a product of the family's ends, not of investment management · Other: Palaveev — a named analytical role for the associate in the room; peer review and sign-off on every plan before it is presented

12 — CCM2 Investment Plan Meeting

The second consultative meeting presents a written investment plan built from the Total Client Profile. It confirms the client's goals in writing, demonstrates the thoroughness of the practice, and asks for a commitment to proceed — but deliberately stops short of taking money. The client takes the plan home and returns a week later for the Mutual Commitment Meeting.

Purpose

  • Present a detailed, actionable investment plan and investment policy statement that maximize the probability of achieving what the client said matters.
  • Clarify and put in writing the goals surfaced at Discovery so both sides are aligned before anything is implemented.
  • Position the Advisor as the expert who addresses wealth preservation first, with advanced planning to follow through the expert network.
  • Obtain a commitment to move forward, without executing anything at this meeting.

Trigger

CCM1 (or the Rediscovery variant) is complete, the client fits the practice, and T05 mode and scope are confirmed. This meeting is scheduled in the room at the end of Discovery.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: AA (drafts the plan per SOP 13; presents one defined analysis in the room), CSA (letter, packet, confirmation, [CRM]) · Consulted: peer reviewer (a second professional — SA, or an ISB colleague — signs off on the plan before it is presented); ISB / [Firm] investment platform for portfolio construction.

Timing

  • +2 weeks after CCM1. The plan is drafted by day 7, peer-reviewed by day 10, packet complete by day 11.
  • Meeting length: 60–75 minutes.
  • CCM3 is scheduled in the room, +1 week after this meeting.

Inputs

  • Total Client Profile (SOP 11) and the Discovery recording/notes.
  • T05 — mode, scope rung, who may instruct, what may be shared.
  • Copies of statements and tax returns gathered at Discovery; held-away asset list.
  • Firm investment philosophy, model portfolios, index and hypothetical-portfolio summaries from the [Firm] platform.
  • Family-level constraints (Mode A entity/trust map; Mode B family policy or trust-instrument terms).

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Investment plan and IPS drafted to the SOP 13 spec using T06; scope banner completed.
  • [ ] Peer review done and signed on the T06 sign-off block; every figure reconciled to source statements.
  • [ ] Fee schedule and firm background sections final; [Firm Compliance] disclosures attached.
  • [ ] Executive summary opens with the client's own words from Discovery (values, goals, relationships) — not with markets.
  • [ ] The AA's named analysis chosen (for example: how the recommended allocation behaves against the client's stated goals across horizons).
  • [ ] Two bound or vault-ready copies of the plan; the client's copy is the one that goes home.
  • [ ] Agenda from T02 (CCM2) sent with the pre-meeting letter (T01); SOP 05 prep complete.
  • [ ] The rest of the process (CCM3, CCM4, first progress meeting, expert-network cycle) ready to explain in one minute.

Procedure

  1. Greet and reinforce. Every team member greets the client by name. The LA reconnects with something the client said mattered at Discovery before any business (SOP 05, SOP 04).
  2. Set the stage. State that today's purpose is to show the client a written road map built from what they told us, and to find out whether it is the right one.
  3. Walk the agenda and the road ahead. Name the remaining steps: this meeting; the Mutual Commitment Meeting in one week; the 45-Day Follow-up; regular progress meetings at the client's chosen cadence; the expert-network cycle that produces the wealth management plan.

  4. Present the executive summary first. Read back the seven areas of the profile as the client's own words. Ask whether anything is wrong or missing — corrections here are the point of the meeting.

    Say something like

    "Before we get to a single number, I want to make sure we heard you correctly — this page is what you told us matters. What would you change?"

  5. Present the recommendations in detail. Go through the plan section by section: goals in writing, the diagnostic of the current situation, the recommended structure, how it maps to each goal, what it costs. Pause for questions after each section. The AA presents the analysis assigned in prep and answers questions on it.

  6. Introduce the IPS without walking through it. Explain what it is (the discipline that governs how we manage money and how decisions get made), where it sits in the notebook, and that it is reviewed annually. Do not read it page by page; most clients want to know it exists, not its detail.

  7. Ask for the commitment — not the check. Ask whether the client is ready to move forward on this basis. If yes, say plainly that we do not execute anything today: the client takes the materials home, thinks it through, and we meet in a week to make the commitment mutual.

    Say something like

    "If this is right, the next step is a short meeting next week where we both commit and sign. I'd rather you take this home and sleep on it than sign anything today."

  8. Solicit and address concerns. Ask directly what worries the client about the plan, the fees, or the process. Record every concern in the notes; answer what can be answered, and commit to a written answer within 48 hours for the rest.

  9. Set the stage for the wealth management plan. Explain that investments are the foundation and only the first layer; once the client is on board, the expert network will look at tax, transfer, protection, and charitable questions and the first progress meeting will present that plan.
  10. Close and schedule. Summarize the decision and any open concerns. Schedule CCM3 in the room, one week out. Send the client home with their copy of the plan and a one-line note of what to look at first.
  11. Confirm in writing within 24 hours (T01). Date and time of CCM3, the list of documents that will be executed there, and written answers to any concerns raised.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours: confirmation and recap sent; concerns answered or dated; [CRM] updated; CCM3 paperwork list handed to the CSA (SOP 14 prep).
  • Within 48 hours: any plan corrections issued as a revised executive summary, marked as such.
  • The one-week gap is deliberate; do not shorten it because the client is eager.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Presented investment plan and IPS (final, peer-signed) [Document vault] — Investment Plan section; [CRM] AA
Corrections to the profile captured in the meeting SOP 11 profile updated in [CRM] AA
Concerns log with answers [CRM] activity; recap LA
CCM3 paperwork list T07 opened by the CSA CSA
Next-meeting confirmation T01; [CRM] calendar CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Present a plan that could only have been written for this client — it should read like Discovery, not like a brochure.
  • Insist the client take the materials home even when they are ready to sign.
  • Give the AA a real part; promote their analysis as their work.
  • Tell the client what the plan does not cover (scope banner) before they ask.

Don't

  • Don't take a check, a transfer form, or a signed agreement at this meeting.
  • Don't present a "financial plan" — advanced planning comes later through the network; claiming expertise in everything is not credible.
  • Don't walk through the IPS line by line.
  • Don't let the platform's model names replace the client's goals as the organizing logic of the presentation.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The plan covers every household and entity in scope on T05; the executive summary carries a family-level page and a household-level page for each household.
  • Where the family's wealth sits in several entities and trusts, present the investor-allocation overlay as a question for the family, not a done deal (SOP 13, SOP 47).
  • Attendance follows the family map (T14); confidentiality between members is checked before household figures are shown in a joint meeting.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Obtain the family-level investment policy or the governing trust instrument before drafting; the plan is consistent with it or carves out explicitly.
  • The executive summary opens with the scope banner: what this plan covers and what the family central team owns.
  • FCT review of the draft happens only if the mandate on T05 says so; otherwise the FCT receives a courtesy summary per consent.
  • Under B-narrow, the "plan" is the mandate-specific IPS and a one-page summary; keep the meeting to 45 minutes.

Metrics

  • Share of CCM2 meetings held within 10–18 days of CCM1.
  • Share of plans peer-signed before presentation (target 100%).
  • Share of CCM2 meetings that ended with CCM3 scheduled (target 100%).

13 Investment plan and investment policy statement — document standard

specOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the two-part investment plan (executive summary + IPS), the four purposes of a written plan, annual IPS review, investment plan is not a financial plan · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 20 — IPS as the family's statement of ends; investor allocation; Family Wealth Ch. 5 — investor allocation across generations and horizons · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes Ch. 5 — conversation prompts on simplicity, fees, decision cadence, concentration vs diversification, break-even hurdle (extension, prompts only)

13 — Investment plan and IPS

The investment plan is the first written deliverable of the relationship and the foundation the wealth management plan is later built on. It has two parts — an executive summary written for the client and an investment policy statement that governs how the practice manages money — and it is scoped, peer-reviewed, and revisited every year.

Purpose

A well-built plan does four jobs: it clarifies and records the client's goals so both sides are working from the same page; it supplies long-term discipline so decisions rest on analysis rather than on reactions to short-term events; it prevents misunderstandings by stating the approach in writing; and it demonstrates the thoroughness of the practice. It is deliberately an investment plan, not a financial plan — advanced planning follows through the expert network and is documented in SOP 30.

Contents

Part 1 — Executive summary (written for the client; 6–12 pages)

  1. Scope banner (first page, boxed): who the client is; which households, entities, and trusts this plan covers; what it does not cover and who owns those areas; the mode and scope rung from T05.
  2. Your profile in your words — the seven areas of the Total Client Profile (values, goals, relationships, assets, advisors, process, interests) summarized from Discovery, goals stated as measurable statements with horizons.
  3. Where you are today — consolidated picture of assets in scope: entities, accounts, custodians, allocation, concentration, liquidity, cost, tax position at a summary level; held-away assets listed for completeness.
  4. How we work — the consultative process, the meeting cadence the client chose, the expert network and what it will address next.
  5. Recommendations — the recommended structure (which accounts/entities, which strategy each, target allocation ranges), how each recommendation maps to a stated goal, what changes from today, transition considerations (taxes, timing, in-kind moves), and what the client must decide.
  6. What it costs — advisory fee basis and schedule, platform and product costs, any fee-sharing disclosures, in one page.
  7. About [Firm] and the Advisor — background, investment philosophy in plain language, the team the client will work with (roles, not names, plus the LA by name).
  8. Next steps — CCM3 date, documents to be executed, the 45-day follow-up, the first progress meeting.

Part 2 — Investment policy statement (governing document; 8–15 pages)

  1. Purpose of the IPS and the parties bound by it.
  2. Objectives and constraints per account group: return objective, risk tolerance and capacity, time horizon, liquidity needs, tax considerations, legal and regulatory constraints, unique circumstances (concentrated positions, restricted stock, family entities).
  3. Asset allocation policy: strategic ranges, rebalancing rules, permitted and excluded asset classes and vehicles.
  4. Investment approach and strategic portfolio process of the practice; roles of the [Firm] platform, the LA, and any third-party managers.
  5. Reference material: summaries of index returns and of the hypothetical portfolios the practice recommends — presented as reference, not as a projection of this client's outcome.
  6. Monitoring and reporting: what the client receives and when (SOP 24), review cadence, criteria for changing the policy.
  7. Per-entity / per-trust addenda where an entity's function differs (T06 addendum table).
  8. Signatures and review log.

Extensions to Bowen's structure

Beyond Bowen

The IPS as a statement of ends. Write the objectives section so the family could recognize it as their decision about what the money is for — not the platform's decision about how to manage it. Goals, horizons, and constraints are the family's; method belongs to the practice.

Beyond Bowen

Multi-entity and trust structure. One IPS per trust or entity whose function differs (a dynasty trust with a 100-year horizon is not a grandparent's income account). Where a trustee holds investment discretion, the IPS records that the trustee adopts it and cannot delegate ultimate responsibility; where [Trust Co.] is trustee, coordinate through SOP 46 and SOP 71.

Beyond Bowen

Mode A investor-allocation overlay. Alongside asset allocation, state who holds what: higher-growth assets sit with the youngest members and the longest-horizon exempt trusts; lower-growth, income-producing assets sit with the oldest members; intermediate generations take the middle. This is presented as a family decision with counsel involved, never applied unilaterally. Mechanics and preconditions are in SOP 47.

Beyond Bowen

Conversation prompts for the objectives section (prompts for the family conversation, not prescriptions — portfolio construction belongs to the [Firm] platform): can each holding be explained to the family in fifteen minutes; are fee-heavy or heavily marketed products excluded on principle; does the family want a cadence of one major investment decision every few years rather than constant activity; concentrate to build, diversify to protect — which phase is this family in; what gross return does the family need simply to preserve purchasing power after tax and inflation.

Standards

  • Voice. Executive summary in the second person and in the client's vocabulary from Discovery; IPS in the third person and precise. No jargon in Part 1 that is not defined on first use.
  • Truth to source. Every number reconciles to a statement or tax return in the file; every goal traces to Discovery notes. The AA keeps a reconciliation sheet.
  • Scope discipline. The scope banner is mandatory; anything outside it is named as outside it, with the owner.
  • No projections as promises. Reference returns are historical and hypothetical, labelled as such; individual projections, if used, show ranges and assumptions.
  • Length. Part 1 under twelve pages; Part 2 under fifteen. If it cannot be short, it is not yet clear.
  • Review. Peer review by a second professional before presentation (sign-off block on T06); [Firm Compliance] review of fees, disclosures, and IPS regulatory items.
  • Format. T06 outline; [Firm] branding; a one-page summary on top for the notebook (T08).
  • Confidentiality. Household-level figures never appear in a family-level document without consent recorded on T05/T14.

Refresh cadence

  • Annual IPS review (mini-procedure): (1) AA pulls the IPS, the prior year's decisions, and any regulatory changes noted by [Firm Compliance]; (2) LA reviews objectives against the current Total Client Profile and any life events (SOP 22); (3) changes drafted and peer-reviewed; (4) reviewed with the client at the first progress meeting of the year; (5) signed and filed with the review log updated. Trust IPS reviews align to the trustee's annual meeting (SOP 46).
  • Event-driven revision: liquidity event, major inheritance, sale of a business, change in trustee, change of mode or scope rung, or any material change in goals.
  • Executive summary is not re-issued annually; it is superseded by the wealth management plan (SOP 30) and the progress-meeting packets.

Owner

LA owns the document and its presentation; AA drafts and maintains; a peer reviewer (SA or ISB colleague) signs; [Firm Compliance] reviews disclosures.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • One executive summary with a family-level page and a page per household; per-entity and per-trust IPS addenda.
  • The investor-allocation overlay is included as a proposal for the family's decision; the family council (where one exists) is the counterparty for family-level policy.
  • Family-level policy language (mission, values, long-term growth commitment) may be quoted into the objectives section once the family has adopted it (SOP 43, SOP 45).

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Obtain the family's investment policy or the governing trust instrument first; this plan is consistent with it or carves out explicitly, and says which.
  • The scope banner states what the family central team owns; the executive summary is delivered to the individual only unless T05 permits more.
  • B-full: full plan for the individual's assets. B-partial: plan for the mandated assets plus a coordination note on how it fits the family's policy. B-narrow: IPS for the mandate and a one-page summary only.
