14 CCM3 — Mutual Commitment Meeting

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — Mutual Commitment Meeting: one-week timing, two objectives, prep, the nine steps, congratulation, buyer's-remorse and financial-media coaching, concentrated nature of gains, first referral ask, schedule the follow-up six weeks out and keep all paperwork · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 9 — the annual fee conversation (clear, written, in context); The Compact — engagement as a freely entered, reciprocal compact; Family Trusts Ch. 6 — conflicts acknowledged, documented, disclosed, managed · Other: Palaveev — fee as policy not negotiation; lead sign-off on proposals

14 — CCM3 Mutual Commitment Meeting

One week after the investment plan is presented, the prospective client returns to become a client. Both sides commit: the client to the plan and the process, the practice to the client's success. Documents are executed, the engagement is scoped in writing, the client is prepared for the emotions of the first weeks, and the first introductions ask is made.

Purpose

  • Make the commitment mutual and explicit — verbally and in signed documents.
  • Execute everything needed to implement the investment plan, cleanly, in one sitting.
  • Inoculate the new client against buyer's remorse and the financial media.
  • Ask for qualified introductions for the first time.

Trigger

CCM2 ended with a commitment to move forward and this meeting scheduled. The client has had the plan for a week.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (paperwork package with sign-here flags, engagement letter, T05, checks/transfer authorizations, confirmation), AA (final plan copy; notes) · Consulted: [Firm Compliance] (engagement letter, disclosures, conflicts register); trustee or [Trust Co.] where a trust is a party.

Timing

  • +1 week after CCM2. Meeting length 45–60 minutes; longer only if the number of accounts demands it.
  • CCM4 scheduled in the room, about six weeks out (the "45-day" follow-up).

Inputs

  • Final investment plan and IPS (SOP 13, peer-signed).
  • T05 completed and ready for signature; engagement letter drafted from it.
  • Account-opening, transfer, and authorization forms per account/entity/trust; beneficiary and titling documents; entity resolutions where needed.
  • Fee schedule; conflicts register entries for this client; disclosures.
  • Concerns log from CCM2 with written answers.
  • Notes on the client's personality and process preference (SOP 04, SOP 11).

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Paperwork package assembled per account with "sign here" flags; every form pre-filled; two-person check completed (SOP 15).
  • [ ] Engagement letter states: the named client(s), mode and scope rung, what is in and out of scope, fee basis and schedule, information-sharing consent, how the engagement ends.
  • [ ] Conflicts register: any fee-sharing, sister-company involvement, or product relationships listed for disclosure; [Firm Compliance] approval on file.
  • [ ] LA has re-read the plan, the Total Client Profile, and every concern raised at CCM2 and can answer without notes.
  • [ ] Copy of the plan for the meeting; the client's copy already at home.
  • [ ] Agenda (T02 CCM3) sent with the pre-meeting letter (T01); SOP 05 prep complete.
  • [ ] Introductions ask prepared: the profile of the family this practice serves best, in one sentence; Mode B variant ready.
  • [ ] Recording not used at this meeting; the AA takes decision notes.

Procedure

  1. Greet and reinforce. As SOP 05. Acknowledge that the client has had time to think.
  2. Collect all questions first, then answer. Ask what came up in the week. List every question before answering any; answer them in order, in full.
  3. Confirm readiness. Ask whether the client is ready to move forward, become a client, and set the plan in motion. If hesitation appears, return to step 2; never push past it.
  4. Walk the engagement letter. Who the client is, what we will do and not do, how we are paid, what we may share and with whom. Sign T05 alongside it.

  5. Hold the fee conversation properly. State the fee in dollars and as a rate, in the context of what it buys; confirm the client understands every way the practice or its affiliates are paid; note that this conversation repeats every year.

    Say something like

    "Here is exactly what you pay, in dollars, and what it covers. We'll go over it again every year, and I'd rather you ask about it than wonder."

  6. Disclose conflicts. Read the conflicts register entries aloud (sister-company involvement, fee sharing, product relationships) and how each is managed. Obtain acknowledgement.

  7. Execute the documents. Take the time to explain each form before it is signed; collect checks and transfer authorizations now. The CSA checks each signature against the package list before the meeting ends.

  8. Congratulate the client. Pause. Mark the moment as an important step toward what the client said matters, in their own words from Discovery.

    Say something like

    "You should be pleased with yourself — this is the step most families put off for years. Everything from here is execution."

  9. Coach for the first weeks. Explain that second thoughts are normal, especially for anyone used to the financial media; suggest treating market commentary as entertainment. Explain that gains arrive unevenly and that missing short periods costs more than staying invested; expect down periods.

  10. Make the introductions ask #1. Describe the kind of family the practice serves best and ask whether anyone comes to mind; then "who else?"; then ask for a personal introduction. Record names; contact details only after the flow stops (SOP 50).
  11. Set up the 45-Day Follow-up. Explain its purpose (organizing everything the transfers generate); ask the client to keep every piece of paperwork and bring or upload it; schedule it about six weeks out.
  12. Close. State what happens next and by when (SOP 15 timeline); thank the client for the trust placed in the practice.
  13. Confirm in writing within 24 hours (T01). Documents executed, transfers initiated, the CCM4 date, what the client will receive from custodians and what to do with it.

Follow-up

  • Same day: CSA opens T07 for every account; documents scanned to the [Document vault]; originals per [Firm] policy.
  • Within 24 hours: confirmation sent; T05 and engagement letter filed; [CRM] updated with commitment date, fee basis, consent, and referral names.
  • Within 48 hours: handwritten thank-you for any introduction given; SOP 50 follow-through begins.
  • Within one week: the LA calls to check for questions that surfaced after signing.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Signed engagement letter and T05 [Document vault] — Agreements; [CRM] CSA
Executed account, transfer, titling, and beneficiary forms Custodian submissions; [Document vault]; T07 CSA
Conflicts disclosure acknowledgement [Firm Compliance] file; [CRM] LA
Fee conversation record (date, amounts stated) [CRM] — repeat annually LA
Introductions received [CRM] referral record; SOP 50 LA
CCM4 confirmation T01; [CRM] calendar CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Have every form ready and checked; the client should sign, not hunt.
  • Explain each document; speed comes from preparation, not from skipping explanation.
  • Say the fee out loud in dollars.
  • Ask for introductions plainly and stop after "who else?" — do not sell.

Don't

  • Don't execute anything the client has not seen explained.
  • Don't hide a sister-company relationship or a fee split behind a disclosure page.
  • Don't shorten the coaching on remorse and media because the client seems confident.
  • Don't leave without CCM4 on the calendar.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • One engagement letter per household plus a family-level letter where the family engages as a unit; T14 (family map, decision rights, confidentiality matrix) signed with T05.
  • Where trusts are parties, the trustee signs the trust's IPS addendum and account documents; [Trust Co.] follows SOP 71.
  • Frame the commitment as a compact the family enters freely and re-affirms each year (SOP 43); introductions ask #1 becomes "which other members or branches should we be serving?"

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Signatories may include a trustee or the family custodian's authorized signer; obtain the FCT's required approvals before the meeting (SOP 33).
  • The engagement letter carries the scope banner from the plan and the information-sharing consent; a courtesy copy goes to the FCT only per T05.
  • Introductions ask #1 is reframed: ask to be introduced into the family team — the family CFO, CIO, trustee, counsel — so coordination starts now. Do not ask for prospects.
  • Fee disclosure extends to any fee sharing with a sister company that also serves the family centrally.

Metrics

  • Share of CCM3 meetings held within 5–10 days of CCM2.
  • Share of packages executed with zero returned forms (NIGO rate at custodian, target < 2%).
  • Share of new clients for whom the introductions ask was made and recorded (target 100%).

Related

  • SOP 02 — Engagement modes · T05 — Engagement scoping worksheet

  • SOP 15 — Implementation and transfers · T07 — Implementation tracker

  • SOP 50 — Asks inside service meetings
  • SOP 33 — Coordinating with outside advisors

Source

  • Hughes, Massenzio & Whitaker, Complete Family Wealth, Ch. 9 — the fee conversation held at least annually, clear and written, put in context (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, The Compact — the engagement as a reciprocal, freely entered compact (paraphrased).
  • Goldstone, Hughes & Whitaker, Family Trusts, Ch. 6 — conflicts of interest acknowledged, documented, disclosed to all parties, and managed (paraphrased).
  • Palaveev, The Ensemble Practice — fee as a policy rather than a negotiation; lead sign-off on proposals (paraphrased).

15 Implementation and transfers — the window between commitment and follow-up

procedureOwner: CSAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the volume of paperwork generated by transfers and the 45-day follow-up's organizing purpose; Ch. 6 — 'client accounts do not suffer from administrative errors' and same-day service-failure resolution (WOW checklist) · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 5 — a one-page plain-language summary and a communication plan for every new structure · Other: Palaveev — client service administrator owns routine execution; 'whoever has the ball is the quarterback'

15 — Implementation and transfers

Bowen's process jumps from the signatures at the Mutual Commitment Meeting to the notebook at the 45-Day Follow-up. In a multi-entity, multi-custodian family the six weeks in between are where administrative errors happen — and administrative error is the fastest way to lose a client who has just said yes. This procedure makes that window a managed project owned by the CSA, with the Lead Advisor accountable to the client.

Purpose

  • Move every account, entity, and trust to its target structure accurately, on time, and with no surprises.
  • Keep the client informed at a steady cadence so the transfer period feels like service, not silence.
  • Produce a plain-language summary and communication plan for every new structure so the family understands what was created and what to tell whom.
  • Arrive at the 45-Day Follow-up with everything collected, filed, and explainable.

Trigger

Documents executed at CCM3 (SOP 14). Also triggered later by any new account, new trust or entity, change of custodian, or restructuring decided at a progress meeting (SOP 20).

Roles

Owner: CSA · Does: CSA (forms, submissions, tracker, custodian follow-up, client updates), AA (in-kind vs liquidate analysis, cost-basis reconciliation, structure summaries), LA (decisions on transition method, client escalation calls, sign-off) · Consulted: [Trust Co.] and trustees for trust accounts; [Firm Compliance] for titling and beneficiary rules; ISB (tax, insurance) where a structure changes ownership; FCT or family custodian in Mode B.

Timing

Day Milestone
Day 0 (CCM3) Forms executed; T07 opened for every account
Day 1 All forms two-person checked and submitted; client sent the "what happens next" note
Days 2–10 Custodian confirmations; account numbers received; transfers initiated
Days 5–25 Assets arrive; cost basis collected; positions reconciled; trades per the transition plan
Weekly Client status update (or per the client's process preference)
Day 30 Reconciliation complete; structure summaries (T21) drafted; notebook (T08) populated
Day 40 Pre-meeting packet for CCM4 assembled; exceptions closed or scheduled
Day ~45 CCM4 (SOP 16)

Inputs

  • Executed forms and the paperwork list from CCM3; T05 (who may instruct, consent).
  • Investment plan recommendations and transition notes (SOP 13): which positions move in kind, which are sold, when.
  • Entity and trust documents: trust instruments, trustee acceptance, entity resolutions, EINs.
  • Current custodian statements for every account moving; contact details of the delivering firms.
  • Beneficiary designations on retirement accounts and insurance; current ownership of policies.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] T07 rows created for every account, entity, and trust, with the target custodian, action, and owner.
  • [ ] Two-person check protocol assigned (preparer and checker named per form).
  • [ ] Transition plan from the AA: for each position, in kind / liquidate / hold, with the tax reason and the LA's initials.
  • [ ] Trust accounts: trustee signatures and, where [Trust Co.] is trustee, the SOP 71 scope memo in place.
  • [ ] Client's preferred update channel and frequency taken from the Total Client Profile.
  • [ ] Notebook (T08) skeleton created in the [Document vault] with permissions matching T05/T14.

Procedure

  1. Open the tracker. Enter every account on T07 the same day as CCM3. Nothing moves that is not on the tracker.
  2. Two-person check every form. Preparer completes; checker verifies names, registrations, account numbers, signatures, dates, and attachments against the plan. Log the check on T07. Submit only after both initials.
  3. Submit and confirm. Send account openings and transfer requests; record submission dates and expected completion. Chase any custodian acknowledgement not received within two business days.
  4. Send the "what happens next" note (T01). Within 24 hours of CCM3: which accounts are opening, roughly when assets will land, what mail or portal messages the client will receive from custodians, and that the practice — not the client — will act on them.
  5. Initiate transfers per the transition plan. Move in-kind positions first; execute liquidations and purchases on the LA's instruction and the platform's process; record every trade decision and its reason on T07.
  6. Collect cost basis. Request cost basis from delivering firms at submission; reconcile against arriving positions; escalate missing lots at day 15. Do not let the first progress report go out with unknown basis.
  7. Complete titling and designations. Retitle trust and entity accounts exactly as the instruments name them; update beneficiary designations on retirement accounts and life insurance to match the plan; obtain entity resolutions where custodians require them; change insurance ownership only with the ISB insurance specialist's confirmation and counsel's sign-off.
  8. Review the tracker daily. CSA reviews every open row each morning: status, next action, owner, date. Anything past its expected date becomes an exception (step 11).
  9. Update the client at the agreed cadence. Weekly by default, or per the process preference: what has arrived, what is pending, what the client need do (usually nothing). Silence during transfers is a service failure.
  10. Draft a structure summary (T21) for every new trust, entity, gift, or plan. The AA drafts, the LA reviews, counsel confirms accuracy where a legal document is summarized. Include the communication plan: what the client should tell whom, when, and how.
  11. Handle exceptions the same day. A delayed custodian, a rejected form, a missing signature: log it, tell the client before they notice, fix it, and record the fix (SOP 23). The person who found the problem owns it to resolution.
  12. Reconcile and close. At day 30, reconcile every account to the plan: positions, cash, basis, registrations, beneficiaries. Populate the notebook (T08) with account confirmations, executed documents, the plan, and the IPS. Hand the CCM4 packet to the LA at day 40.

Follow-up

  • Day 1: submissions confirmed; client note sent.
  • Weekly: status update sent; T07 reviewed with the LA in the team meeting.
  • Day 30: reconciliation signed by the AA; T21 summaries reviewed by the LA.
  • Day 40: exceptions closed or scheduled with the client's knowledge; CCM4 agenda (T02) drafted from the tracker.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
T07 tracker — complete history per account [CRM]; [Document vault] — Implementation CSA
Custodian confirmations, account numbers, executed forms [Document vault] — Accounts CSA
Transition-plan decisions and trade rationale T07 notes; [CRM] AA / LA
Cost-basis reconciliation [Document vault] — Accounts; reporting system AA
Structure summaries and communication plans (T21) [Document vault] — Wealth Management Plan; notebook section AA
Client status updates [CRM] activity CSA
Exceptions log T07; service-failure log (SOP 23) CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Treat every form as a two-person job; the checker is not a formality.
  • Tell the client about a delay before the custodian's letter does.
  • Save every confirmation, every notice, and every executed document — the notebook is built from them.
  • Write the structure summary in words a rising-generation member could understand.

Don't

  • Don't submit a form the same person prepared without a second check.
  • Don't liquidate a position without the LA's initials on the transition plan.
  • Don't leave beneficiary designations for "later"; a mismatch between the plan and the designation is a plan failure.
  • Don't let a specialist, custodian, or sister company become the client's contact for status — the CSA owns communication.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Track by household and entity; the family-level summary of what moved and what was created goes to the family's designated contact per T14.
  • Trust accounts follow the trustee's instructions; where [Trust Co.] is trustee, it acts under the SOP 71 scope memo and the CSA still owns client communication.
  • T21 summaries are the raw material for the family's staged-disclosure conversation (SOP 43); do not distribute them to members until the principal has decided the communication plan.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Obtain FCT or trustee approvals before initiating any transfer that touches family-controlled accounts; record the approval on T07.
  • The custodian may be the family's; adapt forms and timelines to their process, and agree a single point of contact there (SOP 33).
  • Copy transfer status to the FCT only per the consent on T05; the individual receives every update regardless.
  • Under B-narrow, the tracker covers the mandated accounts only; do not collect information about accounts outside the mandate.

Metrics

  • Not-in-good-order (returned) forms as a share of forms submitted (target < 2%).
  • Accounts fully reconciled — positions, basis, registration, beneficiaries — by day 30 (target 100%).
  • Client updates sent on schedule during the transfer window (target 100%).

Related

  • SOP 16 — CCM4 45-Day Follow-up

  • SOP 46 — Trustee–beneficiary relationship · SOP 71 — Engaging borrowed expertise

  • Hughes, Massenzio & Whitaker, Complete Family Wealth, Ch. 5 — the one-page summary and communication plan families should ask their advisers for (paraphrased).
  • Palaveev, The Ensemble Practice — routine execution owned by the client service administrator; whoever receives a request owns it (paraphrased).
  • Extension — the managed transfer window, two-person check, and cadence are ours.

16 CCM4 — 45-Day Follow-up Meeting

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — 45-Day Follow-up: purpose, the tabbed notebook built for five years, the seven steps, the annualized-returns trap and the long-term reframe, second referral ask, scheduling the first progress meeting at the client's stated cadence · Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 11 — the one-week follow-up call; The Compact — engineer small early joint successes; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 5 — review the plain-language summaries of new structures

16 — CCM4 45-Day Follow-up Meeting

About six weeks after commitment, the transfers have generated a stack of confirmations, statements, and notices. This meeting turns that stack into an organized, explained record the client can use for years; it demonstrates the practice's standard of service; it defuses the first short-term performance number; and it makes the second introductions ask.

Purpose

  • Organize and explain every document the implementation produced, in a notebook designed to last the relationship.
  • Place the first 45 days of performance in a lifetime perspective before annualized figures mislead the client.
  • Review the plain-language summaries of any new structures.
  • Ask for introductions a second time, and schedule the first Regular Progress Meeting at the cadence the client chose.

Trigger

Scheduled at CCM3 for roughly six weeks out; implementation (SOP 15) has reached day-30 reconciliation.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (notebook assembled, documents indexed, packet), AA (performance context, structure summaries) · Consulted: none usually; trustee or [Trust Co.] if a trust's first statement needs explaining.

Timing

  • ~45 days (six weeks) after CCM3. Meeting length 45–60 minutes.
  • First Regular Progress Meeting scheduled in the room, about 90 days out or per the client's stated preference.

Inputs

  • Completed T07 with the day-30 reconciliation signed; exceptions closed or scheduled.
  • Notebook (T08) populated: investment plan overview, IPS, wealth-management-plan placeholder, statements and confirmations, executed documents, structure summaries (T21).
  • The paperwork the client saved and brought or uploaded.
  • First-period performance report with the annualization issue understood by the AA.
  • Client's process preference (cadence and channel) from the Total Client Profile.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Notebook built to the T08 index with permissions set per T05/T14; a physical binder if the client prefers paper.
  • [ ] Every custodian document since CCM3 filed and indexed; the client's own stack matched against ours.
  • [ ] One-page reading guide for each document type (statement, confirmation, tax notice) ready.
  • [ ] Performance figure for the period known; the reframe prepared regardless of whether it is up or down.
  • [ ] Structure summaries (T21) final for every new trust, entity, or designation.
  • [ ] One small joint decision identified for a family to make together at this meeting (Mode A).
  • [ ] Introductions ask prepared; agenda (T02 CCM4) sent with T01; SOP 05 prep complete.

Procedure

  1. Greet and reinforce. As SOP 05.
  2. Gather questions first. Ask what has happened since commitment and what questions the paperwork raised. List them; answer in order.
  3. Explain the notebook. Walk the sections: why each exists, what goes in it, and how it will grow over five-plus years. Show where the plan, the IPS, and the coming wealth management plan live.
  4. Organize together. Take the client's saved documents and ours, and place each in its section, explaining how to read it — what a statement shows, what a confirmation confirms, what a tax notice means and who acts on it. The client leaves knowing where everything is and that the practice will keep it that way.
  5. Review the structure summaries. For each new trust, entity, or designation: what it is, who is involved, what happens next, and the communication plan the client owns (T21). Confirm the client is comfortable with what to tell whom.

  6. Put the first 45 days in perspective. Before the client reads an annualized figure, explain that six weeks of returns say nothing about a lifetime plan; that no one can call the market short term; and that the plan works by making sound decisions and staying invested through both kinds of period.

    Say something like

    "You'll see a number on this page that looks either brilliant or alarming — it's six weeks annualized, and it tells us nothing. What matters is the goals on page one, and the decisions we make over years."

  7. Make one small decision together (Mode A). Choose a modest, low-stakes item the family can decide jointly today — a reporting format, a meeting rhythm, a first family-meeting date — so the family banks an early success before harder questions arrive.

  8. Make the introductions ask #2. Describe the family the practice serves best and ask who comes to mind; "who else?"; ask for a personal introduction (SOP 50). Record names.
  9. Confirm the cadence and schedule the first progress meeting. Restate the contact preference the client gave at Discovery; confirm it still holds; schedule the first Regular Progress Meeting (about 90 days out or per preference) and explain that it will present the advanced-planning plan.
  10. Close. Summarize what was organized, what the client should do with future documents (send to us; keep nothing you cannot find), and what comes next.
  11. Confirm in writing within 24 hours (T01). Next-meeting date, the notebook index as sent, any open items.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours: confirmation and index sent; [CRM] updated; introductions recorded and handwritten thanks sent (SOP 50).
  • Within one week: the LA calls to catch questions that surfaced after the client re-read the notebook.
  • Within two weeks: the AA opens the expert-network case brief (T09) so the advanced-planning plan is ready for the first progress meeting (SOP 32).

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Populated notebook with index (T08) [Document vault]; physical binder if requested CSA
Reading guides for document types Notebook — Miscellaneous; reusable CSA
Reviewed structure summaries (T21) with communication decisions [Document vault]; [CRM] AA
Introductions received [CRM]; SOP 50 LA
Confirmed cadence and first progress meeting [CRM] calendar; T01 CSA
Expert-network case brief opened T09 draft AA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Design the notebook for the length of the relationship, not for this quarter.
  • Explain every document; assume nothing about what the client can read.
  • Deliver the reframe whether the number is good or bad — a good number teaches the wrong lesson just as well.
  • Keep the meeting about organization and perspective; save advanced planning for the next meeting.

Don't

  • Don't skip the notebook because the client "isn't a paperwork person" — build the digital version and walk it.
  • Don't quote annualized short-period returns as evidence of anything.
  • Don't let the introductions ask slide because the client is busy; describe, ask, "who else?", stop.
  • Don't leave without the first progress meeting on the calendar.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The notebook has a family level and a household level; access permissions follow T14's confidentiality matrix.
  • The joint decision in step 7 is deliberate and small; record it as the family's first decision under this engagement (SOP 43 builds on it).
  • Structure summaries feed the principal's staged-disclosure plan; the LA offers to attend the conversation with the rising generation when asked.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The notebook covers mandated assets only; do not gather or file family-level documents the individual cannot access.
  • Agree the reporting format with the FCT before the first progress report so the individual's package fits the family's consolidated reporting (SOP 24, SOP 33).
  • Introductions ask #2 stays reframed toward the family team; ask about other members only through the individual and per T05.
  • Under B-narrow, this meeting may be a 30-minute call with the trustee to walk the trust's first statement.

Metrics

  • Share of CCM4 meetings held 40–50 days after CCM3.
  • Share of clients with a complete, indexed notebook at CCM4 (target 100%).
  • Share of CCM4 meetings with the first progress meeting scheduled in the room (target 100%).

Ongoing service — CCM5 and service standards

20 CCM5 — Regular Progress Meeting

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — Regular Progress Meetings: three purposes, first-meeting agenda, drop/defer/do coaching, subsequent meetings, critical success factors; Ch. 5 — asking for additional assets and introductions at every progress meeting · Hughes: Compact — alternating knowledge and courage questions; 80% do nothing; Family Wealth Ch. 21 — unintended-consequences questions before perpetual structures; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 9 — annual fee conversation · Other: Palaveev — peer review and sign-off on every plan; one meeting a year as a second-chair/rotation slot

20 — CCM5 Regular Progress Meeting

The Regular Progress Meeting is the engine of the relationship. The first one, ninety days after the follow-up meeting, presents the advanced-planning plan; every one after that reviews progress against the investment plan and the advanced-planning tracker, captures what has changed in the client's life, and is the moment for the additional-assets and introductions asks. It runs inside the meeting protocol in SOP 05.

Purpose

  • Review the client's progress toward the goals recorded in the Total Client Profile and answer questions, especially in difficult markets.
  • Deepen the relationship: learn what has changed in the client's life and keep the process preference honored.
  • Present (first meeting) and then execute (every meeting after) the wealth management plan, one recommendation at a time, with the client choosing drop, defer, or do.

Trigger

  • First RPM: ninety days after CCM4 (SOP 16), once the expert-network meeting (SOP 32) has produced the draft advanced-planning plan.
  • Subsequent RPMs: at the cadence the client stated in Discovery (quarterly, semi-annual, or annual) and confirmed at CCM4; never less than annually.
  • An RPM is also convened early when a life event in SOP 22 changes the plan.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: AA (progress report, tracker extract, previous-quarter figures, packet), CSA (agenda, confirmation, logistics, [CRM], follow-through on asks), SA (co-attends; leads routine RPMs once the relationship-manager test in SOP 73 is met) · Consulted: ISB / EEN expert for any complex recommendation; [Firm Compliance] for the fee and disclosure items.

Timing

When What
Cadence First RPM at +90 days; then per the client's stated preference
T−10 business days Agenda (T02) drafted; annual items checked against T15 (IPS review, fee conversation, T05 review, survey)
T−7 Pre-meeting letter (T01) with agenda; client invited to add items
T−3 Packet complete; any material change since last contact already communicated; expert confirmed for complex items
T+0 Meeting — 60–90 minutes
T+1 Recap, confirmation of the next RPM, [CRM] log
T+2 Advanced-planning tracker (T10) updated with every decision

Inputs

  • Total Client Profile (SOP 11) and the last recap.
  • Investment plan and IPS (SOP 13); previous-quarter closing statements or the reporting package (SOP 24).
  • The advanced-planning plan (SOP 30) — for the first RPM, the draft from the expert-network meeting; afterwards the current tracker (T10).
  • Implementation tracker (T07) for anything still in transfer.
  • T05 (who may attend, what may be shared, whether asks are permitted) and the personality note (SOP 04).
  • Annual-calendar items due this quarter (T15).

Prep checklist

  • [ ] SOP 05 prep complete (agenda, letter, packet, attendees, roles, no surprises).
  • [ ] Progress report drafted against the goals in the profile, using the previous quarter's closing figures.
  • [ ] Tracker current: every item has a status and a next step; completed items since last meeting listed.
  • [ ] Any plan or recommendation to be presented has been peer-reviewed and signed off (see Procedure step 4).
  • [ ] Expert available — in person or by phone — for any complex recommendation on the agenda.
  • [ ] Annual items due: fee conversation packet; IPS review; T05 re-scope; survey reminder.
  • [ ] Second-chair or rotation designation recorded if this is the year's development slot.
  • [ ] Asks permitted per T05; the ideal-client description ready for the introductions ask.

Procedure

  1. Open per SOP 05. Greet by name, reinforce the client's personality note, walk the agenda, ask for additions. Hold questions the progress report will answer in sequence.

  2. Ask what has changed.

    Say something like

    "What has happened since we last got together?" — then, if needed: "Has anything happened in your life or the family's that affects your finances and that I should know about?"

    Listen for career and business changes, births, marriages, divorces, deaths, health, disputes, sales. Note anything that requires a change to the investment plan or the advanced-planning plan. 3. Report progress. Walk the progress report: goals, the investment plan, the previous quarter's results placed in the long-term frame. Reinforce the long view whenever short-term performance is down. 4. Present the advanced-planning plan (first RPM). Confirm the plan has been peer-reviewed and signed off before it enters the room.

    Beyond Bowen

    Every plan or proposal is reviewed by a second professional (SA, AA, or a bench expert) and signed off by the LA before it is presented. No exceptions for time pressure.

    Then, in order: the four areas at a high level; the highest-priority items in each; the specific challenges the client faces and how the recommended solutions address them; then each recommendation with as much detail as the client needs to decide. 5. Coach each recommendation to a decision. For each item the client chooses drop, defer, or do (Mode B adds refer to family team). Take complete notes of the response and the reasoning. Summarize the next step for every item before moving on. 6. Review the tracker (subsequent RPMs). Completed items acknowledged; in-progress items with owner and date; future items re-prioritized. Keep the high-priority items prominent and educate the client on the aspects of the plan that matter now. For a complex item — a family partnership, a dynasty trust, a business-succession structure via [ESOP Co.] — the relevant expert explains it directly. 7. Run the consequences check before anything long-term is executed.

    Beyond Bowen

    Before a perpetual or multi-generational structure moves from "do" to execution, ask together: what unintended consequences could this have for the people it is meant to benefit; have we taken the long view and hastened slowly; what harm might we do before we try to do good; how will the beneficiaries experience this; what happens if it turns out to be wrong? Record the answers with the decision.

  3. Pace the conversation to what the client is ready for.

    Beyond Bowen

    Alternate questions that supply knowledge with questions that call for courage — the ones the client already knows the answer to but has not acted on. When the family is not ready, most of the time the right move is to wait; note the item and return to it next meeting.

  4. Answer remaining questions about the plan.

  5. Make the asks (SOP 50): first additional assets, then introductions. Thank the client whatever the answer.

  6. Annual items when due. Hold the fee conversation — in writing, in context, with the client leading the questions; review the IPS; re-scope T05; confirm the survey is on its way.

    Beyond Bowen

    Discuss fees at least once a year, in a written form the client can keep, put in the context of what the practice does for the family, and treat the client's questions as a normal part of the relationship rather than a wedge.

  7. Close per SOP 05. Summarize decisions and next steps by owner and date; ask what would make the next meeting better; schedule it in the room.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours: written recap and confirmation (T01); [CRM] log of life changes, decisions, asks and outcomes; handwritten thank-you for any introduction.
  • Within 48 hours: tracker (T10) updated; expert follow-ups assigned; implementation items opened on T07.
  • Within one week: calls to any introduced prospect; report back to the client on the outcome; any "refer to family team" item packaged for the FCT.
  • Before the next RPM: every "do" item has visible progress or a documented reason it does not.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Progress report Client [Document vault]; [CRM] activity AA
Decisions per recommendation (drop / defer / do / refer) T10 tracker; [CRM] AA
Life-change notes and profile updates SOP 11 record in [CRM] LA
Asks made and outcomes [CRM] opportunity records CSA
Fee-conversation record (annual) [CRM]; client file LA
Next RPM date [CRM] calendar; confirmation letter CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Use the most recent quarter-end figures; never present stale numbers.
  • Tell the client of any major change before the meeting.
  • Bring the expert into the room for anything complex rather than paraphrasing them.
  • Treat every RPM as the first: same preparation, same energy.
  • Let the client decide; coaching is not persuading.

Don't

  • Don't skip the asks because the meeting ran long — move them earlier next time.
  • Don't execute a long-term structure in the same meeting it was first agreed; the consequences check and counsel come first.
  • Don't let the tracker become a list of everything; it stays prioritized by impact on the client's life.
  • Don't present a plan nobody else has reviewed.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The RPM for a household sits alongside the family-level annual meeting (SOP 43); items that belong to the family as a whole move to the family-level tracker.
  • Trust and entity recommendations are routed to the trustee or decision-maker named on T14 before being recorded as "do."
  • The introductions ask is framed as other members or branches the family would like the practice to serve, via the elders or council where they exist.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The agenda adds a coordination update: changes on the family side that affect this individual.
  • Recommendations touching family-level structures are drafted as items to take to family counsel or the FCT — the fourth coaching outcome, refer to family team — and are not executed by the Advisor.
  • Asks are limited to assets within the individual's own discretion and to introductions made through the individual, per SOP 02 and SOP 50; nothing is solicited around the FCT.
  • Recap distribution follows the consent on T05.

Metrics

  • Share of RPMs held within the client's stated cadence (target 100%).
  • Share of tracker items with a recorded client decision and a dated next step (target 100%).
  • Asks made per RPM (target: both, whenever T05 permits).

Related

  • SOP 30 — Wealth management plan · T10 — Advanced-planning tracker
  • SOP 32 — Expert-network meeting
  • SOP 50 — Asks inside service meetings · T13 — Scripts sheet
  • SOP 22 — Event-driven contact · SOP 24 — Quarterly reporting package

  • Bowen, Breaking Through, Ch. 5 — asking for additional assets and introductions at every progress meeting (adapted).
  • Hughes, The Compact — knowledge versus courage questions; the discipline of waiting (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, Family Wealth, Ch. 21 — the unintended-consequences questions to put before any perpetual structure (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, Massenzio & Whitaker, Complete Family Wealth, Ch. 9 — the annual fee conversation (paraphrased).

21 Service standards and the contact plan

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the Process area of the Total Client Profile: honor the client's stated preference for the life of the relationship; Ch. 6 — contact frequency of wealth managers vs. investment generalists; the seven satisfaction factors; the WOW service checklist; agenda for every meeting; red-flag methodology · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 6 — both spouses should be able to speak directly with the family's advisers; The Compact — confidentiality and discretion for hyperagent families; the Morgan creed · Other: Palaveev — service standards productized per segment; whoever receives a request owns it; 'who you call for what'

21 — Service standards and the contact plan

Every client told us in Discovery how they want to be worked with. This procedure turns that answer into a written contact plan, sets the response-time and communication standards the whole team is held to, and defines what "service" means for each scope of engagement so that staffing, pricing and the client's expectations all describe the same thing.

Purpose

  • Honor each client's stated process preference for the life of the relationship, in writing, so it survives staff changes.
  • Fix the practice's service standards — response times, agendas, ownership of requests, confidentiality posture — as rules, not habits.
  • Define service by scope (what a B-narrow mandate receives vs. a Mode A family) so the team can plan capacity and the client knows what to expect.
  • Make the practice's contact rhythm deliberately about the client's life, not only the portfolio.

Trigger

  • A new client signs at CCM3 (the contact plan is drafted from the Discovery notes and confirmed at CCM4).
  • An existing client's Rediscovery meeting updates their process preference.
  • Annually, at the first progress meeting of the year (T15), and whenever a life event (SOP 22) or a service failure (SOP 23) reveals the plan is wrong.
  • A new team member joins and must be written into "who you call for what."

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (drafts and maintains the contact plan in [CRM]; sends the written version with the CCM4 confirmation; monitors the touch log and response-time standard), SA/AA (execute assigned touches and deliverables) · Consulted: FCT contact in Mode B for the communication protocol.

Timing

When What
Before CCM3 Draft contact plan from the Discovery "Process" notes (SOP 10, T03)
At CCM4 Confirm the plan with the client; issue in writing with the notebook (T08)
Monthly CSA reviews the touch log against the plan; flags gaps to the LA
Quarterly Contact plan reviewed alongside the reporting package (SOP 24)
Annually (Q1) Full review with the client at the first progress meeting; T05 reviewed at the same time
Within 1 business day Any change to a client's preference is recorded in [CRM] and told to every team member who touches the account

Inputs

  • Discovery notes on process preference: preferred channel, frequency, meeting cadence, who in the household is the primary contact, what they never want (SOP 10, T03).
  • T05 — mode, scope rung, who may instruct, consent for who may receive what.
  • The personality note (SOP 04) — how the client likes to be paced and addressed.
  • Family map and communication map for Mode A families (T14).
  • The annual service calendar (T15) and the segment/scope service definition below.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Process-preference notes transcribed from the Discovery recording into [CRM] fields (channel, frequency, cadence, primary contact, "never").
  • [ ] T05 consent matrix checked so the plan does not promise to send anything to anyone not authorized.
  • [ ] Household members who may speak directly with the Advisor listed (default: both spouses; adult children only with consent).
  • [ ] "Who you call for what" table filled with the current team, including borrowed specialists by name for active matters.
  • [ ] Scope-based service definition selected (table in step 5) and any customization priced or declined.

Procedure

  1. Write the contact plan. One page per client in [CRM] and in the notebook: preferred channel; how often they want to hear from us and about what; meeting cadence and format (in person / video); primary and secondary contacts in the household; who on our team they call for what; what they have asked us never to do (for example, never call at the office, never send unsolicited market commentary).

  2. Confirm it with the client at CCM4 and read it back. Change anything they want changed. The plan is theirs, not ours.

    Say something like

    "You told me in our first meeting how you like to work with an advisor; here it is in writing so that everyone on our team follows it. Tell me what to change."

  3. Set the rhythm of contact. Plan the year's touches from the client's preference and the calendar (T15). Wealth managers who keep their best clients loyal reach them roughly fifteen times a year, most of those touches being about the client's life, family and interests rather than the portfolio. Treat that as a design target for the plan, never as a quota: a client who asked for quarterly contact gets quarterly contact, done well.

  4. Apply the response-time standard. Every message from a client is acknowledged the same business day by the person who received it, with a time by which the answer will come. The answer arrives by that time or the client hears before the deadline that it will be late and why. Whoever received the request owns it to completion — nobody in this practice says "let me put you through to someone else."

  5. Apply the service definition for the client's scope. Service is a product, not a word. The default definition by scope:

    Scope Meetings per year Planning depth Reporting Held-away assets Family layer
    Mode A — whole family Quarterly household RPMs (client may choose semi-annual); annual family meeting Full wealth management plan across all four areas; family-level plan Consolidated across entities and trusts; custom family statement Reviewed every RPM; consolidation offered SOPs 40–48 in full
    Mode B — B-full Quarterly or semi-annual per preference Full plan for the individual's own assets; family-structure items referred to the FCT Individual consolidated; compatible with family reporting Personal held-away only On invitation
    Mode B — B-partial Semi-annual Investment plan plus liaison into the FCT's planning Individual accounts; data feed to the FCT if mandated Not solicited On invitation
    Mode B — B-narrow Annual, plus trustee meetings as mandated Investment plan for the mandate only Mandate accounts only Not solicited None

    Anything the client wants beyond the definition — custom reporting formats, manually tracked outside assets, exception custodians, one-off analyses — is either priced into the fee (SOP 14) or declined, never absorbed silently. 6. Put an agenda in front of every meeting (SOP 05, T02), including calls the client thinks of as quick. A written agenda is the visible sign the practice runs on process. 7. Write "who you call for what." A short table in the contact plan and in every confirmation letter (T01): the LA for advice and decisions; the SA for the plan and routine reviews; the CSA for paperwork, money movement and scheduling; a named specialist for an active matter. Update it within one business day of any team change. 8. Make sure both spouses can reach us. Each partner in a couple may speak directly with the Advisor and should be able to; the plan names both as contacts unless the client instructs otherwise in writing. This protects the household if one partner is suddenly unable to act and it gives each partner a first-hand relationship rather than a relayed one. 9. Hold the confidentiality posture. Very wealthy families attract attention; the practice's job includes not adding to it. Never acknowledge a client relationship in public or to another client. Never confirm to a third party that the family is a client without written consent on T05. Do not discuss one family in front of another, even anonymized, where the details would identify them. Discretion is a value the team is hired for. 10. Design the experience around the seven satisfaction factors. Clients assume competence; it does not differentiate. What does: reliability (promises kept on time); no surprises (problems and their fixes communicated first, and complaints actively invited); first-to-know (clients hear about their affairs, the markets, and the firm from us before anyone else); warmth (genuine, not merely polite); listening (patience while explaining, attention while hearing); client-centered work (their specific needs, with real alternatives). Every standard in this SOP maps to one of these. 11. Audit twice a year against the WOW self-audit (T12) and fix the gaps before the satisfaction survey goes out (SOP 25). 12. Record everything in [CRM]. The contact plan, every touch, every request and its resolution time, every change of preference. The red-flag methodology in SOP 22 runs off these records.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours of CCM4: the written contact plan is in the notebook and in [CRM]; "who you call for what" is in the confirmation letter.
  • Monthly: the CSA reports touch-plan adherence and response-time misses to the LA; misses go to the service-failure log (T12).
  • Annually: the plan is reviewed with the client; changes are re-issued in writing within a week.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Contact plan (one page per client) [CRM] client record; client notebook (T08) CSA
"Who you call for what" table Contact plan; every confirmation letter (T01) CSA
Touch log and response-time record [CRM] activities CSA
Scope-based service definition selected; customizations priced T05; engagement letter (SOP 14) LA
Semi-annual WOW self-audit T12; SOP 25 file LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Read the contact plan before every call with a client you do not speak with weekly.
  • Reach clients about their lives — a note after a child's graduation, an article on something they collect — more often than about their money.
  • Tell a client before the meeting when something material changed; the meeting is for decisions, not surprises.
  • Keep the same standards for a B-narrow trust mandate as for a Mode A family; the definition changes, the quality does not.

Don't

  • Don't let the touch target become a quota that produces hollow contact; a client who asked for quiet gets quiet.
  • Don't send anything to anyone the consent matrix on T05 does not authorize.
  • Don't absorb custom work silently; price it or decline it.
  • Don't use possessive language about clients in front of them or among the team.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The contact plan is written per household and rolled into a family communication map (T14): who is the primary contact per household, who receives family-level communications, and who may not be copied on what.
  • The annual family meeting (SOP 43) and family-level reporting are part of the service definition; the plan states which members attend which meetings.
  • Where a family council exists, the council's chair or the family's designated contact is named for family-level matters; individual households keep their own contacts.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Response-time commitments extend to the FCT's designated contact for the matters within the mandate; the standard is the same as for the client.
  • A written communication protocol (SOP 33) sits beside the individual's preference: who contacts whom, what is copied to the FCT under the T05 consent, single-thread communication for anything touching family structures.
  • "Who you call for what" includes the FCT's contact for family-level matters so the client is never bounced between teams.
  • Service definition follows the scope rung; nothing outside the mandate is offered without re-scoping T05.

Metrics

  • Response-time adherence: share of client requests acknowledged same business day and resolved within the promised time (target ≥ 95%).
  • Contact-plan adherence: share of planned touches completed per client per quarter (target ≥ 90%).
  • Preference changes recorded within one business day (target 100%).

22 Event-driven contact — red flags, shocks, and life events

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 6 — red-flag methodology in the client database; immediate contact when a major external event occurs; the no-surprises and first-to-know factors; clients must not hear of firm changes from a competitor; Ch. 4 — the 'what has changed in your life' questions at progress meetings · Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 16 and 17 — prenuptial disclosure months ahead (disclosure is not access); transitions; revisiting preambles on material change; addiction leverage model; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 16 — family meetings during difficult transitions (sale of a business, succession, death or disability); Family Wealth Ch. 3 — rituals for passages including death · Other: Extension — the trigger table and the death/incapacity checklist are ours

22 — Event-driven contact

The calendar covers the year we can plan. This procedure covers everything we cannot: the signals in the data that something has changed, the market and the world doing what they do, changes inside the firm, and the events in a family's life that decide whether the relationship deepens or ends. Each trigger has an owner, a clock, a message, and a record.

Purpose

  • Make sure the client hears about anything that touches their affairs from us first, fast, and in a consistent voice.
  • Turn red flags in the data into contact before they become problems.
  • Route life events into the right planning work — the prenuptial timeline, a family meeting, a preamble revision — instead of leaving them to the next scheduled meeting.
  • Give the team a checklist for the hardest moment, the death or incapacity of a principal.

Trigger

Any item in the trigger table below is observed by any team member, reported by the client or the family, or surfaced by the monthly red-flag review.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (monthly red-flag review; first acknowledgment; logging), SA/AA (analysis behind the message; tracker updates) · Consulted: [Firm Compliance] for death, incapacity, and any account restriction; FCT contact in Mode B; ISB ([Trust Co.]) where a trust is involved; EEN counsel for prenuptial, addiction, and estate items.

Timing

Trigger class First contact Follow-through
Red flag in the data Same business day the flag is seen Resolved or explained within 3 business days
Market shock Same day, top relationships first; all clients within 2 business days Follow-up note within the week; agenda item at the next RPM
External disaster affecting the client Immediately; then daily until stable Log; adjust the contact plan if needed
Firm or staff change Before the change is visible to anyone outside the firm Written note within 24 hours of the call
Life event reported Same day acknowledgment by the LA personally Planning task opened within 5 business days
Death or incapacity of a principal Same day Checklist runs over 30–90 days; closing ritual within a year

Inputs

  • Monthly red-flag review of [CRM] and [Custodian] activity (SOP 21 records).
  • The contact plan and personality note for the client (SOP 21, SOP 04).
  • T05 — consent for what may be shared with whom; the FCT protocol in Mode B.
  • The family map and communication map (T14) for Mode A families.
  • The advanced-planning tracker (T10) and any letters of wishes or preambles on file (SOP 46).

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Red-flag rules configured in [CRM] and reviewed monthly by the CSA: large cash movement, statement anomaly, missed or cancelled meeting, change of address or marital status, death notification, beneficiary or trustee request, unusual login or contact from an unknown third party.
  • [ ] Market-shock message template drafted and approved by [Firm Compliance] in advance, with a blank for the day's facts.
  • [ ] Death/incapacity checklist (below) on file with the named contacts per client: executor, trustees, counsel, CPA, family contact, FCT in Mode B.
  • [ ] Every team member knows the rule: the LA personally makes the first call on any life event or shock; the CSA never delivers difficult news alone.

Procedure

  1. Detect. The CSA runs the red-flag review monthly and watches daily activity; any team member who hears of an event tells the LA the same day.

  2. Classify using the trigger table and open a task in [CRM] with the trigger, owner, and clock.

    Trigger Owner Message Planning task opened
    Large or unusual cash movement CSA → LA Confirm the client authorized it; verify by callback on a known number, never by reply to the request Fraud check; update T07 if a transfer
    Statement anomaly (missing account, unexpected position, fee error) CSA Explain what happened and what we did about it, before the client notices Service-failure log if ours (SOP 23)
    Missed or cancelled meeting, repeated CSA → LA LA calls: "Is everything all right?" — not a rescheduling email Contact-plan review
    Change of address, employment, or marital status seen in data LA Acknowledge personally; ask what it means for them Life-event branch below
    Beneficiary or trustee request LA Acknowledge same day; route to SOP 46 Distribution-request process (T23)
    Third party asking about the client CSA → LA Nothing confirmed; client told the same day Consent check on T05

  3. Market shock. On the day, the LA calls the top relationships personally (Mode A principals and household leads; Mode B individuals) with one consistent message: what happened, what it means for their plan, what we are doing, and when they will hear from us next. The CSA sends the approved note to every other client within two business days. Nobody on the team sends their own market commentary.

    Say something like

    "I wanted you to hear from me today rather than from the news: here is what happened, here is what it does and does not mean for your plan, and here is what we are doing about it."

    Mode B

    Align the message with the FCT before sending. Two teams telling the same family different stories on the same day destroys confidence in both; when they differ, the LA and the FCT contact agree the wording, or the LA sends only what is within the mandate.

  4. External disaster (a storm, fire, civil emergency, a public event affecting the client's community or business). Contact immediately to ask whether they and their family are safe and whether we can do anything — money movement, documents, a hotel. Stay in touch daily until stable. This is the moment relationships are made or lost.

  5. Firm or staff change. Clients hear about a departure, a merger, a new custodian, or a new team member from the LA before it is visible anywhere else. Sequence: team told first; then a call to each affected client; then a written note within 24 hours; then the change. Never let a client learn of a personnel change when they call in need or from a competitor's outreach.

  6. Life events — the planning branch. Acknowledge personally the same day. Then open the planning task:

    Event What it triggers
    Birth or adoption Beneficiary designations and trust provisions reviewed; a note to the family; rising-generation entry on the family map (T14)
    Engagement The prenuptial timeline starts now: the conversation with the couple and the parents months before the wedding, never in the final weeks; disclosure of trust interests to both partners, with the rule that disclosure is not access; the family's spouse policy applied if one exists (SOP 45); counsel selected to fit the couple
    Marriage Contact plan updated (both spouses may speak directly with the Advisor); consent matrix reviewed; welcome as a new member (SOP 42)
    Divorce or separation Confidentiality between the parties enforced from the first call; [Firm Compliance] consulted; conflicts assessed; the Advisor never mediates a marriage
    Job or career change; new business Compensation and equity terms reviewed; plan updated; tracker items opened
    Sale of a business, succession, retirement of a principal A family meeting convened (SOP 43): what the liquidity event means for the family, not just the balance sheet; expert-network case brief (T09); [ESOP Co.] consulted where an employee-ownership path is live
    New life stage or health change of a trustee, beneficiary, or principal Preambles, letters of wishes, and beneficiary designations revisited (SOP 46); incapacity documents checked
    Signs of addiction or crisis The LA raises it privately with the appropriate family member; the leverage-model conversation with counsel about protective trust provisions and treatment funding; never a moral judgment, always a plan (SOP 46, SOP 30)
    Death of a family member Checklist below

  7. Death or incapacity of a principal — run the checklist.

    • [ ] Day 1: LA calls the surviving spouse or the designated family contact; condolences first, logistics only when asked. Nothing else that day.
    • [ ] Day 1–3: [Firm Compliance] and [Custodian] notified; accounts restricted as required; recurring transfers paused; authorized signers confirmed from the file, never from a phone call.
    • [ ] Week 1: executor, trustees, counsel, and CPA identified and contacted; documents located (will, trusts, powers of attorney, letters of wishes, legacy letter); date-of-death valuations ordered.
    • [ ] Week 1–2: the household's immediate cash needs covered; a single point of contact on our team named for the family.
    • [ ] Month 1–3: estate and trust administration coordinated with counsel and [Trust Co.]; investor-allocation and trust-funding items reviewed; the family map updated; the contact plan rewritten with the survivors.
    • [ ] Within the year: a family meeting that includes remembrance (SOP 43); the closing ritual for any trust that terminates (SOP 48); the deceased's story captured for the family archive.
    • [ ] Incapacity: the same sequence with the agent under the power of attorney and the successor trustee; the annual protector check-in brought forward (SOP 46).

    Mode B

    The FCT leads estate administration for the family; the Advisor supports the individuals he serves, coordinates through the single thread in SOP 33, and shares nothing beyond the T05 consent.

  8. Record. Every trigger, message, and task is logged in [CRM] with dates; life events update the Total Client Profile (SOP 11) and the family map.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours: written note where a call was made; task opened with owner and date.
  • Within one week: planning branch confirmed with the client; trackers updated; the next RPM agenda amended.
  • At the next RPM: the event reviewed and the plan changes presented.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Trigger log (event, date, owner, message, resolution) [CRM] activities CSA
Planning tasks opened [CRM] tasks; T10 tracker LA
Updated profile, family map, contact plan SOP 11 file; T14; SOP 21 CSA
Death/incapacity checklist, completed Client [Document vault] LA
Market-shock message sent [CRM] mass activity; copy in the notebook CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Make the first call yourself on anything that hurts; delegate the paperwork, never the empathy.
  • Say what you know, what you do not know, and when they will hear from you again.
  • Start the prenuptial conversation the day you hear of an engagement.
  • Treat a beneficiary's request as a relationship moment, not an administrative one.

Don't

  • Don't send market commentary that has not been approved and aligned.
  • Don't verify a money-movement request by replying to the message that made it.
  • Don't let a client learn of a staff change from anyone but the LA.
  • Don't attempt to mediate between spouses; enforce confidentiality and bring in the right professional.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Family-wide events (a death, a business sale) are communicated through the communication map (T14): the LA calls household leads; the family contact or council chair coordinates family-level messages.
  • Family meetings are the vehicle for transitions; convene within weeks of a sale, succession, or death, not at the next annual meeting.
  • Confidentiality between members governs what each household hears about another's event.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Market and shock messages aligned with the FCT; the LA sends only what is within the mandate if agreement is not reached in time.
  • Life events shared with the FCT only under the T05 consent; the individual decides what the family learns and when.
  • On a principal's death or incapacity, the FCT leads; the Advisor's checklist runs only for the accounts and individuals in his mandate.
  • Firm changes affecting the mandate are told to the client first, then to the FCT contact under the protocol.

Metrics

  • Red flags resolved or explained within 3 business days (target ≥ 95%).
  • Market-shock outreach to top relationships completed same day (target 100%).
  • Life events with a planning task opened within 5 business days (target 100%).

23 Service failure recovery

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 6 — resolve service failures the same day where possible; treat a failure as an opportunity by communicating the problem and the solution; interview every lost client; occasional mystery shopper; no administrative errors as a service-satisfaction item · Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 21 — the protector's question, 'what have I contributed to this?', turned on ourselves; The Compact — 80% of the time do nothing; respond rather than react · Other: Palaveev — clients dislike unpleasant surprises more than failures; the firm owns the client experience; never blame another party in front of the client

23 — Service failure recovery

Failures will happen: a transfer stalls, a report is wrong, a promise is missed, a call is not returned. Clients forgive the failure; they do not forgive learning about it late, being blamed for it, or seeing it happen again. This procedure fixes the failure fast, tells the client first, repairs the process, and learns from the clients who leave.

Purpose

  • Resolve every service failure the same day where possible and never later than the time promised.
  • Make sure the client hears the problem and the fix from us, together, before they discover the problem themselves.
  • Convert each failure into a change in a procedure so it does not recur.
  • Learn systematically from lost clients and from an occasional outside test of our own service.

Trigger

  • Any team member notices or is told of an error, a missed deadline, an unreturned message, a wrong document, a mishandled request, or a client expressing dissatisfaction.
  • A red flag in SOP 22 turns out to be our mistake.
  • A client gives notice, moves assets away, or cancels the relationship.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (intake and log; fixes administrative failures; tracks to closure), SA/AA (fixes analytical or reporting failures; drafts the explanation) · Consulted: [Firm Compliance] where money, documents, or regulatory items are involved; [Custodian] and ISB where the failure sits with them; FCT contact in Mode B through the agreed channel.

Timing

Step Clock
Intake and log Within 1 hour of discovery
LA informed Same hour for anything the client can see; same day otherwise
Client told (problem + fix + timing) Same day, by the LA, by phone
Resolution Same day where possible; otherwise by the time promised, with a progress call if it slips
Root-cause note and SOP change Within 5 business days
Lost-client interview Within 2 weeks of notice

Inputs

  • The service-failure log (T12, part c).
  • The contact plan and personality note (SOP 21, SOP 04) — how this client wants to be reached and how they take bad news.
  • The relevant SOP and tracker (T07 for transfers, T10 for planning items).
  • T05 and the FCT protocol in Mode B.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Every team member knows where the log is and that logging is never punished; hiding a failure is.
  • [ ] The apology-call rule is understood: the LA makes it personally, whoever caused the failure.
  • [ ] Standing arrangement with [Custodian] and ISB partners for escalation contacts and turnaround times.
  • [ ] The mystery-shopper check scheduled once a year (a trusted outsider tests a call, an email, and a document request).

Procedure

  1. Log it. The person who discovers the failure records it in the log within the hour: what happened, who is affected, when it was promised, what the client knows. No judgment yet.
  2. Contain. Stop any further harm: pause a transfer, correct a document, hold a report. If money or documents are involved, tell [Firm Compliance] now.
  3. Diagnose fast. Establish what actually happened and what it will take to fix, in enough detail to give the client a date. Do this before the call; do not call with "we are looking into it" unless the client will otherwise find out first.

  4. Call the client — the LA, personally, the same day. Problem, cause in one sentence, the fix, the date, and what we are changing so it does not recur. Apologize once, clearly, without excuses.

    Say something like

    "I am calling because we made a mistake on your account and I want you to hear it from me, together with what we have already done to fix it and when it will be complete."

  5. Never blame. Do not attribute the failure to the custodian, a sister company, the client's other advisors, or the client, in front of the client. The practice owns the client experience whoever caused the problem; escalation and cost recovery happen behind the scenes through the agreed channel.

  6. Fix it by the date promised. If the date slips, the client hears before the date, not after. Track to closure in the log and the relevant tracker.
  7. Confirm closure in writing the day the fix lands, and check at the next contact that the client considers it closed.
  8. Root cause. Within five business days, the LA and the person closest to the failure write a two-line root-cause note: the step in the SOP that failed or was missing, and the change. Amend the SOP (SOP 60). If the same failure recurs, treat it as a system failure, not a person's.
  9. Turn the protector's question on ourselves. Before assigning cause elsewhere, ask what we did or did not do that contributed. Most "custodian problems" have a missing check on our side.
  10. Review the log monthly at the team meeting (SOP 74): patterns, open items, changes made. Feed themes into the semi-annual WOW self-audit (T12) and the survey action list (SOP 25).
  11. Lost-client interview. When a client gives notice or moves assets away, the LA asks for a thirty-minute conversation within two weeks, using the interview guide in T12: what changed, what we missed, what they would tell a friend about us, and whether anything could bring them back. Thank them for the time regardless of the answer. Record the findings; act on them.
  12. Mystery-shopper check. Once a year, a trusted outsider tests the practice — a call to the main line, an email request, a document request — against the response-time standard. Results go into the self-audit.

Follow-up

  • Same day: log entry, client called, fix under way.
  • Within 5 business days: root-cause note; SOP amended; team told what changed.
  • Monthly: log reviewed; open items closed or re-dated with the client informed.
  • Annually: lost-client findings and mystery-shopper results reviewed with the satisfaction survey.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Service-failure log entry (T12 c) [CRM] CSA
Client notification (call logged; written confirmation of closure) [CRM]; client notebook LA / CSA
Root-cause note and SOP amendment SOP 60 change log LA
Lost-client interview record [CRM]; SOP 25 file LA
Mystery-shopper results SOP 25 file LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Tell the client before they find out; the surprise hurts more than the error.
  • Give a date and keep it; if you cannot, call before the date.
  • Fix the process, then the person's understanding of it — in that order.
  • Ask a departing client for the interview even when the reason is obvious.

Don't

  • Don't send the apology by email; the LA calls.
  • Don't explain the failure by naming who else was involved.
  • Don't let a failure sit unlogged because it was small; small failures are the pattern.
  • Don't overreact to a single failure with a new rule that slows every other client; respond, don't react.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • If a failure touches more than one household, each affected household lead is called separately; the family contact is told only what the consent matrix allows.
  • A failure in a trust or entity account is reported to the trustee and the beneficiary as the trust's communication protocol requires (SOP 46).

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The Advisor owns recovery for his client even when the failure sits with the FCT, the family's custodian, or a sister company; the client hears one accountable voice.
  • Escalation goes through the agreed channel in SOP 33; the FCT contact is told what happened and what was done, never that they caused it, in front of the client.
  • If the failure reveals a gap in the mandate (something nobody owned), the LA raises it with the FCT and re-scopes T05.

Metrics

  • Failures resolved same day or by the promised date (target ≥ 95%).
  • Repeat failures of the same root cause within 12 months (target zero).
  • Lost-client interviews completed within 2 weeks of notice (target 100%).

Source
