  • Goldstone, Hughes & Whitaker, Family Trusts, Ch. 21 — the "what have I contributed to this?" question, applied to ourselves (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, The Compact — respond rather than react; most problems resolve with time and care (paraphrased).
  • Palaveev, The Ensemble Practice — unpleasant surprises hurt more than failures; the firm owns the client experience; take responsibility and fix it fast (paraphrased).

24 Quarterly reporting package

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — regular progress reports as a section of the client notebook; use the previous quarter's closing statements; reinforce the long-term perspective; notify the client of material changes before the meeting; Ch. 6 — timely information and regular briefings (first-to-know factor) · Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 7 and 20 — beneficiaries should be able to read a trust statement and know how and how much everyone is paid; the Office of the Beneficiary reviews fees; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 9 — fee transparency and the annual fee conversation · Other: Palaveev — custom reporting and manually tracked outside assets are unpriced customization; consolidated reporting is a core deliverable of team-based firms

24 — Quarterly reporting package

Every client receives a written picture of where they stand each quarter, whether or not a meeting happens that quarter. The package consolidates every account, entity and trust we serve, measures progress against the client's own objectives rather than against last quarter's index, shows what we did and what comes next, and states plainly what they paid. It is the backbone of the notebook and the pre-read for every progress meeting.

Purpose

  • Give the client a single, consolidated view across custodians, entities and trusts.
  • Measure against the investment policy statement's objectives and the plan's milestones, reinforcing the long-term perspective.
  • Report transparently on fees paid to everyone.
  • Carry the advanced-planning tracker and implementation status so the meeting can be about decisions.
  • Produce it on a fixed schedule so the client is never waiting for information.

Trigger

  • Quarter-end statements are available from [Custodian] and any other custodians (typically 10–15 business days after quarter end).
  • A year-end version adds an annual summary.
  • An interim package is produced on request or after a major event (SOP 22).

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (data gathering, assembly, delivery, filing), AA (analysis, performance vs objectives, tracker extract, draft cover summary) · Consulted: SA for the plan status; ISB ([Trust Co.]) for trust accounting extracts; FCT contact in Mode B for format and data feeds.

Timing

Business day after quarter end Step
+1 to +10 Statements and data gathered; outside-asset values requested where the client has authorized us to track them
+11 to +15 AA analysis; draft package built on T11
+16 to +18 LA review and sign-off; cover summary finalized
+18 to +20 Delivered per the contact plan; filed to the notebook; agenda for the next RPM updated
Year-end Same clock plus the annual summary; delivered before the first progress meeting of the year

Inputs

  • Quarter-end statements from every custodian; trust accounting extracts from [Trust Co.] where applicable.
  • The investment policy statement and plan objectives (SOP 13).
  • The advanced-planning tracker (T10) and implementation tracker (T07).
  • The annual service calendar (T15) for upcoming items.
  • Fee records: our fee, custodian and platform fees, third-party manager fees, trustee fees, any fee-sharing disclosed under SOP 31.
  • The contact plan (SOP 21) — format, channel, and who receives what under T05.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Account list reconciled against the engagement: every account, entity and trust in scope is present; nothing out of scope is included.
  • [ ] Outside assets: only those the client has authorized us to track, with a note that values are client-supplied and as-of dates.
  • [ ] Any customization (a special format, an extra schedule, manual outside-asset tracking) is on the priced-customization list from T05 or has been declined — nothing absorbed silently.
  • [ ] Tracker extracts current: T10 statuses coded; T07 open items dated.
  • [ ] Fee schedule and the quarter's actual fees reconciled.
  • [ ] Anything in the package that will surprise the client has already been told to them by the LA (SOP 22).

Procedure

  1. Gather. CSA collects statements and data feeds from every custodian, trust extracts from [Trust Co.], and authorized outside-asset values. Missing items are chased on day +5; the package never waits past day +15 for a straggler — it goes out with a clearly marked gap and a follow-up date.
  2. Reconcile. CSA reconciles holdings and cash across sources; discrepancies go to the AA the same day and, if unresolved by day +12, to the LA.
  3. Analyze. AA produces performance against the IPS objectives (the client's required return, the spending or distribution rate, the risk band), the allocation against policy ranges, and a plain-language note on what drove the quarter. Short-period returns are shown but framed: what matters is progress toward the objectives over the horizon the plan set, not any single quarter.
  4. Report fees. Every fee the client paid this quarter, by payee, in dollars and as a rate: ours, custodian and platform, third-party managers, trustee, any disclosed fee-sharing. The client should never have to ask what they paid.
  5. Pull the trackers. T10 extract: each advanced-planning item with its status (done / in progress / scheduled / deferred / dropped) and next step. T07 extract: open transfers, titling, beneficiary designations.
  6. Write the cover summary (AA drafts, LA rewrites): three short blocks — what changed, what we did, what is next — plus any decision the client will be asked to make at the next meeting.
  7. Assemble on T11. Order: cover summary; consolidated holdings by entity and trust; performance vs objectives; fees; tracker extract; implementation status; upcoming calendar; questions for the next meeting.
  8. LA review. Accuracy, tone, and whether the summary would make sense to a family member who was not in the last meeting. Sign off by day +18.
  9. Deliver per the contact plan: [Document vault] posting with a personal note, or printed and mailed where the client prefers; a copy to each authorized recipient on T05. Trustees and beneficiaries receive the trust sections as the trust's protocol requires (SOP 46).
  10. File to the notebook (T08) and [CRM]; update the next RPM agenda (T02) with the questions raised.
  11. Flag customization. Any request for a new format, extra schedule or manual tracking is logged; the LA decides at the next fee conversation whether to price it or decline it (SOP 14).

Follow-up

  • Day +20: delivery confirmed in [CRM]; next-meeting agenda updated.
  • Within one week of delivery: CSA checks that the client received and can open the package (a call for clients who prefer print).
  • At the next RPM: the package is the pre-read; questions from it lead the agenda after the life-changes question.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Quarterly reporting package (T11) Client notebook (T08) / [Document vault]; [CRM] CSA
Reconciliation notes and gaps [CRM] activity CSA
Fee reconciliation Package fee section; [CRM] AA
Customization log T05 priced-customization list LA
Updated RPM agenda T02 CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Report against the client's objectives first; indices are context, not the scorecard.
  • Show every fee, including the ones we do not receive.
  • Write the cover summary in the client's language, not the platform's.
  • Deliver on the same day each quarter so the client can plan around it.

Don't

  • Don't hold the package for a late custodian; ship with a marked gap.
  • Don't include accounts outside the mandate, even when the client mentions them.
  • Don't let a manual outside-asset schedule become an unpriced standing job.
  • Don't let the package be the first place a client sees bad news.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • One consolidated family package at the family level (entities, trusts, households as the consent matrix allows) plus a household package per household; each household sees only what T14 authorizes.
  • The family-level tracker (family goals, family-level planning items) is a separate section; the year-end version feeds the family balance sheet and income statement inputs (SOP 44).
  • Trust sections go to trustees and beneficiaries per the trust protocol.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Format compatible with the family's consolidated reporting; where the FCT provides a template or data specification, use it, and supply data feeds if the mandate requires.
  • Only mandated accounts appear; family-level assets are referenced by name only if the client asks and the FCT agrees.
  • Copies to the FCT follow the T05 consent; fee reporting covers our fees and any fee-sharing disclosed to the individual and, where the FCT gatekeeps, to the FCT.

Metrics

  • Packages delivered by business day +20 (target 100%).
  • Reconciliation discrepancies unresolved at delivery (target zero).
  • Customizations absorbed without pricing or a decline decision (target zero).

25 Annual client satisfaction survey

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 5 — conduct a formal client survey every year as part of reviewing the relationship; Ch. 6 — the sequence: audit against the service checklist, close the gaps, then survey; share results with the team; act; tell clients what will change; interview lost clients; the seven satisfaction factors · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 9 — clients should take the lead in the annual fee conversation; the adviser's response to hard questions is itself evidence · Other: Extension — the instrument in T12 and the Mode B coordination check are ours

25 — Annual client satisfaction survey

Once a year the practice asks every client, formally, how it is doing — and only after it has first checked itself against its own standards and fixed what it found. The survey gives clients permission to say what they would not say in a meeting, tells them we want to hear it, and produces an action list that we report back to them. The instrument is ours, built from the seven factors that actually separate satisfied clients from dissatisfied ones.

Purpose

  • Hear the complaints clients would otherwise keep, before they act on them.
  • Measure the practice on the factors that drive loyalty — reliability, no surprises, timely information, warmth, listening, understanding needs, providing alternatives — not on the competence clients already assume.
  • Close the loop: team session, action items, and a specific "what will change" message to clients.
  • Feed the lost-client interviews and the mystery-shopper results into the same annual review.

Trigger

  • Calendar: Q2 (T15) — the WOW self-audit in May, the survey in May–June, results and the client message in July.
  • A new client's first survey is sent at the first Q2 after CCM4, never earlier than six months into the relationship.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (self-audit logistics; survey distribution and collection; response tracking), AA (tabulation and distillation) · Consulted: whole team for the results session; FCT contact in Mode B for the coordination check.

Timing

When Step
Early May WOW self-audit (T12 a) completed by the LA with the team
Mid May Gaps assigned and closed or scheduled before the survey goes out
Late May Survey (T12 b) sent to every client household per the contact plan
June Responses collected; one reminder at two weeks; LA personally calls non-responders among top relationships
Early July Tabulation; team results session; action list
Mid July "What will change" letter to every client; individual follow-up calls where a response warrants it
Ongoing Action items tracked at the monthly team meeting; reviewed at next year's self-audit

Inputs

  • The WOW self-audit results (T12 a) and the gap list.
  • The service-failure log for the year (T12 c) and any lost-client interviews (T12 d).
  • The mystery-shopper results (SOP 23).
  • The survey instrument (T12 b), personalized only with the client's name and the team members they work with.
  • The contact plan and T05: who in each household receives the survey; the Mode B coordination check recipient.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Self-audit completed and gaps closed or scheduled — the survey is not sent while known gaps sit open.
  • [ ] Survey list reconciled: every client household; both spouses invited to answer separately where the contact plan names both.
  • [ ] Delivery channel per contact plan (secure link via [Document vault]; paper for clients who prefer it).
  • [ ] Anonymity decision recorded: responses are attributed unless the client asks otherwise; the cover note says so and offers an anonymous option.
  • [ ] [Firm Compliance] has seen the instrument and the cover note.

Procedure

  1. Audit first. The LA and team score the practice against the self-audit (T12 a): met / partly / not for every item. Assign every "not" and "partly" an owner and a date. Close what can be closed in two weeks; schedule the rest and tell the team.

  2. Send the survey with a short personal note from the LA: why we ask, that we read every answer, that criticism is what we most want, and how long it takes (ten minutes).

    Say something like

    "Once a year I ask every family we serve to tell us plainly what we should do better. Your candid answers shape how we work next year."

  3. Collect. CSA tracks responses; one reminder after two weeks. For the top relationships and any client with a recent service failure, the LA calls personally to ask for the response or to take it by phone.

  4. Tabulate and distill. AA scores by factor, lists every open-ended comment verbatim (with the client's name unless anonymous), and flags any score of 2 or below on any item for individual follow-up.
  5. Follow up individually first. Before any team session, the LA calls every client whose responses flag a problem: thank them, ask what happened, and say what we will do. This is a service-recovery moment (SOP 23), not a data point.
  6. Hold the team results session. The whole team, including borrowed staff who touch clients regularly: results by factor, themes from comments, the failure log and lost-client findings for the year, the mystery-shopper results. Everyone contributes to the action list; the people who do the work usually know the fix.
  7. Write the action list. Each item: the change, the SOP it amends (SOP 60), the owner, the date. Distinguish what changes for everyone from what changes for one client.
  8. Tell clients what will change. A letter to every client within two weeks of the session: what we heard, in their words where possible; the specific changes we are making; thanks. Clients who asked for something particular hear it personally from the LA.
  9. Track the action list at the monthly team meeting (SOP 74) until every item is closed; carry the results into next year's self-audit as the baseline.
  10. Run the lost-client interviews for anyone who left during the year, if not already done (SOP 23), and include the findings in the results session.

Follow-up

  • Within two weeks of the results session: the "what will change" letter is out; individual calls made.
  • Monthly: action items reviewed; closed items reported to the team.
  • Next May: last year's actions verified in the self-audit before the new survey.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Self-audit scores and gap list SOP 25 file; T12 a LA
Survey responses (attributed or anonymous) [CRM] client records; SOP 25 file CSA
Tabulation by factor; comment list SOP 25 file AA
Individual follow-up calls [CRM] activities; failure log if applicable LA
Action list with SOP amendments SOP 60 change log; [CRM] tasks LA
"What will change" letter [CRM]; client notebook CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Fix known gaps before asking clients to point them out.
  • Read every comment aloud in the team session, including the uncomfortable ones.
  • Tell clients specifically what changed; generic thanks devalue their effort.
  • Treat a low score as a call to make today, not a statistic for July.

Don't

  • Don't survey a client mid-crisis or within weeks of a service failure that is still open; call them instead.
  • Don't survey a new client before six months.
  • Don't let the action list die after the letter goes out.
  • Don't ask questions about investment performance as if it were the point; ask about the relationship.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Each household receives its own survey; both spouses may answer separately. Family-level questions (family meetings, communication across the family, the family-level plan) are added for families with an active family layer.
  • Results are shared with the family contact or council chair only in aggregate and only under the T14 consent; individual households' answers stay with those households.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Survey the individual only; questions about family-level matters are omitted unless within the mandate.
  • Optional coordination check (T12 e): three questions to the FCT's designated contact about how the working relationship is functioning — responsiveness, information flow, surprises — sent with the client's knowledge.
  • Findings that concern the FCT's own service are raised through the SOP 33 channel, never in the client's letter.

Metrics

  • Response rate by household (target ≥ 70%; 100% among top relationships, by phone if necessary).
  • Share of action items closed within 90 days (target ≥ 80%).
  • Year-on-year change in the average score on the three lowest factors (target: improving).

Advanced planning and the expert network

30 The wealth management plan — document standard

specOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the wealth management plan in three parts; the four advanced-planning areas and their definitions; the advanced-planning mind map with completed / in-progress / future coding; SMART priorities · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 5, 8, 20, 21 — gift vs transfer, staged disclosure, structure summaries, investor allocation, philanthropy placement rules; Family Trusts Ch. 10, 14, 15, App. 6 — preambles and purpose language, distribution philosophy, addiction provisions, perpetual-trust counterweight; Family Wealth Ch. 5, 7, 12 — investor allocation, family bank, philanthropy as governance training · Other: Bonner — wealth-transfer technique menu, insurance objections, jurisdictional review, family properties (deltas only)

30 — The wealth management plan

The wealth management plan is the document that turns the practice from investment consulting into wealth management. It has three parts — the profile, the investment plan, and the advanced-planning plan — and the third part is a living tracker that is presented at the first Regular Progress Meeting and revisited at every one after. This spec defines what the document contains, how it is written, and how often it is refreshed.

Purpose

  • Give the client one integrated view of everything the practice is doing and proposing across investments, tax, transfer, protection, and giving.
  • Give the Advisor and the expert network a single prioritized list of actions, each with an owner, a status, and a next step, so nothing is lost between meetings.
  • Make the plan safe to present: every recommendation has a rationale, an expert, a consequence check, and a client decision recorded against it.

Contents

Part 0 — Cover and scope banner

  • Client(s) and households or entities covered; plan version and date; the mode and scope rung from T05.
  • Scope banner: one paragraph stating what the plan covers and what it does not (for example, trusts administered by another fiduciary, assets managed by the family's central team). Mode B: every Part 3 section is tagged in scope / family-team-owned / coordination-only.
  • The one-page "big picture": the four areas with their completed, in-progress, and future items on a single page (T10 summary block).

Part 1 — Total Client Profile summary

The seven areas of SOP 11 in one to two pages: values, goals, relationships, assets (including held-away assets and where they sit), advisors, process preference, interests. In Mode A, the family-level map is summarized here and the household detail sits in an appendix.

Part 2 — Investment plan

A pointer to the investment plan and IPS (SOP 13, T06) with the current version date and any changes since the last plan. Do not duplicate the IPS here.

Part 3 — Advanced-planning plan

One section per area, each with the same structure:

  1. Definition (Bowen's four areas, in the practice's words): wealth enhancement — the best return consistent with the client's risk tolerance after tax; wealth transfer — passing assets to the next generations tax-efficiently and in the way the client wants; wealth protection — shielding the family from creditors, litigants, divorcing spouses, and catastrophic loss; charitable planning — fulfilling the family's giving intentions, often while supporting the other three.
  2. Current situation — two to five sentences from the profile and the documents reviewed.
  3. Recommendations, prioritized by the impact each would have on the client's life, each with: the recommendation; the expert responsible (ISB / EEN / COA); the rationale; the consequence check (what could go wrong, who is affected); the client decision — drop / defer / do (Mode B: refer to family team); the status — completed / in progress / future; a SMART next step with owner and date.
  4. Open questions for counsel or the family — items the practice cannot decide.

The four areas are not silos; the plan cross-references items that belong to two areas (a trust that is both transfer and protection).

Agenda menus by area

The following are checklists of what to consider, not recommendations. Each item enters the plan only after the expert-network meeting (SOP 32) and counsel where required.

Beyond Bowen — wealth enhancement menu

Investor allocation: which family member or entity holds which asset, matched to the 20 / 50 / 100-year horizons (SOP 47) · family bank and intra-family loans, documented arm's-length with counsel · a tax-drag and fee audit across all managers and structures · deferral over income where the client's goals allow · reserve mechanisms in trusts for recurring obligations.

Beyond Bowen — wealth transfer menu

Estate-tax exposure above the exemption and the generation-skipping picture · gift versus transfer: purpose, message, and the recipient's readiness decided before the vehicle · who-before-what: the giver's own goals, then the recipient, then the structure · the equality default and early, clear communication of any exception · staged disclosure: existence and purpose of structures first, numbers later · a preamble or letter of wishes and purpose language beyond the standard distribution formula · a one-page plain-language summary and a communication plan for every new trust, gift, or plan (T21) · the do-no-harm consequences check and the perpetual-trust counterweight conversation before any dynasty or long-term structure · addiction and behavioral-health provisions reviewed with counsel · fund growth assets into trusts before they appreciate · for counsel's consideration: leveraged sale to a trust, intentionally defective grantor trust, valuation discounts, trust situs review · the insurance-objections checklist as devil's advocate for any ILIT or premium-finance proposal (fees compounding, long-horizon certainty, counterparty lock-in, cash payouts consumed) · business succession, including the ESOP path assessed with [ESOP Co.].

Beyond Bowen — wealth protection menu

The humane trustscape: distribution committee, office of the beneficiary, a narrow mediative protector, institutional trustee (SOP 46, SOP 48) · protector provisions and a workable trustee-succession mechanism · the prenuptial process — months before the wedding, disclosure of trust interests, family policy set in advance · asset-protection structures with counsel · property and casualty review, identity-theft exposure, personal security · jurisdictional and residency review as a counsel-only conversation; expatriation is out of scope · family properties treated as an identity anchor: a property map, a policy against dividing them, and a plan for who uses and maintains them.

Beyond Bowen — charitable planning menu

Placement rules: a section on the family's responsibility to the outside world in the mission statement; the share of financial and qualitative capital devoted to giving on the family balance sheet; a formal vehicle broad enough for every member to participate · the seven readiness questions (tradition, obligation or choice, organizations supported, sectors, board roles, giving at death, giving as much as wished) · donor-advised fund versus private foundation · a grandchild–grandparent giving program with age-scaled participation · young-adult engagement rules: open process, minimal restrictions, subjects that draw them in, let a disappointing grant teach · philanthropy as the family's governance rehearsal.

Part 4 — Decision log and next steps

A dated log of every client decision (drop / defer / do / refer) with the reasoning recorded at the meeting, and a consolidated next-steps table by owner and date.

Part 5 — Appendix

Expert-network contributors and their roles; documents reviewed (returns, estate documents, trust instruments, policies, entity documents); glossary of structures named in the plan; Mode A: the household-level profiles.

Standards

  • Length: the big picture fits one page; Part 3 is as long as the family's situation requires but each recommendation fits half a page.
  • Language: plain English; every structure is named in the glossary; no product names in the body.
  • Completeness: no recommendation without an expert, a rationale, a consequence check, and a next step. "Establish additional priorities" is a legitimate future item in each area.
  • Ownership: the Advisor is the author and quarterback; experts contribute sections and are named; the client hires the attorney directly and legal fees are never shared.
  • Review: peer-reviewed by a second professional and signed off by the LA before presentation; drafted from the expert-network meeting output, never from a single specialist's proposal.
  • Disclosure: any fee or commission arrangement with a contributing expert is disclosed in the plan and cleared with [Firm Compliance].
  • Confidentiality: the plan respects the consent matrix on T05 / T14; Mode A household detail is not circulated to other households.
  • Sequence: the plan is presented only at a Regular Progress Meeting (SOP 20); nothing in it is executed before counsel and the consequences check.

Refresh cadence

  • Tracker (T10) updated within 48 hours of every RPM and every expert-network meeting.
  • Full plan re-issued annually, or on any trigger in SOP 22 (liquidity event, death or incapacity, marriage, business sale, relocation).
  • Part 1 refreshed whenever the profile changes; Part 2 on the annual IPS review.

Owner

LA owns the document; AA maintains the tracker and drafts sections from expert input; CSA files each version to the [Document vault] and the client notebook (T08).

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The plan has a family level (structures, governance items, philanthropy, family bank) and household levels; family-level items are presented at the annual family meeting (SOP 43) and tracked on the family-level T10.
  • Trust items are routed through the trustee relationship in SOP 46; the family's other advisors are named in Part 5 and coordinated under SOP 33.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The scope banner is mandatory; each Part 3 section carries an in scope / family-team-owned / coordination-only tag from T05.
  • Items touching family-level structures are written as questions or recommendations for the FCT or family counsel, never as actions the Advisor will execute.
  • Distribution of the plan follows the consent on T05; family-team-owned sections may be shared with the FCT only when the individual has authorized it.

31 Expert network — build, vet, and maintain

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — building the professional network: minimum core, extended roster, four traits, compensation sidebar, keeping the network running well; Ch. 7 — partner selection questions, anti-captivity rule, annual review of external relationships · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 9 — counselor/coach selection criteria and the two-meeting trial; personne de confiance qualities; Family Trusts Ch. 20-21 and App. 3 — Distribution Committee and Office of the Beneficiary boundaries; conflicts acknowledged, documented, disclosed, managed; Family Wealth Ch. 3 — welcoming ritual for new advisers · Other: Palaveev — internal cross-referral economics, written terms for shared resources, six vendor questions; Extension — the Internal Specialist Bench roster and scorecard are ours

31 — Expert network

Advanced planning cannot be delivered by one person. This procedure builds the team of specialists the Advisor brings to each family — an external core, an extended external roster, and the sister-company bench inside [Firm] — vets them, puts them on written terms, and keeps them working as one team with the Advisor in charge.

Purpose

  • Put the two core external experts in place before advanced planning is promised to any family.
  • Turn [Firm]'s trust, ESOP, tax, insurance, and lending capabilities into a named, scored, on-call bench.
  • Fix the rules of engagement: the clients are the Advisor's, fees are disclosed, conflicts are managed, and no expert becomes a client's default contact.

Trigger

  • The practice commits to offering advanced planning (initial build).
  • A Total Client Profile or network meeting reveals a need no current member can meet.
  • A member fails a review, leaves, or a conflict cannot be managed.
  • Annually, on the service calendar (T15), for the review of every external relationship.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (roster, scorecards, written terms on file, disclosure filings), AA (shortlist research, reference calls, brief preparation) · Consulted: [Firm Compliance] (licensing, fee sharing, disclosures), sister-company leaders for bench nominations.

Timing

Stage Target
Core two external members identified and on terms before the first family is told advanced planning is part of the service
Internal bench mapped within 30 days of this SOP's adoption; refreshed each quarter
Extended roster built need by need, each within 60 days of the need appearing
Vetting one candidate shortlist to decision in 4–6 weeks; trial matter within the following quarter
Annual review Q3 on the service calendar, before the Q4 planning cycle

Inputs

  • The four advanced-planning areas (wealth enhancement, transfer, protection, charitable) and the issues currently open across all families (T10 trackers).
  • [Firm]'s directory of sister companies and their specialists; [Firm Compliance] rules on fee sharing, gifts, and licensing.
  • Existing relationships: the client's own advisors (mapped on T05) — potential members, never automatically excluded.
  • Referrals from other advisors and from the clients' own professionals.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Needs inventory: for each family, which of the four areas has an open item that needs expertise the practice does not hold.
  • [ ] Bench nominations requested from each sister company with a one-paragraph description of what the practice needs from them.
  • [ ] Vetting interview guide and reference-call script ready (below).
  • [ ] Written-terms template reviewed by [Firm Compliance].
  • [ ] Roster and scorecard set up in [CRM].

Procedure

Build

  1. Define the network from the clients' needs, not the market. List the open issues by area; group them into capabilities. Every capability gets exactly one route: core external member, extended external member, internal bench, or the client's own advisor.
  2. Fill the core two first. A private-client attorney who is a partner in a high-end boutique (not a trust officer inside a bank or insurer) and a truly independent insurance specialist who receives no carrier incentives. The attorney addresses tax, estate, and legal questions; the insurance specialist works alongside the attorney on risk-transfer structures. Until both are on terms, advanced planning is described to clients as "coordinated," not "delivered."

  3. Map the Internal Specialist Bench. For each sister company, name the person, what they solve, how to engage them (SOP 71), the economics [Firm] applies, and the confidentiality wall if that company also serves a client's family centrally.

    Bench member Solves Typical trigger
    [Trust Co.] — trust officer / fiduciary lead trust administration, trustee services, distribution process, trust reviews any trust in the family map; SOP 46 and 48
    [ESOP Co.] — transaction lead business succession and liquidity via an employee-ownership sale a closely held business with no successor or a sale under consideration
    Sister RIA — planning analyst plan modelling, IPS drafting capacity, second-chair analysis capacity gaps before the first hire (SOP 70)
    Tax specialist complex income tax, entity structure, state residency multi-entity families; a liquidity event
    Insurance / risk property-casualty review, liability exposure wealth-protection items on T10
    Lending intra-family and secured credit structuring investor allocation and family-bank funding (SOP 47)

  4. Extend the external roster as needs appear. Rely on the core two to bring in their own experts first (an actuary behind the insurance specialist, a corporate tax lawyer or valuation specialist behind the attorney). Add a direct member only where the practice will use them more than once a year: credit, corporate tax, derivatives and concentrated-stock strategies, securities law, income tax, actuary, valuation.

    Beyond Bowen

    Families at this level need members Bowen's roster does not include: a family-governance facilitator for first family meetings, mission sessions, and crises; a counselor or coach for individual members; people able to sit on a Distribution Committee (advising a trustee, never deciding) or in an Office of the Beneficiary (chosen and paid by the beneficiary — never housed inside a family office or inside [Firm]). Vet these on the personne-de-confiance qualities: an interest in the family's culture, belief in orderly evolutionary change, and willingness to be a "number two."

Vet

  1. Shortlist five. Sources: the core members' own recommendations, other advisors, professional bodies, the clients' existing advisors. Never run a one-candidate search.
  2. Interview for the four traits — specific expertise, integrity, professionalism, chemistry — plus the practice's own fit. Ask:
    • Describe the last three matters like ours you handled; what did the client decide and why?
    • How do you work when another professional quarterbacks the relationship?
    • Whom do you bring in when a matter is outside your depth, and how are they paid?
    • How do you communicate with clients between milestones?
    • What would make you decline a matter we send?
    • How are you compensated on the work we would send, in full?
    • What does a family that is unhappy with you say about you?
  3. Check references the candidate did not choose. Ask each reference whom else the candidate works with, then call those firms; ask a client-side reference how the candidate handled a disagreement.

  4. Run a trial. A meaningful but not mission-critical matter, or — for counselors, coaches, and facilitators — the two-meeting trial: two sessions to assess fit on both sides before any standing engagement; either party may stop without cost.

    Beyond Bowen

    Counselor / coach selection criteria: training; a medically accepted license where the work touches mental health; experience in both practice and counseling; a match between that experience and the family's actual challenge. Readiness on the client side matters as much as the professional's credentials.

Onboard

  1. Put the relationship in writing. Scope of what the practice will send; the rule that the Advisor remains the client's point of contact and decision coordinator; communication protocol (who contacts the client, cc rules, turnaround); confidentiality and the internal wall where relevant; compensation and disclosure; conflicts declared at signing; how either side ends the relationship.

  2. Welcome the member into how the practice works. A one-hour session on the consultative process, the five-meeting sequence, the family layer, the trackers, and the network-meeting format (SOP 32). Introduce them to the CSA who will schedule and chase.

    Beyond Bowen

    Mark the arrival of a new adviser with a small ritual — an introduction at the next network meeting and, for a family-facing member, a named introduction to the family at the next meeting. People who are formally welcomed perform their roles better.

  3. Add to the roster and open a scorecard: responsiveness, quality of work, client feedback, fee transparency, willingness to collaborate, conflicts declared. Score after every matter.

Maintain

  1. Run the quarterly network meeting (SOP 32). This is where the team bonds and where most disagreement about approach is worked out before it reaches a client.
  2. Keep the network running well — five rules: hold a common vision (comprehensive, client-centered work with capable peers and fair reward); be clear who is in charge (the clients are the Advisor's; the Advisor decides what is best for them); formalize how and when members communicate; improve the meetings by asking members for feedback; keep members motivated by making sure good work becomes income for them.
  3. Review every external relationship annually. Six questions per member: is the fit still strategic; exclusive or one of several, and what does that cost or buy; how concentrated is our business with them and does it buy priority; how durable are they (ownership change, retirement, exit); how much do they customize for us; how do clients perceive them? Never become captive — keep the practice's own process even where a member does most of the work.
  4. Maintain the conflicts register. For every member: the conflict (fee sharing, dual roles, sister-company relationships, drafting attorney named as trustee), the management step, who has been told. Acknowledge, document, disclose to all affected parties, manage — never assume away.
  5. Replace or remove when a scorecard falls below standard for two matters, a conflict becomes unmanageable, or a client asks. Do it directly and respectfully, in writing, with a handover of open items.

Follow-up

  • Within one week of any new member joining: written terms signed, roster updated, disclosure filed with [Firm Compliance], introduction scheduled.
  • Within one week of every matter closing: scorecard updated; client feedback captured at the next progress meeting.
  • Annually: review results and roster changes recorded; conflicts register re-confirmed; the family told of any change that affects them (SOP 21 first-to-know rule).

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Network roster (core, extended, internal bench) with engagement path and economics [CRM] · shared with the team CSA
Written terms per external member [Document vault] — practice records LA
Scorecards [CRM] CSA
Conflicts register and disclosures [CRM] · copy to [Firm Compliance] LA
Annual review memo practice records LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Have the core two in place before promising advanced planning.
  • Let the core members bring their own sub-experts before adding direct members.
  • Disclose every fee arrangement to the client in writing; keep the practice properly licensed for anything it is paid on.
  • Charge a premium for the investment work that carries the coordination, and a project fee for strategies with no product.

Don't

  • Don't accept any share of legal fees — the client hires the attorney directly.
  • Don't use an insurance specialist who is incented by a carrier.
  • Don't let a member become the client's primary contact, or contact a client outside the agreed protocol.
  • Don't house an Office of the Beneficiary inside [Firm] or a family office; the beneficiary owns it.

Compensation and disclosure norms

Typical arrangements: a split of insurance commissions between the practice and the specialist; a finder's fee or points on credit; a share of commissions on derivative transactions; no share of legal fees ever. All of it is disclosed to the client, approved by [Firm Compliance], and recorded on the conflicts register. Internal cross-referral economics inside [Firm] follow firm policy and are always set below what an external referral source would receive.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The client's incumbent CPA and attorney are candidates for the network, not competitors; invite them into the standing advisory board (SOP 33).
  • Family-facing members (facilitator, counselor) are introduced through the family map's communication rules (T14).

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The family's counsel and trust company are the private-client attorney and the fiduciary. The practice's network fills gaps only, with the FCT's knowledge, and never duplicates a role the FCT already holds.
  • Any fee sharing is disclosed to the individual and, where the FCT gatekeeps professional relationships, to the FCT.
  • Where a sister company of [Firm] sits on the FCT, the internal wall is stated in the written terms and in the scope memo (T25).

Metrics

  • Core two on terms: yes/no (a gating metric).
  • Share of open advanced-planning items with a named expert assigned within 30 days.
  • Average scorecard across members; number of unmanaged conflicts (target zero).

32 Expert-network meeting — quarterly case review

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the wealth management network meeting: quarterly to monthly cadence, agenda in advance, one to six clients per meeting, scenario thinking, the advanced-planning mind map coded completed / in progress / future, bringing the expert to the progress meeting · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 1 — five capitals as part of the case picture; Family Trusts Ch. 17 — transition points that should trigger review · Other: Extension — the named UHNW scenario prompts and the case-brief format are ours

32 — Expert-network meeting

The quarterly meeting at which the Advisor presents one to six families to the expert network and leaves with a draft advanced-planning map for each. It is the engine behind Part 3 of every wealth management plan and the place where the network becomes a team.

Purpose

  • Convert each family's Total Client Profile into prioritized, expert-assigned actions across wealth enhancement, transfer, protection, and charitable planning.
  • Give every family the benefit of several specialists thinking together, without the family paying for a roomful of hourly time.
  • Bond the network through regular, structured collaboration.

Trigger

  • Standing: quarterly on the service calendar (T15), monthly if the family count justifies it.
  • Gating: the two core external members (SOP 31) are on terms.
  • Per family: a family's investment plan has been accepted (CCM3) and its first advanced-planning plan is due for the first progress meeting; or a life event on T10 or in SOP 22 opens a new set of questions.

Roles

Owner: LA (facilitates; presents every case) · Does: AA (case briefs, scenario worksheet, draft map), CSA (agenda circulation, attendance, minutes, follow-up tasks) · Consulted: EEN members, ISB members invited for the cases that need them.

Timing

When What
T−3 weeks Families selected (one to six); consent confirmed for each; experts invited by need
T−2 weeks Case briefs drafted by the AA from the Total Client Profile and T10
T−1 week Agenda and briefs circulated (T09); conflicts declaration requested
T+0 Meeting — 90 minutes for up to three families; half a day for six
T+3 days Draft advanced-planning map per family sent to the assigned experts for correction
T+2 weeks Map finalized; recommendations scheduled into each family's next progress meeting

Inputs

  • Total Client Profile (SOP 11) and, in Mode A, the family map and five-capitals summary (T14, SOP 44).
  • The current tracker (T10) — what is completed, in progress, or planned.
  • Consent status on T05 / T14: which facts may be shared, and whether the brief must be anonymized.
  • Prior-quarter statements and the investment plan's scope banner (SOP 13).
  • Open questions raised by the client at the last progress meeting.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Case list agreed: which families, in what order, and the one decision each case needs.
  • [ ] Case briefs (T09) complete: seven areas in summary, structures, issues, and the questions for the network — one page each.
  • [ ] Anonymization applied where consent is limited; names replaced by case codes in circulated material.
  • [ ] Experts confirmed for each case; the attorney and insurance specialist attend every meeting.
  • [ ] Conflicts declaration collected from each attending member.
  • [ ] Agenda circulated with time allotted per case.
  • [ ] Video or phone bridge tested; in person for the first two meetings with any new member.

Procedure

  1. Open (5 minutes). Restate the purpose — decisions and priorities for the families on the list — and the confidentiality rule for the room. Confirm conflicts declarations.
  2. Present the case (LA, 10 minutes). Walk the one-page brief: who the family is, what they value and want, the structures in place, the issues, and the specific questions. Do not present solutions.
  3. Identify the key issues (all, 10 minutes). Let each expert name what they see from their discipline; the AA records issues on the scenario worksheet.
  4. Build scenarios (15 minutes). For the two or three issues that matter most: what happens if the family does nothing; what happens under each credible course of action; what the family has said they care about that constrains the answer.
  5. Identify opportunities (10 minutes). Concrete actions per area — enhancement, transfer, protection, charitable — with the expert who would carry each.

  6. Prioritize (5 minutes). Rank by impact on the family's stated goals, then by urgency and cost. Mark each as completed / in progress / future on the draft map. Prioritization is the Advisor's call; the experts advise.

    Beyond Bowen

    Scenario prompts to run when they apply: a liquidity event ahead (sale, IPO, settlement); a concentrated position; business succession, including whether an employee-ownership sale through [ESOP Co.] fits; a generational transition in leadership or ownership; a member marrying in (prenuptial timing, disclosure of trust interests); incapacity of a principal; a trust termination or large distribution within ten years; family-office formation. Add the family's five-capitals picture to the brief: an action that grows only financial capital while draining human or social capital is not a good recommendation.

  7. Assign owners and next steps (5 minutes). Every "in progress" or "future" item gets an expert, a next step, and a date. Decide which items warrant the expert joining the family's next progress meeting in person or by video.

  8. Close the case by reading back the draft map. Move to the next family.
  9. Close the meeting: five minutes for what worked and what to change next time; schedule the next meeting.

  10. Debrief (LA and AA, same day): finalize the draft maps, note anything to tell the family before the progress meeting so there are no surprises.

    Say something like

    "For this family, if we could only get one thing done this year, which item would you choose and why?"

Follow-up

  • Within three days: draft maps to assigned experts for correction; minutes to attendees.
  • Within two weeks: maps final; T10 updated; each family's next progress meeting agenda updated with the items to present and which expert attends.
  • Before each progress meeting: the LA calls any expert who will present to align on how the recommendation will be framed.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Case briefs and scenario worksheets (T09) practice records; case codes only if anonymized AA
Draft and final advanced-planning map per family T10 in [CRM] and the client's [Document vault] AA
Expert assignments with dates [CRM] tasks CSA
Meeting minutes and conflicts declarations practice records CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Present the family, not a product; let the room find the solutions.
  • Keep to one to six families per meeting; depth over coverage.
  • Bring the relevant expert into the family's meeting for complex structures rather than relaying their advice second-hand.
  • Ask members every quarter how to make the meeting better.

Don't

  • Don't circulate identifiable client detail beyond what consent allows.
  • Don't let an expert take a recommendation directly to the family before the Advisor has presented the map.
  • Don't turn the meeting into a pitch session for any member's products.
  • Don't skip a quarter because "nothing changed" — transitions are usually visible in the room before the family names them.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Family-level items (governance, family bank, trusts across households) are presented as family cases; household-level items as household cases, with the family map's confidentiality matrix (T14) governing what each expert sees.
  • Recommendations that touch family structures are routed through the family council or the annual family meeting (SOP 43), not to individual members.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • B-full: run the meeting scoped to the mandate; the brief is anonymized and limited to the individual's own affairs; anything touching family structures becomes a question for family counsel, framed as a recommendation to take to the FCT.
  • B-partial: the case is reviewed only if the FCT invites the practice's input; otherwise an annual internal scoping check replaces the network review.
  • B-narrow: not run; the mandate is delivered and reported.

Metrics

  • Families reviewed per quarter against families due.
  • Share of "in progress" items with an owner and a date (target 100%).
  • Median days from meeting to final map (target ≤ 14).

33 Coordinating with outside advisors — the family's central team and incumbent professionals

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — relationship management's three tasks, including working with the advisors the client already has and other advisors managing other parts of their finances · Hughes: Family Wealth Ch. 8 — the family's advisers convened as a board with a facilitator at the first meeting; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 2 and Ch. 9 — annual owners meeting with all advisers present; one-page summary and communication plan to ask advisers for; The Compact — the family council as the family's voice to outside professionals; Family Trusts Ch. 16 — the translator role between family and adversarial counsel · Other: Palaveev — never assign blame; whoever receives the request owns it; Extension — the protocol itself is ours; Bowen names the task without a method

33 — Coordinating with outside advisors

Every family at this level already has professionals, and the largest have a central team — a family office, a trust company, counsel, a lead advisor. Bowen names working with them as one of the three tasks of relationship management but gives no method. This procedure is the method, written first for Mode B (where the Advisor serves individuals inside a family with its own team) and then for Mode A (where he coordinates the family's incumbent professionals himself).

Purpose

  • Make the Advisor a reliable, low-friction colleague to the family's central team so that his individuals get better outcomes and the FCT never feels bypassed.
  • Give the client one thread of communication, one map of who does what, and no surprises from any direction.
  • Handle disagreement between advisors privately and let the client decide.

Trigger

  • Engagement scoping (T05) identifies an FCT or incumbent advisors — before CCM2 in every new engagement.
  • A new advisor enters the picture (new counsel, a family office is formed, a trustee changes).
  • Any recommendation on T10 touches something another advisor owns.
  • A service failure or dispute involves another advisor.
  • Quarterly, by the coordination call; annually, by the advisor-map review.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (advisor map upkeep, consent letters, call scheduling, cc discipline), AA (data packages, reconciliation of positions between advisors) · Consulted: [Firm Compliance] on any information-sharing question; the FCT contact.

Timing

Step When
Advisor map drafted after CCM1, before CCM2
Introductions and consent letter between CCM2 and CCM3; confirmed in the engagement letter
Communication protocol agreed within 30 days of CCM3
Coordination call quarterly, two weeks before the client's progress meeting
Advisor-map review annually at the first progress meeting of the year

Inputs

  • T05 Parts 2, 4, and 5: who the client is, what may be shared, and the counterparties.
  • The Total Client Profile's Advisors area (SOP 11): what has worked and not worked with each advisor.
  • The scope banner of the investment plan (SOP 13) and the area tags on the wealth management plan (SOP 30).
  • Documents the client has authorized us to receive from other advisors: trust instruments, family investment policy, entity charts, prior plans.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Advisor map drafted: for each advisor — name, firm, function, what they own for this client, how they prefer to communicate, and whether the client wants us in contact with them.
  • [ ] Consent letter drafted from T05 Part 4 for the client to sign, naming what we may share with whom and what we may receive.
  • [ ] The three questions answered on T05 (who pays, who is the client, who advocates for the rising generation).
  • [ ] Any conflict between the practice or a sister company and an outside advisor logged in the conflicts register (SOP 31).

Procedure

Mode B first — the Family Central Team

  1. Map the advisors. Complete the advisor map from CCM1 and T05. Distinguish who owns a function (decides), who executes it, and who is informed. Confirm the map with the client before contacting anyone.

  2. Let the client make the introductions. Ask the client to introduce the Advisor to the FCT contact by a short message or a three-way call. Never introduce yourself to a family's central team unannounced.

    Say something like

    "So your family office is never surprised by anything we do, would you introduce me to the person there who coordinates your affairs? A short note from you is all it needs."

  3. Send the consent letter. One page, signed by the client, stating what the practice may share with the FCT and receive from it, for what purpose, and for how long. Copy to [Firm Compliance]. Nothing is shared before it is signed.

  4. Hold a first coordination call. Purpose: state the mandate (scope rung from T05), learn the FCT's own process and calendar, agree the communication protocol, exchange the documents each side needs (family investment policy and trust constraints inbound; the individual's IPS scope banner outbound), and identify anything already under way that affects the individual.
  5. Write the communication protocol. Who contacts whom for what; single thread per topic; cc rules (the client is copied on substantive exchanges unless they have asked otherwise); turnaround expectations; how urgent matters are escalated; what is confidential from the FCT under the client's consent.
  6. Coordinate before acting. Any recommendation touching a family structure is drafted as a recommendation to take to family counsel or the FCT, presented to the client that way, and — with consent — previewed with the FCT before the client's progress meeting. The FCT should never learn of a recommendation from the client after the fact.
  7. Run the quarterly coordination call. Twenty minutes, two weeks before the client's progress meeting: changes on either side, items in flight, calendar for the family (meetings, reviews, tax deadlines), anything the FCT needs from the practice's reporting (SOP 24).
  8. Handle disagreement privately. If the practice disagrees with an FCT position, raise it with the FCT first, in writing, with the analysis; document both positions; present both to the client neutrally; the client decides. Never argue the point in front of the client, and never assign blame for another advisor's failure — the practice still owns recovery for its client (SOP 23).
  9. Review the map annually and on every trigger in SOP 22: new advisors, departures, changes in who decides.

Mode A — the family's incumbent professionals

  1. Map and meet the incumbents. The client's CPA, attorney, other managers, and trustees. Ask what has worked and what has not; state that the practice's role is to coordinate, not replace, and that the client has authorized contact.

  2. Convene the advisers as a standing advisory board. Propose to the family that its outside advisers meet together once or twice a year with the Advisor as convener. Bring a professional facilitator to the first meeting so that professional defensiveness does not derail it. Agenda: the family's goals in the advisers' words; the map of who owns what; open items across the four planning areas; the calendar.

    Beyond Bowen

    Families are routinely surprised that their advisers have never met; when they do, problems no single adviser could solve get solved. The first joint meeting sets the tone — hence the facilitator. This is Bowen's expert network convened as the family's own board rather than issue by issue.

  3. Use the annual owners meeting. Where the family holds an annual owners or family meeting (SOP 43), invite all advisers for the relevant portion so owners know whom to call for what. Provide each adviser's one-page summary of anything new they have done for the family, in plain language, with a communication plan (T21).

  4. Work through the family council when one exists (SOP 45): it is the family's voice to outside professionals; the Advisor coordinates the advisers on the council's behalf and reports to it, without displacing individual households' direct relationships.
  5. Act as translator in adversarial processes. In prenuptial negotiations or contested estate matters, help the family articulate its positive intent and convey it to both sets of lawyers, so legal process does not damage the relationship the structures are meant to protect (SOP 22, SOP 46).

Follow-up

  • Within one week of each coordination call: notes to the FCT contact and the client; tasks in [CRM]; advisor map updated.
  • Before each progress meeting: the LA checks that every recommendation touching another advisor's domain has been previewed with them.
  • Annually: advisor map and consent letter re-confirmed with the client; conflicts register updated.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Advisor map [CRM] client record; copy in T05 Part 5 CSA
Consent letter [Document vault]; copy to [Firm Compliance] LA
Communication protocol [CRM] client record; shared with the FCT CSA
Coordination call notes [CRM] activities CSA
Disagreement memos (both positions) [Document vault] LA
Advisory board agendas and minutes (Mode A) [Document vault] CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Let the client introduce you; let the client decide when advisors disagree.
  • Preview anything that touches another advisor's domain with them before the client hears it.
  • Keep one thread per topic and copy the client on substance.
  • Ask the FCT what they need from the practice, not only what the practice needs from them.

Don't

  • Don't share anything the consent letter does not cover, including the existence of the relationship.
  • Don't solicit assets managed by the FCT or a sister company of [Firm] (SOP 50).
  • Don't let a coordination failure become the client's problem to referee.
  • Don't take a family-structure recommendation to the family without counsel's knowledge.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The Advisor is the coordinator; incumbent professionals may join the expert network (SOP 31) with the client's agreement.
  • The standing advisory board (step 11) and the annual owners meeting (step 12) are the two coordination forums; the family council, where it exists, is the interface.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Steps 1–9 in full. The scope rung sets the depth: B-full — quarterly call and preview of every structure-touching item; B-partial — quarterly call and participation in the FCT's process on invitation; B-narrow — reporting to the mandate's owner on the agreed schedule and nothing more.
  • On the death or incapacity of a principal, the FCT leads; the Advisor supports his individuals and follows the FCT's communication plan.

Metrics

  • Advisor map current for every client (annual review completed).
  • Share of structure-touching recommendations previewed with the relevant advisor before the client meeting (target 100%).
  • Disagreements escalated to the client without a written two-position memo (target zero).

Family layer — Mode A

40 Family engagement model — who the client is, the family map, and the Advisor's stance

specOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — Relationships, Advisors and Process areas of the Total Client Profile; both names in the center for a couple · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 2 — family of affinity; Ch. 9 — who pays, who is the client, who advocates for the rising generation; The Compact — personne de confiance conduct: confidentiality for hyperagent families, never mediate a marriage, do nothing most of the time, small joint successes first; Family Wealth Ch. 8 — the homme d'affaires; Ch. 18 — the family council as the family's executive · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes Ch. 8 — a family office exists only once assets are formally designated as family rather than personal; council-level policies set in advance

40 — Family engagement model

When the whole family is under the Advisor's umbrella (Mode A), the unit of engagement is no longer a household but a multi-household system with entities, trusts, generations, and in-laws. This spec fixes what the practice must know and agree about that system before it runs the consultative sequence on it, and how the Advisor conducts himself inside it.

Purpose

  • Define who the client is when the client is a family.
  • Standardize the family map and the four matrices (decision rights, confidentiality, communication, transitions) that every family-layer procedure reads from and writes to (T14).
  • State the Advisor's stance — the conduct that makes a family willing to let one outside professional see the whole picture.
  • Draw the boundary between what the practice runs and what it refers.

Contents

1. Who is the client

  • One relationship, several clients. The family is served as one relationship, but the clients are named people and named entities. Every household gets its own engagement letter; every entity and trust has a named decision-maker recorded on T14. "The family" never signs anything.
  • Three questions, answered in writing on T05 and reviewed annually: who pays the fee; who is the client; who is advocating for the rising generation. If the first two answers are the senior generation and the third is "no one," the Advisor raises it with the principals before the plan is built — the rising generation's interests must have a voice, and if no one else holds it, the Advisor says so.
  • When governance exists (a family council, an assembly, a family office), the council is the Advisor's institutional counterparty for family-level matters. Individual households remain clients in their own right, with their own confidentiality.
  • A couple is one client unit with two people who may each speak directly with the Advisor. Either spouse may hold something in confidence from the other only where the engagement letter says so and [Firm Compliance] has approved.

2. Family of affinity — the working definition

The practice defines the family the way the family defines itself: descendants of a named ancestor and the people the family has chosen to include — spouses and partners, adopted members, and, where the family says so, long-serving trusted advisers. The test is shared purpose and a felt sense of belonging, not bloodline alone. Practical consequences:

  • Both surnames appear at the head of a couple's file and agenda.
  • In-laws are included in learning and in meetings by default (see SOP 43); the family's own policy on spouses, set in advance, governs exceptions.
  • A member who has formally left (divorce, estrangement, a written exit) is removed from the map and the matrices at the next review; an ex-spouse with an ongoing interest through children or a trust is recorded as a counterparty, not a member.

3. The family map

The map (T14, Part 1) lists every member with: generation, household, roles held, entities and trusts in which they have an interest or a power, and contact preference. Roles are assigned per person, and one person usually holds several:

Role Meaning in this practice
Principal A wealth creator or senior holder whose decisions set the family's direction
Household lead The member who speaks for a household's day-to-day financial matters
Decision-maker The person empowered to instruct on a named entity or account
Trustee / protector / committee member A fiduciary or advisory role in a trust or family entity
Beneficiary A current, contingent, or remainder interest in a trust
Elder Recognized by the family for mediation, memory, and ritual (not simply the oldest)
Council member Elected or appointed to a family governing body
Rising generation Any member still forming an identity and calling apart from the wealth — not defined by age

The entity and trust map (T14, Part 2) draws the trustscape: each entity and trust, its purpose, trustee, beneficiaries, protector, advisors, and next review date. Together the two maps are the family-level layer of the Total Client Profile (SOP 11).

4. Decision rights

A matrix (T14, Part 3) states, for every recurring matter, who decides and who is consulted: investment policy for each pool; distributions from each trust; sale or financing of a family asset; a new family loan; hiring or dismissing a family advisor; who attends family meetings; what the rising generation is told and when. Where the family has never decided this, the Advisor records the de facto answer, labels it as such, and raises it at the next family meeting. Principle: members are bound by rules they helped make; the Advisor never invents decision rights on the family's behalf.

5. Confidentiality matrix

  • Default: private per adult. Nothing an adult tells the Advisor is shared upward, sideways, or with a trustee or a family office without that adult's written, specific consent recorded on T14 (Part 4).
  • Opt-in sharing. Consent states what may be shared (existence of the relationship; plan; values; recaps; personal circumstances), with whom, and for what purpose. Summary-only is a valid setting.
  • Structural knowledge is family knowledge. The existence and terms of trusts, entities, and family policies are shared with every adult member entitled to know them under the family's own rules; the Advisor encourages staged disclosure rather than secrecy, and never becomes the instrument by which one branch keeps another uninformed.
  • Inside [Firm]. Where a sister company serves a trust or another branch, the same wall applies between the Advisor's team and that company's staff; the scope memo (T25) states it.

6. Communication map

For each household: the primary contact, the process preference of each member (channel, frequency, meeting cadence — honored for the life of the relationship), who is copied on what, and who you call for what inside the practice (LA, SA, CSA). For the family as a whole: who convenes, who circulates minutes, and how the Advisor's team is told about births, deaths, marriages, illnesses, and moves. The map lives in T14 (Part 5) and is mirrored in each household's contact plan (SOP 21).

7. Conflict rule

Family members' interests diverge — senior and rising generations, trustee and beneficiary, one branch and another, a spouse and a family of origin. The rule:

  1. Name it. The moment the Advisor sees that serving one member well could disadvantage another, he says so to both, in general terms that respect confidentiality.
  2. Hold the whole. The Advisor's fidelity is to the family relationship and to each client's stated interests, not to whoever pays the largest fee or speaks loudest.
  3. Separate when needed. If the conflict cannot be held by one professional — a divorce, a contested distribution, a business buy-out between siblings — the Advisor arranges separate representation for the member(s) affected and continues for the rest only with everyone's informed agreement, documented and cleared with [Firm Compliance].
  4. Never mediate a marriage. The relationship between spouses is not the Advisor's to mediate; he refers to a qualified professional and steps back.

8. The Advisor's stance

The role the family needs is closer to a trusted counsellor than a product provider. The practice says which it is selling — knowledge and products, or the courage and judgment that help a family act on what it already knows — and never markets one while delivering the other. Conduct that follows:

  • Do nothing, most of the time. Many family problems resolve with time and new information; the Advisor's first instinct is to wait, ask, and let the family work, intervening only when waiting would do harm.
  • Small joint successes first. Before the family faces its hardest question, engineer a few decisions it can make together and win — a shared giving decision, a modest family loan, a meeting that ends on time with minutes.
  • Confidentiality as a security measure. The Advisor does not acknowledge a client family in public, does not discuss one family with another, and tells families at the outset that discretion protects their privacy and their safety.
  • External-elder functions only when asked. A family may ask the Advisor to hold a story, chair a difficult conversation, or remind the family of its own rules. He does so only when invited, and hands the function back to a family elder as soon as one emerges.
  • Transitions, not transactions. Every recommendation is judged by how it fits the family's long transitions (generational, ownership, leadership), not by this year's tax saving alone.
  • Who advocates for the rising generation. If the answer is "no one," the Advisor makes sure the question stays on the table until someone does.

Caution

The Advisor is never the family's judge, therapist, or referee. When a matter needs mediation, counselling, or adjudication, he refers (SOP 31) and supports the process from the side.

9. Out of scope — refer via the network

Drafting a family constitution; designing or chairing a family council or assembly; mediation of disputes; therapy or addiction treatment; legal documents of any kind. The practice helps the family decide whether it is ready for these (SOP 45) and brings the right specialist (SOP 31); it does not deliver them.

10. Scoping procedure (Mode A, brief)

  1. At handoff, the CSA opens T05 and a blank T14 with everything known.
  2. After the household Discovery (SOP 10) and the family discovery (SOP 41), the LA completes T14 Parts 1–2 (map and trustscape) with the principals.
  3. Before the first family meeting (SOP 43), the LA drafts Parts 3–5 (decision rights, confidentiality, communication) from what the family already does, labels every de facto entry, and asks each adult to sign the confidentiality row that concerns them.
  4. At the family meeting, the family confirms or changes decision rights and communication; the LA records the result.
  5. The engagement letters (SOP 14) reference T14; the plan (SOP 30) is scoped from it.

Beyond Bowen

Ask the principals early whether any asset has ever been formally set aside as the family's rather than someone's personal property. Until that separation is made and written down, there is no family money to govern — only individuals' money that others hope to inherit.

Standards

  • Every adult on the map has a signed confidentiality row before the Advisor discusses that adult with anyone else.
  • Every entity and trust has a named decision-maker and a next-review date.
  • Every de facto decision right is labeled as such until the family confirms it.
  • No family-level document (plan, executive summary, meeting minutes) is circulated beyond the recipients the communication map allows.
  • The stance in §8 is reviewed against the service-failure log at the annual SOP review (SOP 60).

Refresh cadence

  • T14 reviewed at every annual family meeting and on any life event in SOP 22 (birth, death, marriage, divorce, incapacity, sale of a business, a member joining or leaving the enterprise).
  • The three questions in §1 re-asked annually at the first progress meeting of the year.

Owner

LA owns the model and the map; CSA maintains T14 in the [Document vault] and [CRM]; AA keeps the trustscape current from trust documents received under SOP 46.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • This spec applies in full; T14 is a required record before SOP 41 concludes.
  • Where the family has a council, the council chair is the counterparty for Parts 3–5; households sign their own confidentiality rows regardless.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The Advisor does not build a family map for a family that has its own central team. He records on T05 the individual's position in the family, the FCT's members and functions, and the individual's consent about what the FCT may be told.
  • If the family later invites him into its meetings or its executive summary, the stance in §8 applies unchanged; the map remains the family's, not his.
