41 Family discovery and the family executive summary

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — Discovery Meeting and the seven areas of the Total Client Profile; the rediscovery variant · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 15 — the family executive summary process; Ch. 1 — the family balance sheet and the qualitative-vs-financial budget comparison; Ch. 2 — three circles; The Compact — the essential questions as a discovery vocabulary; generational position; Family Wealth Ch. 17 — the two opening questions (passion, mentor) · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes Ch. 2 and 8 — the seven pitfalls, the culture inventory, the three Ds, the family-vs-personal asset question

41 — Family discovery and the family executive summary

Bowen's Discovery Meeting profiles one household in ninety minutes. A family of several households, entities and generations cannot be profiled that way: no single interview reveals the system, and no single member is entitled to speak for the others. This procedure is the Mode A extension — confidential interviews with every adult and key stakeholder, one qualitative instrument to every adult, and a written executive summary the family then discusses together. It produces the family-level layer of the Total Client Profile and the raw material for the wealth management plan.

Purpose

  • Understand the family as a system — its strengths, pressures, decision habits and transitions — from every member's point of view, not only the principals'.
  • Give every adult a confidential voice before the plan is built, so the plan is the family's, not the patriarch's.
  • Produce a document the family can discuss at its first meeting, and the inputs for SOP 11, SOP 30 and SOP 43.

Trigger

  • A Mode A engagement is confirmed on T05, after the principals' household Discovery (SOP 10).
  • An existing Mode A family that has never had a family-wide discovery (run it as the family's rediscovery).
  • A trigger in SOP 22 that changes the system: a death, a business sale, a governance decision, a new generation reaching adulthood.

Roles

Owner: LA (kickoff, every interview, synthesis, presentation) · Does: AA (interview scheduling support, notes typing from recordings, first draft of the summary tables, T18 scoring), CSA (invitations, consent forms, logistics, [Document vault]) · Consulted: an external facilitator (EEN) where the family prefers a non-family, non-advisor interviewer, or where the family is in conflict; [Firm Compliance] on recording and consent.

Timing

Step When
Kickoff with the principals Within 2 weeks of the household Discovery
Invitations and consent Week 1 after kickoff
Interviews (60–90 minutes each) Weeks 2–6; no more than three per day for the LA
T18 instrument out and back Sent with the invitation; due before each interview
Synthesis and draft summary Weeks 6–8
Leader review Week 8–9
Presentation at a family meeting (SOP 43) Weeks 10–14, at the family's convenience
Feed SOP 11 and SOP 30 Immediately after the family meeting

Inputs

  • T05 (mode, scope, who is the client, the three questions) and the household Total Client Profiles already built (SOP 11).
  • A first-draft family map and trustscape (T14 Parts 1–2) from what the principals disclosed.
  • Trust instruments, entity documents and any existing family documents (mission statements, constitutions, meeting minutes) the principals will release.
  • T17 (kickoff checklist, interview guide, notes form, report outline) and T18 (the instrument).
  • The two-way confidentiality rule from SOP 40: interview content is confidential to the interviewee; the summary reports themes, never who said what.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Principals have agreed the goals of the process, the interviewee list, and the timeline (T17 Part 1).
  • [ ] Every interviewee has received the invitation letter (T01), the confidentiality statement, the interview topics, and T18.
  • [ ] Recording consent obtained for each interview or notes-only agreed; consents filed.
  • [ ] Interpreter or facilitator arranged where needed; video links tested for remote members.
  • [ ] The LA has reviewed each household's profile and the trustscape before that household's interviews.
  • [ ] Discovery overlay menu (below) selected for this family — no more than five overlays per interview.

Procedure

  1. Kickoff with the family leaders. Meet the principal(s) (and the council chair if one exists). Agree: why the family is doing this; the outputs; the steps and dates; who will be interviewed — every adult member, adult in-laws by default, and the key non-family stakeholders (family counsel, the CPA, a family-office executive, a long-serving trustee); who will see the summary and in what form. Record the answers on T17 Part 1.

    Say something like

    "Before I can advise the family well, I need to hear from everyone in it — privately, and on the same questions. What comes back to you is what the family thinks as a whole, never who said what."

  2. Build the interviewee list and the invitations. CSA sends each person a letter: the purpose, the confidentiality promise, the five topics, the T18 instrument with a return date, and a choice of interview times. Rising-generation members receive the same letter as everyone else.

  3. Send the instrument. Every adult completes T18 (the family balance sheet) before their interview. The AA scores returns as they arrive; scores are not shared until the summary.

  4. Interview each person for 60–90 minutes, using T17 Part 3. Open with the two questions that reveal a person fastest — what they are passionate about, and who they learn from. Then work the five topics:

    Topic What we are listening for
    A. What's working The family's strengths; what this person would protect at any cost
    B. What's coming Pressures they see in the next two years and the next twenty
    C. What they'd do How they think the family should respond, and what they would need
    D. What they'd learn What they hope to understand about themselves and the family from this
    E. What they'd give What they want out of the process, and what they are willing to contribute

    Add the household-level Bowen areas (values, goals, relationships, assets, advisors, process, interests — T03) for any adult who has not had a household Discovery. Close by asking what else you should have asked.

  5. Apply the discovery overlays the LA selected in prep — as conversation, not as a questionnaire:

    Overlay Use it to surface
    Essential-questions menu (our wording): does the family decide together; is each member growing; is each generation finding its own dream; does stewardship come after calling; does the family attract or obligate; are elders being cultivated; is the long view alive The family's self-understanding as a system
    The two opening questions — passion, mentor Whether each member has a calling and the means to pursue it
    Generational position — G1 household, G2 siblings, G3 clans, G4+ tribe What governance the family will soon need
    Three-circle attention check — family / ownership / management Which circle is starved
    Qualitative-vs-financial budget comparison What the family actually spends on people vs on money
    "Has any asset been formally set aside as the family's?" Whether family money exists yet

    Beyond Bowen

    Two further overlays, both from Bonner: the seven-pitfalls probe (do heirs get advance notice of what is coming; does every heir have a role; is sibling competition capped; do the parents send one message; is ownership passing in time; is spouse fit discussed; is succession a shared vision or a decree) and the culture inventory (values, business, hobbies, education, marriage, philanthropy, politics, history, motto, traditions, reputation, vacations, properties, investments — which of these does the family actually share?). Use the three Ds — division, dissatisfaction, distance — as a temperature check at the end of each interview.

  6. Record and secure. Notes typed within 48 hours from the recording or the LA's notes (T17 Part 4); recordings and notes stored in a restricted folder of the [Document vault]; nothing attributable to a person leaves that folder.

  7. Synthesize. The LA (with AA support on tables) writes the four-section summary on T17 Part 5: themes (what most people said, including contradictions between generations or branches); strengths; challenges and opportunities; recommendations and next steps. Attach the T18 results — per capital and family averages only, with the range shown, never per person unless that person agreed. Add the draft family map and trustscape (T14) and the transitions inventory.

  8. Review with the leaders. Walk the principals (and council chair) through the draft. Correct facts; do not soften themes. Agree how the summary is shared: full document to all adults (preferred), full document to a working group, or a presentation only — and record the choice and the reason.

  9. Present at a family meeting (SOP 43): the LA presents themes and strengths first, challenges second, recommendations last; the family discusses; the meeting adopts one to three next steps and owners.

  10. Feed the profile and the plan. Update SOP 11's family-level layer and T14 Parts 1–6; carry the recommendations into the advanced-planning tracker (T10) and the wealth management plan (SOP 30); open learning plans (T19) where the summary named them.

  11. Close the loop with every interviewee. A short note from the LA: thank you, what the family decided, what happens next.

Follow-up

  • Within 48 hours of each interview: notes typed and filed; T18 score entered.
  • Within one week of the family meeting: minutes (T16) and the adopted next steps circulated per the communication map; T14 updated.
  • Within one month: the plan (SOP 30) reflects the recommendations; the annual meeting date is in every calendar.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Kickoff record and interviewee list (T17 Parts 1–2) [CRM]; family [Document vault] CSA
Interview notes and recordings Restricted folder, [Document vault] AA
T18 scores (per capital, per member, family) [Planning software] or spreadsheet; restricted AA
Family executive summary (T17 Part 5) Family [Document vault]; distribution per the sharing plan LA
Updated T14 and SOP 11 family layer [CRM] LA / CSA
Recommendations in T10 [CRM] tracker AA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Interview in-laws and rising-generation members with the same seriousness as principals.
  • Keep every interview to the topics; the LA listens far more than he talks.
  • Report contradictions between generations as themes — they are usually the most valuable finding.
  • Offer an outside facilitator where the family is in conflict or where members would not be candid with the Advisor.

Don't

  • Don't let the principals edit themes out of the summary; facts yes, themes no.
  • Don't attribute a view to a person, in writing or in the room.
  • Don't rank members or households on the T18 results.
  • Don't run the family meeting before every interview is done — a missing voice will be noticed.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Required before the wealth management plan is presented to a family; the household Discoveries alone are not sufficient.
  • For an existing Mode A family that has never had one, run it as the family's rediscovery in the first year.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The Advisor does not run a family executive summary for a family that has its own central team.
  • If the FCT invites him to contribute, he provides input on his individual's behalf with that individual's consent, and may be one interviewee among many. If asked to conduct interviews for the family, treat it as a separate, scoped engagement on T05 with its own confidentiality terms.

Metrics

  • Share of adult members and in-laws interviewed (target 100%).
  • Weeks from kickoff to family-meeting presentation (target ≤ 14).
  • Recommendations adopted at the family meeting that appear in T10 within one month (target 100%).

Related

  • SOP 10 — CCM1 Discovery Meeting · SOP 11 — Total Client Profile
  • SOP 40 — Family engagement model · SOP 43 — Family meetings · SOP 44 — Family capitals assessment
  • SOP 30 — Wealth management plan
  • T03 — Discovery interview guide · T14 — Family map and matrices · T17 — Family executive summary · T18 — Family balance sheet and income statement · T19 — Rising-generation learning map

Source

  • Bowen, Breaking Through, Ch. 4 — the Discovery Meeting and the seven areas; discovery run with existing clients (adapted).
  • Hughes, Massenzio & Whitaker, Complete Family Wealth, Ch. 15 — a facilitated, confidential, multi-interview executive summary shared at a family meeting; Ch. 1 — the family balance sheet and the budget comparison; Ch. 2 — the three circles (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, The Compact — a vocabulary of essential questions for families and their advisors; the generational arc (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, Family Wealth, Ch. 17 — two questions at the start of every family engagement: what a person is passionate about and who mentors them (paraphrased).
  • Bonner & Bonner, Family Fortunes, Ch. 2 and 8 — the pitfalls checklist, the culture inventory, the three Ds, the family-vs-personal asset question (paraphrased).
  • Extension — the five-topic frame, the overlay menu, and the sequencing with the Bowen household Discovery are ours.

42 Family member onboarding

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the consultative sequence CCM1–CCM4; Process preference honored for the life of the relationship · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 4 — individuation, work outside the family enterprise, the questions a rising-generation member asks of themselves; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 5 and 6 — staged disclosure, communication plan for every gift, both spouses able to speak with the advisers; Family Wealth Ch. 3 — rituals of welcome for new members and new advisers; Compact — beginner's mind; small early joint decisions · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes — advance notice to heirs; six engagement channels; the managed-slice training allocation (paraphrased); Extension — the compressed path and the onboarding sequence are ours

42 — Family member onboarding

When an individual member of a family the practice already serves — a rising-generation adult, a new spouse, a sibling's household, a branch — becomes a client in their own right, the consultative sequence runs again for that person, inside the family's existing profile and confidentiality rules. This procedure scales the sequence to the member, adds the family-specific steps (welcome, map, consent, learning plan), and protects the member's own identity and agency throughout.

Purpose

  • Give each member the same disciplined experience the principals received, sized to their situation.
  • Bring the member into the family map, the confidentiality matrix, and the contact plan without breaching anyone else's confidences.
  • Onboard in a way that strengthens the member's own path (individuation) rather than binding them to the wealth.
  • Make sure no member ever learns of a trust, gift, or inheritance by accident.

Trigger

Any of: a principal asks the Advisor to "bring in" a child, in-law, or branch; a member asks for their own relationship; a trust in which the member is a beneficiary becomes distributive or the member reaches an age of notice; a marriage, divorce, or new household changes who is a decision-maker; a member is added to a family bank, investment committee, or council role.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (scheduling, T05 for the member, [CRM] and [Document vault] set-up, welcome logistics), AA (member-level profile draft, plan draft) · Consulted: the principals (only within their own consent), the trustee where a trust is involved, the family's elder or council chair for the welcome ritual.

Timing

Step Relative timing
Sponsor conversation and advance-notice plan Before any contact with the member
Member Discovery (CCM1) Within 30 days of the member's agreement
Investment plan (CCM2) +2 weeks — or combined with Discovery on the compressed path
Mutual commitment (CCM3) +1 week
Follow-up (CCM4) +45 days
First progress meeting +90 days, then at the member's stated cadence
Welcome ritual At the next family gathering after CCM3

Inputs

  • Family-level Total Client Profile (SOP 11) and the family map, decision rights, confidentiality matrix, and communication map (T14).
  • What the member is entitled to know: trust instruments naming them, gifts planned, any structures already in place (checked with counsel and the trustee).
  • The parents' or principals' intentions for disclosure and the one-page structure summaries already prepared (T21).
  • The discovery interview guide (T03) and the member-level profile outline (T04).
  • The rising-generation learning map (T19) if the member is under about 30 or new to financial responsibility.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Sponsor conversation held with the principal(s): why now, what they hope for, what they are willing to disclose, what they want kept private. Recorded on T14.
  • [ ] Advance-notice plan agreed: who tells the member what, in what setting, before the Advisor's first meeting (SOP 15 and T21 for any structure involved).
  • [ ] Confidentiality check: nothing from another member's profile appears in this member's packet unless that member consented on T14.
  • [ ] T05 opened for the member as a client in their own right — named client, who pays, who may instruct, who advocates for them.
  • [ ] Trustee informed and invited where the member is a beneficiary and the trust is relevant to the conversation (SOP 46).
  • [ ] Pre-meeting letter (T01) written to the member directly, not via the parents, with the agenda and an invitation to add items.
  • [ ] Personality and process notes: how this person prefers to be contacted; whether a spouse or partner attends.

Procedure

  1. Hold the sponsor conversation. Meet the principal(s) alone. Establish that the member becomes a client in their own right, with their own confidences, and that the Advisor will not report on the member to the parents without the member's consent. If the principals cannot accept that, do not proceed; refer the member to another advisor.

  2. Plan the disclosure before the meeting. With the principals (and counsel if a trust is involved) decide the content, tone, and process of what the member will be told: the existence of structures first, then their workings, then figures as the member's questions warrant. Prepare or update the one-page summary (T21). The parents deliver the news; the Advisor explains the mechanics afterward.

    Caution

    Never let a trustee's letter or a statement in the mail be the first a member hears of a trust. The advance-notice rule is absolute.

  3. Invite the member directly. The CSA sends T01 to the member. The letter says who asked for the introduction, that the member's relationship is their own, what will be covered, and what to bring.

  4. Run Discovery (SOP 10) for the member. Use T03 in full. Add the two opening questions in the family overlay — what they are passionate about and who they learn from — and the member's own view of the family's values and of the structures that touch them. Record the member's process preference and honor it for the life of the relationship.
  5. Choose the path.
    • Standard path — the member has meaningful assets, entities, or a trust with distributions: CCM1 → CCM2 (+2 weeks) → CCM3 (+1 week) → CCM4 (+45 days) → progress meetings.
    • Compressed path — a rising-generation member with modest assets and no current trust distributions: Discovery and a short investment plan in one 90-minute meeting; commitment by signed letter within a week; a 45-day call in place of a meeting; the first progress meeting at 90 days. Say in the room that the pace will slow down as their situation grows.
  6. Build the member's profile (T04) inside the family profile. Household level for the member; link to the family level only for the nodes the member is entitled to see. Flag every node with its confidentiality level.
  7. Draft the plan with the member's own ends. The investment plan (SOP 13) states what belongs to the member, what is held for them in trust, and who decides what. For beneficiaries, the plan names the trustee and the distribution process (SOP 46) as inputs, not as the member's money.

  8. Offer, never impose, the development conversation. If the member wants it, work through the "setting off" questions over several meetings: whether they feel free or dependent; whether they have found work that matters to them; whether they are a good friend and have good friends; whether they can be compassionate with themselves, express gratitude, and enjoy themselves; whether they take part in the wider community; where they want to grow. Record only what the member chooses to record.

    Say something like

    "Some members find it useful to talk about the life they want before we talk about the money that will support it. We can do that, or not — it's your call."

  9. Set the norms that protect individuation. Discuss, with the principals' agreement, the family's norms: working outside the family enterprise for a period before joining it; building an identity and a livelihood that would stand without the wealth; avoiding public prominence about the family's affairs. Frame them as the family's choices, not the Advisor's rules.

  10. Choose an engagement channel. Offer the six channels a member can take up in the family enterprise — a role in the business, in the family philanthropy, a seat on the investment committee, management of a family property, an administrative role in the family office function, or a funded venture through the family bank (SOP 47). Record the choice on T14 and T19.
  11. Consider a managed slice. With the principals and any trustee, offer the member a small allocation — roughly half to one percent of family financial capital, or a fixed sum — to manage personally with the Advisor's coaching, so mistakes are affordable and real. Record it on T19.
  12. Run CCM3 for the member (SOP 14). The engagement letter names the member as client, states the mode and scope, and records consent (T05). The fee basis is explained in the member's own terms. The introductions ask is reframed: "Who else in the family should we be serving?"
  13. Add the member to the family map, matrices, and contact plan (T14, SOP 21). Update decision rights, the communication map ("who calls whom for what"), and the annual calendar (T15). Both spouses of a new household are told they may speak directly with the Advisor and are given enough understanding to do so.
  14. Arrange the welcome ritual. Ask the family's elder or council chair to mark the member's entry at the next gathering — a few words, a story, an introduction of the member's own dreams — and mark the practice's side with a note from the LA and the member's own notebook (T08).
  15. Run CCM4 and the first progress meeting (SOPs 16 and 20). Include one small joint decision the member and the principals can make together early (a charitable grant, a property question, a family-bank policy) so the first shared experience is a success.
  16. Build the learning plan (T19). For members under about 30 or new to financial responsibility, agree the next twelve months of learning: what they will read, which meetings they will attend, what they will manage, who mentors them, and how progress is reviewed at the annual family meeting.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours of each meeting: recap to the member only (unless consent says otherwise); [CRM] updated; T14 and T19 updated.
  • Within one week of Discovery: the one-week call (SOP 05) — new questions always surface once a young member has slept on it.
  • Within 30 days of CCM3: welcome ritual scheduled; contact plan live; the member's notebook set up.
  • Annually: the member's process preference, consent, and learning plan reviewed at their first progress meeting of the year.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Member's T05 (client, mode, scope, consent) [CRM]; [Document vault] LA
Member-level profile linked to the family profile (T04) [CRM]; [Planning software] AA
Member's investment plan and engagement letter [Document vault] LA
Updated family map, decision rights, confidentiality and communication matrices (T14) [CRM] family record CSA
Learning plan and managed-slice record (T19) [Document vault]; reviewed at the annual family meeting LA
Welcome ritual note and date [CRM] family record CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Treat the member as a client with their own confidences from the first minute.
  • Ask what the member already knows and believes about the family's wealth before telling them anything.
  • Let the parents deliver news; let the Advisor explain mechanics.
  • Keep the first shared decision small and winnable.

Don't

  • Don't diagnose. The "Black Hole" patterns in SOP 04 are awareness cues for the Advisor, never labels used with the member.
  • Don't give the member only the "small" parts of the family's affairs to learn on; the large, complex structures are where the teaching value is.
  • Don't report a member's spending, choices, or requests to the parents — not even as reassurance.
  • Don't let a welcome become a performance review.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The full procedure applies. The family map, matrices, and calendar are the practice's own records and are updated here.
  • Where the family has a council, inform it of the member's entry as the constitution provides; the member's affairs remain their own.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • When another member of a large family asks to work with the Advisor, inform the FCT as agreed on the existing client's T05, then open a separate mandate with its own T05, its own scope rung, and its own consent — nothing flows between the two mandates without both members' consent.
  • The family's own welcome and governance practices are theirs; the Advisor takes part only when invited.
  • The learning plan is offered only where the mandate includes the member's own affairs (B-full or B-partial).

Metrics

  • Members onboarded in the year and share on the compressed path.
  • Share of member Discoveries preceded by a documented advance-notice plan (target 100%).
  • Learning plans reviewed at the annual family meeting (target 100% of plans).

Related

  • SOP 10 — CCM1 Discovery · SOP 14 — CCM3 · SOP 16 — CCM4
  • SOP 40 — Family engagement model · SOP 41 — Family discovery
  • SOP 46 — Trustee–beneficiary relationship · SOP 47 — Family bank and investor allocation
  • T14 — Family map and matrices · T19 — Rising-generation learning map · T21 — Structure summary and communication plan

Source

  • Bowen, Breaking Through, Ch. 4 — the consultative sequence and the rule that the client's process preference is honored for the life of the relationship (adapted).
  • Hughes, Massenzio & Whitaker, Complete Family Wealth, Ch. 4 — individuation, working outside the family enterprise, the self-questions of a member setting off (paraphrased); Ch. 5–6 — staged disclosure, planning the communication of every gift, both spouses able to speak with the advisers (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, Family Wealth, Ch. 3 — welcome rituals for new members and new advisers (paraphrased). Hughes, The Compact — small early joint successes (paraphrased).
  • Bonner & Bonner, Family Fortunes — advance notice to heirs, the six engagement channels, the managed-slice allocation (paraphrased). Bonner disagrees with Hughes on guiding versus freeing a member's path; this procedure follows Hughes.
  • Extension — the compressed path, the sponsor conversation, and the onboarding sequence are ours.

43 Family meetings — standing rules, the first meeting and mission session, the annual family meeting

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — Regular Progress Meeting agenda and critical success factors (applied at family level) · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 16 — meeting design frame, ground rules, conflict handling, attendance, facilitation, cadence, venue; Ch. 17 — stories and rituals; Ch. 18 — mission statements; Family Wealth Ch. 2 — the mission-statement session and meeting rules; Ch. 1 — the four qualitative questions; Ch. 13 — the next-generation conversation; Ch. 18 — annual review of representatives; The Compact — youngest speaks first; allies/friends/others · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes Ch. 8 — a timed first council meeting with pre-work profiles and a takeaway round

43 — Family meetings

A family meeting is owned by the family: it is about the whole of the family's wealth, not only the money, and the family — not the Advisor — sets its agenda. The Advisor designs, prepares and (until the family can) facilitates. This SOP holds three procedures: the standing rules every family-attended meeting runs on; the first meeting and the mission/values session; and the annual family meeting, which is the family-level counterpart of the Regular Progress Meeting.

Purpose

  • Give the family a safe, disciplined way to stay connected, learn, and decide together.
  • Turn the executive summary (SOP 41) and the capitals assessment (SOP 44) into shared decisions.
  • Establish the rhythm — rules, roles, minutes, cadence — that lets the family govern itself later without the Advisor in the room.

Trigger

  • A family executive summary is ready to be presented (first meeting).
  • The family's annual meeting month (annual meeting).
  • A transition or crisis in SOP 22 — a business sale, a leadership change, a death or incapacity — where the family needs to meet within weeks.

Roles

Owner: LA (design, preparation, facilitation until handed over) · Does: CSA (invitations, venue, materials, childcare arrangements, minutes circulation), AA (packet: T18 results, T10 family-level tracker, reporting extracts) · Consulted: external facilitator (EEN) for the first meetings, for conflict, and for annual tune-ups; specialists (ISB/EEN) attend only their portion.

Timing

Meeting When Length
First meeting 10–14 weeks after the family-discovery kickoff Two half-days (about 3 hours each) with a free afternoon and evening between, or one full day with long breaks
Mission/values session Same retreat as the first meeting, or within six months 4–6 hours
Subsequent meetings while the practice forms Every six months for two or three cycles Half-day to one day
Annual family meeting Same month each year, fixed in the family calendar (T15) One to two days
Preparation Agenda out 4 weeks ahead; pre-work due 2 weeks ahead; packet 1 week ahead
Minutes Draft within 5 days; final within 2 weeks

Inputs

  • The family executive summary (T17 Part 5) and T18 results (first meeting); the annual capitals refresh (SOP 44) and the family-level advanced-planning tracker (T10) thereafter.
  • T14 (map, decision rights, confidentiality, communication) — attendance and what may be discussed in front of whom.
  • Pre-work from every attendee (T16 Part 3): one-page member profile; ten-year statement.
  • The family's mission statement, values statement, and governance documents if any exist.
  • T16 for the design frame, rules sheet, run-sheets, agendas, exercise menu, story prompts, rituals calendar, minutes template.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Design frame completed (T16 Part 1): why this meeting, what it must produce, who attends, when, how (format and learning styles), where.
  • [ ] Attendee list agreed with the leaders against T14; spouses invited unless the adult children asked otherwise; members under fourteen provided with childcare or a parallel program; specialists booked for their portion only.
  • [ ] Agenda drafted with the family's items first; circulated 4 weeks ahead with pre-work forms.
  • [ ] Packet assembled 1 week ahead in the formats members learn from (numbers on paper for some, one-page visuals for others); heavy content split across two sessions.
  • [ ] Venue meets the rules below; audio works; breaks scheduled every 75–90 minutes.
  • [ ] Facilitator briefed (or the LA has rehearsed the run-sheet); chair and secretary for this meeting nominated from the family and briefed.
  • [ ] Any weighty disclosure the leaders intend (an estate plan, a sale, a new trust) has been discussed with the LA beforehand, with time reserved for members to react.
  • [ ] Ground rules sheet printed for signature (first meeting) or for reading aloud (later meetings).

Procedure

Part A — Standing rules and the conflict protocol (every family-attended meeting)

  1. Open with the rules. At the first meeting the family discusses and adopts its own ground rules from the draft on T16 Part 2 and signs the sheet; at later meetings the chair reads them aloud. The practice's draft, in our words:

    Rule In practice
    Be here Devices away; on time; pre-work done
    One voice at a time Let people finish; no finishing sentences for them
    Play it back before you push back Show you understood before you answer
    Say "I" Own your view; no "everyone thinks"
    Hold your outcome loosely Come to decide together, not to win
    Drop the "but" Begin a reply with what you heard, not with the objection
    Candor with care Say the hard thing so it can be heard
    Park, don't drop Not everything is settled today; parked items get an owner and a date
    What's said here stays here Unless the family agrees otherwise
    The rules bind everyone Including the people paying for the meeting

  2. Appoint a chair and a secretary from the family for this meeting, after the agenda is set so that a member with a major report is not also chairing. Roles rotate. The chair facilitates as a peer; the secretary keeps minutes (T16 Part 10) and circulates a draft within five days.

  3. Speaking order. Where a decision affects the young most, offer the family the practice of hearing the youngest adults first and the eldest last.
  4. Enforce the rules. The chair (or the LA, until the family can) names a breach the moment it happens, kindly and without exception. Rules enforced on everyone counteract entitlement; rules ignored teach that the meeting is theater.

  5. Run the conflict protocol when disagreement turns destructive.

    1. Ask whether the disagreement is producing better discussion or stopping it.
    2. Understand first: ask clarifying questions only, until each side can state the other's position.
    3. Separate the people from the problem; name the source of the conflict (a misunderstanding, different needs, different values, a structure that isn't working) and ask the group to confirm the name.
    4. Invoke the relevant ground rule.
    5. Look for common ground and legitimate difference — differing values are allowed.
    6. Map allies, neutrals and opponents privately before the next vote; there are no enemies inside a family.
    7. Call a break when stuck. If the matter cannot be settled in the room, hand it to the family's elders or, failing them, to an outside mediator (SOP 31). The Advisor never adjudicates.

    Caution

    A disagreement between spouses is not for this room. Pause it, and refer privately (SOP 40 §7).

Part B — The first meeting and the mission/values session

  1. Pre-work. Every attendee sends, two weeks ahead: a one-page profile (what a good friend would know about you — passions, current mentors, what you are working on) and a ten-year statement (where you want to be, and what the family could do to help). The CSA compiles a profile book for the meeting.
  2. First meeting — presenting the executive summary. Chair opens; rules adopted (step 1); profile round (each person, one minute); the LA presents themes and strengths, then challenges, then recommendations; discussion in the family's own order; the family adopts one to three next steps with owners; takeaway round; close.
  3. A family standing up its own family office or council uses the timed agenda instead (T16 Part 5): about four hours in eight blocks — open and celebrate recent accomplishments; roll call and profiles; the family office idea and the family balance sheet; break; the family-office budgets (support, property, travel to family events); constituting an investment committee and the investor-allocation idea (SOP 47); break; how decisions get made — decision rights and confidentiality (T14); close with takeaways and the next date.

  4. The mission/values session (T16 Part 4), in our version of the classic sequence, with clock times for a family of up to about twenty (larger families break into groups that report back):

    Step Minutes What happens
    1. Rules and roles 10 Read the rules; chair and secretary confirmed
    2. Profiles 15 Each person: passions and mentors from their profile
    3. Values lists 25 Each person writes the handful of values the family's long-term success depends on; posted on the wall; clustered into a shared list
    4. The long view 20 Each person writes what they would want the family to remember mattered most, looking back from very old age; shared in small groups
    5. Twenty years out 30 Each person describes the family two decades from now; read aloud
    6. Family history 45–60 A small committee's draft of the family's story — crises, opportunities, memorable ancestors, past decisions good and bad — reviewed and corrected
    7. How we will decide 30 The forms of family government, briefly; the family chooses how it will decide together and who represents whom

    Add either or both quick exercises where energy allows: what matters most to me and why (a round the table, then aggregated into the values list); founding values vs present values (the whole family names the founders' values, each generation separately names today's, and the two are compared). A drafting committee of two or three, spanning generations, writes the first draft of the mission/values statement from the wall; the family treats it as a first draft and revisits it annually. Keep the whole session enjoyable — food, breaks, a walk.

  5. Follow the first meetings with a short cycle. Meet again in six months, then six months after that, before moving to an annual rhythm; the facilitator attends the first two or three and then returns for annual tune-ups or new skills.

Part C — The annual family meeting

  1. Design the agenda in three tracks (T16 Part 6): individual — each member's update on life, work, plans; generational — each generation caucuses on what it wants to share with and learn from the others, then reports; family-wide — the business of the family enterprise.
  2. Run the family-wide track as a progress meeting.
    1. Chair opens; rules read; agenda additions.
    2. A rising-generation member reads the mission/values statement aloud.
    3. The four health questions, in our words: Is each person here thriving? Do the leaders of each generation give their peers reason to stay and to listen? Does everyone know how they could leave the family enterprise, so that no one stays because they cannot? Are those who represent the family looking after all of its capitals, and do members feel that they are?
    4. Capitals review — the T18 results (SOP 44) year on year: what grew, what shrank, what the family will do about it.
    5. Family-level advanced-planning tracker (T10) — status of wealth transfer, protection and giving items; the family confirms drop / defer / do on each open item.
    6. Money and structures — the year's family-level reporting (SOP 24 extracts), any change to trusts or entities, the investor-allocation and family-bank report (SOP 47), the family's giving.
    7. Review of representatives — council members, trustees the family can influence, the family's advisors including this practice: what worked, what to change; the fee conversation for the practice is held here or in the principals' progress meeting, never skipped.
    8. Decisions requested — each with a proposer, the options, and a recommendation; decided by the family's own rules (consensus preferred; vote where the family has agreed to).
    9. The rising generation — a short, separate conversation, never tied to money decisions in the same session: what is your dream, and how can the family invest in it? Learning plans (T19) updated.
    10. Next steps with owners and dates; the next meeting date fixed; takeaway round.
  3. Stories and rituals in every annual meeting. Reserve time for one or two stories from a designated storyteller who received the prompts in advance (T16 Part 8); keep the grandparent–grandchild lunch from which parents are absent; mark the year's passages — a birth, a coming of age, a marriage, a new elder, a death, the welcome of a new advisor — with the family's own rituals (T16 Part 9); close with a gratitude round in which each person names someone they will thank, and how.
  4. Attendance rules. Spouses attend by default — the organizing generation asks the adult children rather than deciding for them, and spouses may join for the general and learning sessions before executive ones. Members under fourteen have childcare or a parallel program (money skills, a service project). Elders are always invited. Experts attend only their portion. A member who wants to opt out of family meetings is met with a conversation, not a shrug.
  5. Facilitation. Use an outside facilitator for the first meetings, for any meeting following a crisis, and once a year thereafter for a tune-up; between those, the family chairs its own meetings and the LA attends as the family's advisor.
  6. Venue. Not a parent's home or office. Somewhere with room for both work and play, convenient for everyone expected, quiet enough for older ears, with food and rest for those who traveled. The cost is a statement that the family invests in itself.

Follow-up

  • Within 5 days: draft minutes (T16 Part 10) from the family secretary, reviewed by the LA for accuracy only, circulated per the communication map.
  • Within 2 weeks: final minutes; decisions entered in T10 and T14; learning plans (T19) updated; the next meeting in every calendar.
  • Within 1 month: every owner of a next step has been contacted once by the CSA.
  • After the first two meetings: the LA and the family's chair review what worked and adjust the design frame.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Design frame, agenda, packet Family [Document vault] CSA
Signed ground rules Family [Document vault]; reprinted for each meeting CSA
Profile book and ten-year statements Restricted folder CSA
Mission/values statement (drafts and adopted version) Family [Document vault]; read at every annual meeting Family drafting committee; LA holds the file
Minutes and decisions Family [Document vault]; T10, T14 updated Family secretary; CSA
Rising-generation learning plans T19 in [CRM], restricted LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Put the family's items first and the Advisor's last.
  • Split heavy content across two half-days; leave the evening between free.
  • Give the young something real to do — reading the statement, presenting a grant, keeping the minutes.
  • Build in silence after a weighty disclosure; people need time before they can respond.

Don't

  • Don't let a performance review of the portfolio masquerade as a family meeting.
  • Don't adopt rules and then let a senior member break them.
  • Don't decide anything the family has not had time to discuss; park it with an owner.
  • Don't let the Advisor's agenda replace the family's; if the family owns nothing on the agenda, the meeting has failed before it starts.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The practice designs and facilitates until the family can; every family has at least one meeting a year and a fixed month for it.
  • Where the family has a council, the council plans the meeting with the LA and the council chair chairs it.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The Advisor does not convene meetings for a family with its own central team. When invited to present, he attends his portion only, presents what his individual has consented to, and follows the family's rules and chair.
  • If his individual asks for help preparing for the family's meeting, he prepares them privately — their update, their questions, their position on decisions.

Metrics

  • Annual meeting held in the fixed month with minutes issued within two weeks (target 100% of Mode A families).
  • Share of adults (including in-laws) attending the annual meeting (target ≥ 85%).
  • Next steps from the previous meeting completed or formally re-decided by the next one (target ≥ 80%).

44 Family capitals assessment — the qualitative balance sheet and income statement

specOwner: LAMode Abeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — Values, Goals, Relationships and Interests areas of the Total Client Profile · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 1 — the five capitals; a self-rated family balance sheet; the qualitative-vs-financial budget comparison; Ch. 2 — the four transitions; Family Wealth Ch. 4 — the family balance sheet and income statement; Ch. 2 — annual résumé and personal mission statement; Ch. 10–11 — beneficiary and trustee annual reports; Ch. 13 — next-generation learning plans · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes Ch. 1 — human-capital liabilities as unfunded liabilities; 'organizational capital'

44 — Family capitals assessment

A family tracks its financial capital monthly and its other capitals never. This spec defines the practice's annual qualitative statements for a Mode A family: a family balance sheet that rates the four qualitative capitals, and a family income statement that records whether the family's people and their knowledge grew or shrank this year. Together they sit beside the financial reporting (SOP 24) so the family's picture of itself is complete.

Purpose

  • Measure the capitals the family cannot see on a custodial statement, in a form that can be trended over years and generations.
  • Give the annual family meeting (SOP 43) a factual basis for the "is each of us thriving" conversation.
  • Surface human-capital liabilities early enough to fund the remedy.

Contents

1. The five capitals — working definitions

Capital What we mean Evidence we look for
Human The members themselves: health, self-knowledge, the ability to find meaningful work and to pursue their own happiness Work that fits; recovery from setbacks; an identity separate from the wealth; freedom to leave
Intellectual What members know and can do, and whether it moves between them Financial literacy suited to each role; mentors; learning funded; knowledge shared across households
Social The quality of members' relationships with each other and with the world outside Voluntary time together; disputes settled; newcomers included; giving; cousins who know each other
Spiritual The family's shared sense of purpose beyond money — humility, gratitude, a long view A stated purpose; stories told; decisions weighed for grandchildren; rituals kept
Financial The property the family owns — the tool that funds the other four Financial statements (SOP 24); the plan (SOP 30)

Beyond Bowen

One source counts a fourth capital differently — "organizational" capital, the family's institutions and processes — and drops the social and spiritual capitals. The practice keeps the five above and records governance maturity separately (SOP 45), so nothing is lost by the choice.

2. The family balance sheet — instrument design (T18)

  • Form. Four sections, one per qualitative capital, each with about eight plain statements written by the practice for a family of substantial wealth; every adult rates agreement 1–5. A one-line definition heads each section.
  • Scoring. Average per capital per member; per capital across the family; the family's overall profile. Show the range as well as the mean — a capital on which the generations disagree by two points is the finding.
  • Assets and liabilities. The statements describe assets. A separate liabilities page lists, per household and without attribution in the family version, the conditions that drain human and intellectual capital — addiction, illness, dependency on distributions, a member without work that fits, unspoken conflicts — each with a status (being addressed / not yet) and an owner.
  • Confidentiality. Individual ratings are seen by the LA and the AA only. The family sees averages and ranges. A member's own scores are returned to them privately with the family's averages for comparison.
  • First use. In the family discovery (SOP 41), before the executive summary. Thereafter with the annual meeting pre-work.

3. The family income statement — the annual change

Compiled each year from four short documents each adult supplies before the annual meeting (forms in T18):

Input What it records Who supplies it
Personal résumé update What a good friend would know: work, passions, current mentors, what was learned this year Every adult
Personal mission statement One paragraph: what I am for; revised or reaffirmed Every adult
Beneficiary self-report For each trust: did I meet my responsibilities as a beneficiary this year (understood the trust; met the trustee; kept financial literacy growing; gave the trustee my assessment)? Each beneficiary
Trustee report For each trust: did I meet mine (purposes honored; annual meeting held; beneficiary education in place; policies implemented)? Each trustee the family controls; [Trust Co.] where applicable

The AA summarizes: members who took on new roles, skills or responsibilities; mentoring relationships formed; learning funded; trusts whose relationships improved or deteriorated; the human-capital liabilities resolved or newly recognized. The LA writes the one-page narrative — did the family's people and knowledge grow this year? — with the year's financial summary on the facing page.

4. Human-capital inventory

A confidential register (T14 Part 1 extended): each member's passions, current mentors, skills, roles held inside and outside the family, and the role the family could offer them. Used to fill roles (a committee seat, a property to manage, a foundation task), to find internal mentors, and to spot the member who has no role at all.

5. Human-capital liabilities as unfunded liabilities

Beyond Bowen

Treat a member's addiction, illness, dependency or unresolved conflict as an unfunded liability on the family balance sheet: it will come due. The family either funds the remedy — the best available treatment, a coach, a role, a loan that builds independence — or insulates the wealth from the liability through trust design (SOP 46, SOP 48). Doing neither is the choice the balance sheet makes visible.

6. The philanthropy share

One line: the share of the family's financial capital, and of its members' time, devoted to giving this year. Recorded whether or not the family gives through a structure; feeds the charitable section of SOP 30.

7. Transitions inventory

The four transitions — family (generation to generation), ownership (who holds what, and in trust or outright), board or council, management (of the business or the money) — each with a stage, a leader, and the decisions it will require (T14 Part 6). Several usually run at once; the inventory is the reason the plan's sequencing exists.

8. Rising-generation learning plans

For each rising-generation member (any member still forming an identity and calling apart from the wealth): the age-staged learning map (T19), this year's steps, who mentors, what the family funds, and how progress is seen — never as a test tied to money. Reviewed in the separate rising-generation conversation at the annual meeting (SOP 43), not in the money session.

9. The qualitative-vs-financial budget comparison

Once a year, two numbers side by side: what the family spent on preserving and growing financial capital (management, advisory, legal, accounting, custody fees) and what it spent proactively on the four qualitative capitals (learning, coaching, treatment, family meetings, mentoring, travel to gather). The ratio is discussed, not judged; the family decides whether it wants a qualitative budget at all.

Standards

  • Every adult member is invited to complete the instrument; participation below three-quarters is reported as a finding.
  • Individual scores never appear in a family document; ranges and averages only.
  • Statements are reviewed by the LA every three years for wording that has dated, and any change is noted so trends remain comparable.
  • The liabilities page always carries an owner and a status per item; a liability without an owner is escalated to the principals.
  • The income-statement narrative is one page; the financial summary faces it.
  • The assessment is presented at the family meeting by the LA, never mailed cold.

Refresh cadence

  • Balance sheet: at family discovery, then every one to three years as the family chooses (annually while the family is in transition).
  • Income statement inputs: annually, due two weeks before the annual family meeting.
  • Human-capital inventory and transitions inventory: at every annual meeting and on any event in SOP 22.
  • Learning plans: annually, and at each rising-generation member's milestone.

Owner

LA owns the design, the narrative and the presentation; AA scores, compiles and maintains the register; CSA distributes and collects the forms and files them in the restricted folder of the [Document vault]. Where [Trust Co.] is trustee, its trust officer supplies the trustee report through SOP 46.

45 Family governance readiness

procedureOwner: LAMode Abeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 7 and 19 — three Ps, humility, confederal default, constitution, assembly, council, Wisdom Council, build sequence; Compact — governance as joint decision-making, eight principles, four authorities of elders, allies/friends/others, transition committee, who is your successor; Family Wealth Ch. 1, 2, 18 — republic as the chosen form, meeting rules, the three branches · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes — three governance stages with member-count thresholds, the tanist, the endowment-model sequence, constitution additions (paraphrased); Extension — the readiness assessment and the LA-runs / refers split are ours

45 — Family governance readiness

Governance is joint decision-making. Most families need clarity about how a few decisions get made long before they need a system; some never need a system at all. This procedure helps a family decide, without pressure, whether to build governance, what to build first, and what the Advisor runs versus refers to a facilitator.

Purpose

  • Assess whether a family is ready for, and would benefit from, formal governance.
  • Sequence the work so principles come before policies and policies before practices.
  • Position the Advisor correctly: convener and translator, not the family's government.

Trigger

Any of: the family discovery (SOP 41) surfaces decisions nobody knows how to make; a transition is approaching (sale of a business, a principal stepping back, death or incapacity, a member coming of age, a branch forming); the family has grown beyond one household's dinner table; a trust or family entity needs a decision body; a principal asks "how do we keep this together?"

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: AA (readiness notes, drafts of options), CSA (meeting logistics, minutes, record of decisions) · Consulted: elders and any council chair; a family-governance facilitator from the EEN for the first meetings and for any charged decision; counsel for anything that becomes a legal document.

Timing

Step Timing
Readiness assessment Within the family discovery cycle or within 60 days of a trigger
Options conversation with principals +2–4 weeks
Foundational retreat Within a quarter of the family's decision to explore governance
Working group 3–9 months, with updates to the whole family at least quarterly
Ratification meeting When the working group and the principals agree the draft is ready
Reviews Annually at the family meeting; the constitution amended only by its own rule

Inputs

  • Family executive summary and Family Balance Sheet results (SOP 41, T17, T18).
  • Family map, decision rights, and communication map (T14).
  • Transitions inventory (SOP 44) and the annual calendar (T15).
  • Any existing documents: letters of wishes, shareholder agreements, foundation bylaws, trust preambles.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] The three questions answered on T05: who pays, who is the client, who advocates for the rising generation.
  • [ ] The family's current decision-making mapped: who decides what today, and which decisions have caused friction.
  • [ ] Member count, generations, and branches counted (the thresholds below depend on them).
  • [ ] The LA's own limits stated in writing: what he will run, what he will refer.
  • [ ] A facilitator identified in the EEN before the first governance meeting is proposed.

Procedure

  1. Assess readiness. Score the family on the signals in the table below. Readiness is not size; it is shared intention and a few decisions that need a home.

    Signal Ready Not yet
    Shared intention to stay together as a family enterprise Stated by most adults Assumed by the founder only
    Decisions that need a home Named (foundation grants, a property, distributions, the business) "Everything" or "nothing"
    Communication Members already talk about money, however awkwardly Money is unmentionable
    Founder's posture Willing to move decisions to a group while alive Wants a structure that enforces his wishes after death
    Elders Someone the family already turns to for disputes and stories None, or the founder only
    Conflict Present and survivable Absent (suspicious) or feud-level (refer first)

  2. Start with the three Ps, in order. Principles (values, purpose, vision) first — the mission/values session in SOP 43 supplies them. Policies (constitution, trust terms, distribution rules) second. Practices (meetings, executive summaries, education) third. A practice adopted without a policy behind it fades; a policy without agreed principles is contested at the first hard case.

  3. Ask whether a system is needed at all. Many families need clarity in three or four areas — where the family gathers, how the foundation decides, how discretionary distributions are handled, who speaks for the family to advisors — and nothing more. Offer that as the first option. A system that does not serve individual members' flourishing is make-work.
  4. Set the confederal default. Each branch or household keeps authority over most matters; only the few matters that are genuinely family-wide go to a family body: oversight of a shared business or foundation, a voice in the direction of shared entities, pooled resources for family learning, relations with outside professionals. Warn against founder-driven centralized designs; they rarely outlive the founder.

  5. Locate the family on the three-stage arc.

    Stage Typical form Decision rule Threshold
    First generation All adults of sound mind vote; founder holds a veto Consensus, founder's veto as backstop Up to one household's children as adults
    Sibling generation Representative democracy of siblings Consensus sought; equal votes Until roughly 15–20 adult members
    Cousins and beyond A family republic: branch representatives on a council; branches caucus before sending them Consensus in the council; supermajority for structural change From roughly 15–20 members; above ~30 branch representation is essential

    Design for the next stage, not the current one, and build in the amendment rule that lets the family evolve without revolution.

  6. Offer sequencing options. One well-tested sequence: council → mission and constitution → family bank → investment committee → education program → philanthropy committee, all sitting over the family's long-term trusts. Another: philanthropy first, as the low-risk rehearsal for joint decisions. Choose with the family based on where a decision is already needed.

  7. Hold the foundational retreat (SOP 43). Questions for the room: why do we want to stay together; what are the strengths and weaknesses of our family culture; how do we want to treat each other; what would a council be responsible for if we had one. Adopt ground rules at this meeting. Use a facilitator.
  8. Form a working group. Three to five members across generations and branches, one of them from the rising generation. Their job: poll every adult, draft the charter, and keep the family informed. The family executive summary process (SOP 41) is the natural polling tool.
  9. Build the communication plan. Regular updates from the working group to every member; ideas tested with non-members of the group before they harden; no one surprised at ratification.
  10. Draft the constitution for counsel. Contents to decide, in the family's words before any lawyer's: statement of purpose; who counts as family (descendants of a named ancestor, spouses, adopted members, partners); values; ground rules for how members treat each other; council charter (purpose, authority — advisory or binding — formation, size, terms, officers, subcommittees, meeting cadence, communication with the wider family); spouse policy (participation, prenuptial expectations, treatment on divorce — set as general policy, never case by case); business-employment policy; conduct-based disqualification from roles and family-bank funds (with treatment funding permitted); dispute resolution; amendment rule (difficult, not impossible).
  11. Define the council's annual duties so it is a working body: plan the annual family meeting; recommend appointments to trust, foundation, and family-office roles; review budgets of the family enterprise's parts; review the governance system's own performance and report to the assembly; propose amendments; supervise outside advisers; coordinate the annual family balance sheet and income statement (SOP 44).

  12. Design the elders' role deliberately. Four functions: mediate disputes (equity for all, not a verdict for one); tell the family that it is not following its own rules; keep and tell the stories; hold the rituals. Four qualities: discernment, discretion, discipline, discovery. Elders are nominated by branches, seated by the assembly, serve longer terms, and cannot act on their own initiative — they must be asked. Until the family grows its own, a trusted outside adviser may serve as an external elder when asked.

    Caution

    A governance design with no active role for the senior generation will be sabotaged by that generation. The elder role is where founders go; design it first.

  13. Name a tanist. Each generation designates an apprenticed successor to the council chair (and a parallel one for the investment committee): no title, no privileges beyond what the council agrees, but the person who learns the family-office matters most deeply, sets the agenda, and keeps discussion on business. Rename any "succession committee" a transition committee.

  14. Teach two decision techniques. Allies / friends / others — before any contested decision, each member maps who agrees, who is neutral, who is likely opposed; there is no "enemy" category. Speaking order — youngest first, eldest last, so the people who will live longest with the decision are heard before the elders weigh in. Use consensus for structural matters; votes for elections and amendments.
  15. Ratify in the open. A meeting convened for the purpose, with vigorous debate and an open vote so no one is voiceless. Then celebrate: a story from the family's history, every member signs, a photograph, the signed copy kept by the youngest council member. The first council election usually happens at this meeting; nominees speak to why they want to serve.
  16. Ask every leader the succession question. "Who is your successor?" — of the council chair, of the operating-company CEO, of the family-office head, of the trustee. Record the answers on the transitions inventory (SOP 44).
  17. Decide what the LA runs and what he refers. The LA convenes, translates, keeps the calendar, and administers the council's financial duties. A family-governance facilitator (EEN) runs the retreat, the ratification, and any decision where members' interests conflict. Counsel drafts. The LA never mediates between spouses (SOP 40).

Follow-up

  • Within one week of each governance meeting: minutes circulated for comment (CSA); decisions logged; open questions assigned.
  • Quarterly during the build: working-group update to the whole family.
  • Annually: the assembly reviews the council's performance; the council reviews the system; the mission statement is read at the opening of the annual meeting.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Readiness assessment and options memo [Document vault] family folder AA
Retreat minutes and adopted ground rules [Document vault]; T16 CSA
Draft constitution (family's words) → counsel's draft → ratified copy Family's own records; a copy in the [Document vault] Working group; counsel
Council charter, roster, terms, tanist designation T14 governance section CSA
Elders' roster and nomination rule T14 CSA
Transitions inventory updated with successors SOP 44 LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Start with the decisions that already need a home.
  • Bring critics inside and give them real roles.
  • Engineer a small joint decision that succeeds before the hard ones.
  • Write the amendment rule before the first amendment is needed.

Don't

  • Don't propose a system to a family that needs three clear policies.
  • Don't let advisers or the founder draft the constitution and hand it down.
  • Don't let the council become the place personal and marital matters are litigated; its mission is the family's shared enterprise.
  • Don't let "we talk all the time" replace meetings with agendas and minutes.

Metrics

  • Decisions with a named "home" (body, rule, cadence) as a share of decisions the family identified.
  • Members participating in the ratification vote as a share of eligible adults.
  • Council annual duties completed on the calendar.

Source

  • Hughes, Massenzio & Whitaker, Complete Family Wealth, Ch. 7 and 19 — humility before systems, three Ps, confederal default, constitution, assembly and council, Wisdom Council, the build sequence and ratification celebration (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, The Compact — governance as joint decision-making, the eight principles, the four authorities and selection of elders, allies/friends/others, speaking order, the transition committee, the succession question (paraphrased).
  • Hughes, Family Wealth, Ch. 1, 2, 18 — the republic as the form families choose, meeting rules, the three branches and their duties (paraphrased).
  • Bonner & Bonner, Family Fortunes — the three governance stages and member-count thresholds, the tanist, the endowment-model sequence, constitution additions on spouses, employment and conduct (paraphrased). Bonner narrows the council's scope to wealth matters and rejects the family of affinity; this procedure keeps Hughes's inclusive definition of family.
