46 Trustee–beneficiary relationship

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — relationship management includes working with the client's fiduciaries; expert in the room for complex items · Hughes: Family Trusts (Goldstone, Hughes & Whitaker) Ch. 2–4, 9–14, 16, 19–21 — the trustscape, narratives, accepting a trusteeship, preambles and letters of wishes, pre-meeting letters, mindset, the meeting, distribution requests, marriage, the highest duty, Office of the Beneficiary, protector; Family Wealth Ch. 10, 11, 19 — beneficiary and trustee responsibilities, the redesigned annual meeting, trustee as mentor; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 6, 8, 14 — spouses and the three-step communication process, humane trustscape, prenuptial agreements · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes — productive-behavior beneficiary terms as a contrasting drafting menu (paraphrased); Extension — the Advisor's position inside the trustscape and the sequencing are ours

46 — Trustee–beneficiary relationship

A trust is a relationship among a creator, a trustee, and a beneficiary that happens to live inside a legal document. Most families the practice serves hold the majority of their financial capital in trust by the third generation, and most beneficiaries experience those trusts as a burden. The Advisor sits inside the trustscape — next to the trustee (often [Trust Co.]), the beneficiary, and the creator — and this procedure defines what he does there: help the parties see the relationship, prepare each side for the other, run a real meeting, and turn the distributive function from an afterthought into the heart of the trust.

Purpose

  • Make every trust the practice touches a human relationship first and a legal one second.
  • Prepare beneficiaries to receive well and trustees to serve well, so that if the trust ended tomorrow the beneficiary could steward what it holds.
  • Give the distribution process a written, transparent, repeatable form.
  • Keep the Advisor's role clear: he advises, prepares, and coordinates; the trustee decides.

Trigger

Any of: a client is or becomes a beneficiary or trustee; a new trust is being drafted; a beneficiary reaches an age of notice or a trust becomes distributive; a distribution request is coming; a trustee–beneficiary meeting is due (at least annually); friction between trustee and beneficiary; a beneficiary's marriage or engagement; a trustee's succession.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: AA (trustscape map, meeting packs T22, request analysis support T23), CSA (scheduling, letters, records) · Consulted: the trustee ([Trust Co.] or individual), the trust protector if any, counsel for every drafting item, a counselor or family-governance facilitator from the EEN where relationships are strained, the ISB for trust administration questions.

Timing

Item Timing
Trustscape drawn and narratives audited At Discovery for any beneficiary or trustee client; refreshed annually
New-beneficiary introductory letters Within 30 days of the beneficiary's notice; first meeting within 60 days
Trustee–beneficiary meeting At least annually; quarterly where distributions are active
Accounting and trustee's questions to the beneficiary Two weeks before the meeting
Beneficiary's agenda additions and questions One week before the meeting
Follow-up call after a first or heavy meeting One week after
Distribution requests On the agreed calendar (quarterly for routine, annually for significant); emergencies as they arise
Relationship preamble and letters of wishes Reviewed every ten years and at any material change
Protector check-in Annually, with each party separately

Inputs

  • The trust instruments and any statements of purpose, letters of wishes, or legacy letters; the trust's investment policy; the last accounting.
  • The beneficiary's Total Client Profile (SOP 11) and, in Mode A, the family map and confidentiality matrix (T14).
  • The trustee's policies and procedures for distributions.
  • The consent on T05 governing what may be shared with the trustee and the family.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Trustscape drawn for each significant trust: every party, every adviser, the lines between them (see step 1).
  • [ ] Each party's narrative about the trust noted — positive and negative assumptions, and where they came from.
  • [ ] The trustee's three functions mapped (administration, investment, distribution) and who actually performs each.
  • [ ] The beneficiary's current literacy in each function noted in words.
  • [ ] Any pending distribution request identified and the request form (T23) started.
  • [ ] Conflicts of interest across the trustscape listed, disclosed, and a management note recorded (SOP 48).

Procedure

A. See the relationship

  1. Draw the trustscape. With the client, lay out the people and institutions around the trust as objects on a page — the client, family members, the trust itself, trustee(s), protector, committees, each party's advisers — placed by closeness and connected by lines. Photograph it. Then draw the trustscape the client would like to have. The gap between the two is the agenda.

  2. Audit the narratives. Ask each party, separately, what they believe about trusts in general, about this trust, about the other party, and where those beliefs came from. Ask which beliefs serve them and which do not. Do not argue with a narrative; name it, and ask what one small step would test it.

    Say something like

    "Everyone arrives at a trust with a story about it. Before we look at the document, tell me the story you've been carrying."

  3. Ask the two destination questions of whoever is in the room: what is the single most important reason this trust exists, and what is the most important outcome you want from it. If nobody can answer, the trust needs a statement of purpose (section C).

B. Prepare the trustee

  1. Brief prospective trustees at drafting time. When a client is about to name a trustee — or is asked to serve — walk the candidate through our selection topics (T24, Part 3): first reactions; document homework; self-inventory; yellow flags (strangers as beneficiaries, litigation history, multiple marriages or branches, addiction, special assets, a family business in the trust); and the deeper questions about oversight, disagreement, compensation, liability, and exit. A candidate who arrives already asking these questions is a good sign.
  2. Run the "which cap is on top" conversation for any family-member trustee: list every relationship the candidate has with the beneficiary (parent, aunt, business partner, friend); the trustee role must outrank all of them whenever the candidate is acting as trustee. Ask the candidate whether they can set the other caps aside; ask the creator whether they believe it.
  3. Position [Trust Co.] correctly. Where the firm's trust company is trustee, its strengths are administration, investment process, and continuity; its weakness is knowing the beneficiary. Compensate with a Distribution Committee and an Office of the Beneficiary (SOP 48) and with the Advisor's own relationship with the beneficiary.

C. Give the trust a voice

  1. Encourage the creator to write purpose language for counsel. A short opening statement of what the trust is for, in the creator's own words — a gift meant to enhance the beneficiaries' lives, not to control them — placed before the mechanics. Counsel drafts; the creator's words lead.
  2. Offer the three letters of wishes. Creator to beneficiaries (why, and hopes); creator to trustees (how to approach discretion, non-binding); and, later, trustee to successor trustees and beneficiaries (what this trust has meant in practice). Offer a legacy-letter outline where the creator wants to say more (purpose, exhibits, an ethical will, messages to each beneficiary, guidance to trustees, distribution principles).
  3. Broaden the purpose vocabulary beyond the customary health, education, maintenance, and support: productivity (a start-up, a lower-paid calling, a period of volunteering, a career coach), education defined to include lifelong learning, family unity (gatherings, facilitators, weddings, adoption), legacy (giving, memberships). Counsel decides what the document can carry; the family decides what it means.
  4. Name the trust deliberately. Five minutes at signing spares decades of statements headed by a surname and a legal phrase.
  5. Write a relationship preamble for existing trusts. Where the creator is gone or silent, trustee and beneficiary write their own short statement of how they will work together and what they understand the trust's purposes to be. Revisit it every ten years and at any material change: a new trustee or beneficiary, a sale of a key asset, a new life stage, a health change.

D. Onboard a new beneficiary

  1. Confirm the advance-notice plan (SOP 42). The parents or creator tell the beneficiary that the trust exists and what it is for; the trustee and the Advisor explain how it works. No beneficiary learns of a trust from a statement.
  2. Exchange introductory letters (T22). Trustee to beneficiary: who they are, when and where, hopes for the relationship, what will be covered, an invitation to add agenda items and bring written questions, and a request that the beneficiary read the instrument first. Beneficiary to trustee: who they are and what is going on in their life, what they hope for, their agenda items, advance notice of any request, a request for the agenda and materials. The Advisor drafts or coaches both sides where asked.
  3. Design the first meeting so that anxieties come before nuts and bolts: introductions; the trustee's short account of the role and the journey ahead; the beneficiary's questions and what they think they already know; then, and only then, the mechanics — roles, how to request funds and how requests are analyzed, a sample statement walked through, investments at whatever depth the beneficiary wants. Schedule the one-week follow-up call before leaving the room.

E. Run the meeting

  1. Prepare the mindset. Before each meeting the trustee (and the Advisor) decide whether this is a situation for caution or for advancement, and shift accordingly; recall meetings that helped someone grow; plan how to respond to the beneficiary's good news with genuine interest and open questions rather than a pivot to the statements; list the beneficiary's strengths, not their problems.
  2. Use the two premeeting checklists (T22). Trustee: instrument, correspondence, prior notes; the meeting's highest purpose and what an excellent outcome sounds like; own narratives; any pending request and the question that would open a deeper conversation; the big questions about the beneficiary's self-awareness, calling, mentor, and civic life — and whether the trustee is equipped to help. Beneficiary: the same documents; the running master list of questions; agenda additions; how a request would enhance their life; own narratives; own strengths.
  3. Run the redesigned annual format. Send the accounting two weeks ahead with a proposed agenda and the trustee's specific questions; the beneficiary reorders the agenda and adds their own questions a week ahead. Meet in the morning, in private (never a restaurant), for the business; keep any social time for afterward.
  4. Follow the standing agenda (T22): opening — what each hopes to accomplish and what success looks like; agenda confirmation; life changes since last time; status of prior to-dos → annual review block — the beneficiary's hopes, challenges, and opportunities for the year; the trustee's; what is working and what could improve; the beneficiary's assessment of the trustee's performance and the trustee's of the beneficiary's; disputes and next steps → technical block — statement, tax, quantitative items → distributions — new, pending, anticipated → close — to-dos, did we achieve what we hoped, what to change next time.
  5. Ask the distribution-readiness question at least annually, in both directions: if this trust had to be distributed tomorrow, would the beneficiary be ready to receive it — and what would each party do this year to make the answer "yes"?

F. Handle distribution requests

  1. Set the calendar. Routine requests quarterly, significant ones annually, emergencies as they arise; the calendar is stated at onboarding and on T23.
  2. Receive the request in writing (T23): purpose; amount; the trust language the beneficiary believes permits it; timing; related follow-on requests; other requests anticipated in the coming year. Supporting documents as appropriate — invoices, a budget, a business plan scaled to the ask, a statement of outside resources. Where apt, a short essay on how approval would enhance the beneficiary's life. In practice much of this is assembled together in conversation; the form is a thinking aid, not a hurdle.
  3. Stage 1 — the conversation. Before or after the written request: what motivates it and whether there is a larger purpose underneath; how it squares with the creator's intent and with the document; whether there is a better route than trust funds; whether the beneficiary will have their own resources in it; the best outcome if approved, short and long term; what changes if declined, and what alternatives would exist. Insert a growth question even in routine budget reviews — what does having the trust pay for this cost the beneficiary in independence?
  4. Stage 2 — the enhancement standard. Is making, or not making, this distribution more likely to enhance the beneficiary's life — meaning their maturation and pursuit of their own aims — or merely to subsidize it? This question will not be in the document; it is the practical expression of the trustee's fidelity to the purpose. It is life-stage dependent: a request from a professional in her forties is not a request from a twenty-one-year-old.
  5. Stage 3 — the document. Would approval be a reasonable exercise of discretion under the trust's language? If the language is narrower than the purpose, note it for the structural review (SOP 48).
  6. Stage 4 — prudence checks. Size relative to the trust; the beneficiary's request history and consistency with past decisions; one-off or part of a plan, and cumulative impact; requests anticipated this year and beyond; effect on other beneficiaries; whether outside resources must be considered; whether a loan, or part-loan part-distribution, would serve better (a residence financed as a mortgage keeps the beneficiary's own stake in it).
  7. Communicate the decision and the reasoning. Transparently, with questions answered. If declined, offer time to brainstorm other routes to the underlying goal. The trustee decides; the Advisor and any Distribution Committee advise.
  8. Write the decision memo (T23). Process, analysis, decision, alternatives offered, follow-up. Three uses: a template for future requests, a record for successor trustees, and evidence if the decision is questioned in the family or in court.

G. Develop the beneficiary

  1. Teach the beneficiary's responsibilities, in our words: understand each trust and its purpose; know what trustees must do; understand the balance between preserving purchasing power and paying a reasonable distribution; grasp asset allocation at a working level; look for evidence the trustee serves all beneficiaries; meet the trustee annually and give an assessment; know how the family's trust structure fits together; read a fiduciary accounting; take up the education offered; know what trustees and professionals are paid.
  2. Build literacy in the three functions — administration, investment, distribution — to the point that the beneficiary could receive the assets. Use the practice's own reporting and IPS as teaching material.
  3. Offer the Office of the Beneficiary (SOP 48). A small group the beneficiary convenes and pays for — an accountant who can teach, an investment expert, later a mentor for the psychological and career side — which the trustee acknowledges and supplies with documents. It may draw on family-office and [Firm] resources; it must not be housed in the family office, or it stops being the beneficiary's own. It is transitory by design.
  4. Practice gratitude deliberately. Once or twice a year, the beneficiary writes to the creator (living or not), or reflects on what the trust has taught them, and where the relationship was difficult, simply on what has been learned. A gift is incomplete until it is acknowledged.
  5. Support the trustee as mentor. The relationship begins as an arranged one; the trustee's early role is mentor, evolving toward representative as the beneficiary participates fully. When the beneficiary asks why they were given this gift and whether they are worthy of it, the answer must be truthful.

H. Guard the relationship

  1. Protector check-in. Where a protector exists (SOP 48), they ask each party separately, once a year, how it is going. In conflict, they ask each party what they themselves did or did not do that contributed, before deciding whether to switch on any power.
  2. Addiction and behavioral provisions. Where the family has any history of addiction or serious mental-health disorder, raise with counsel — before a problem exists — whether the trust carries workable provisions: discretion to withhold, authority to fund evaluation and treatment, a requirement of compliance and releases, testing, a defined recovery period, distributions to dependents while the beneficiary's are suspended, and an updating mechanism. Principles only; counsel drafts.
  3. Marriage. On any engagement, run the seven-step prenuptial communication (SOP 22): the family establishes what the member actually brings to the marriage as opposed to what is in trust; each parent clarifies their own feelings; the parents decide whether to leave the decision to the member; the member and the fiancé(e) clarify their own; parents and member talk for understanding; the couple talk; then decide how the process can support the new marriage. Trust interests are disclosed — disclosure is not access — and framed as family history, not protection against a person. Offer the Advisor or a counselor as translator between the family and both sets of lawyers.
  4. When to bring the expert into the room. For any complex solution — a decanting, a family limited partnership, a distribution committee — the relevant expert joins the beneficiary meeting in person or by phone.

Beyond Bowen — a contrasting drafting menu

Some families prefer trusts with no age-triggered distributions, eligibility conditioned on productive behavior, a short list of permitted purposes (career start, education, ventures, arts or humanitarian work, emergencies) and reciprocal duties (serve on committees, help manage property, help protect the enterprise). This is a legitimate design for counsel to consider, but it sits in tension with the beneficiary-agency model above — it substitutes rules for the trustee's discernment and the beneficiary's growth. Say which the family is choosing and why.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours of any meeting: recap to the parties as consent allows; to-dos assigned; T22 pack filed.
  • Within one week: follow-up call after a first or heavy meeting.
  • Within two weeks of a distribution decision: decision memo filed; beneficiary's notebook updated (T08).
  • Annually: the trustscape, narratives, and mutual assessments refreshed; the distribution-readiness question asked; letters of wishes reviewed against life changes.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Trustscape drawings (current and aspirational) [Document vault] trust folder AA
Narrative notes per party [CRM], restricted per T05 LA
Purpose statement, letters of wishes, legacy letter (drafted for counsel) Family's records; copy in the [Document vault] Creator; counsel
Introductory letters and first-meeting design (T22) [Document vault] LA / CSA
Meeting packs, agendas, mutual assessments (T22) [Document vault]; [CRM] activity AA / CSA
Distribution requests and decision memos (T23) Trustee's records; copy in the [Document vault] Trustee; AA
Beneficiary literacy notes and Office of the Beneficiary roster [CRM] LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Start the analysis of a request at the start of the relationship, not when the request arrives.
  • Put the beneficiary's questions before the statements.
  • Treat a beneficiary in their sixties as an adult; "newly notified" is not "young."
  • Document every discretionary decision.

Don't

  • Don't let the Advisor, a committee, or a protector make the distribution decision; the trustee decides.
  • Don't let a trustee's letter be the beneficiary's first notice of a trust.
  • Don't equate a beneficiary with their problems; list their strengths.
  • Don't sell perpetuity as a tax product (SOP 48).

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The Advisor coordinates the whole trustscape: trustee ([Trust Co.] or individual), protector, committees, and the family's counsel; the trust map is part of the family profile (T14).
  • Where a family member is trustee for a sibling, the "which cap is on top" conversation is repeated annually.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The Advisor supports his individual as a beneficiary within the family's trustscape: prepares them for meetings, helps them draft requests, and attends when invited; he does not redesign the family's trusts.
  • Requests and recaps go to the FCT or trustee only as the individual's consent on T05 allows.
  • Where [Trust Co.] is the family's trustee and also the Advisor's sister company, the confidentiality wall applies and is stated in writing.

Metrics

  • Trustee–beneficiary meetings held per beneficiary per year (target ≥1; quarterly where distributive).
  • Distribution requests with a written request and a decision memo (target 100%).
  • Beneficiaries with a documented "ready to receive" plan (target 100% of adult beneficiaries).

procedureOwner: LAMode Abeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — wealth enhancement and wealth transfer as advanced-planning areas; the expert network for structuring · Hughes: Family Wealth Ch. 5 and 7 — investor allocation, intrafamily lending, the family bank and its two loan types; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 20 — investor allocation preconditions, the family bank's governance guidelines and transparency rule; Compact — small joint successes; beginner's mind · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes — interest-free-but-repayable loans, the no-bailout rule, cost-elimination rationale, the managed slice, family investment-policy prompts (paraphrased); Extension — the Advisor's operating role and the procedure's sequencing are ours

47 — Family bank and investor allocation

Two family-level practices sit on top of ordinary asset allocation. Investor allocation decides which family member or entity holds each investment so that growth accrues where it is taxed least and held longest. The family bank lends to family members on terms no commercial lender would offer, because the return the family wants is the borrower's independence and competence as much as the interest. Both need counsel, a policy, and an administrator — the Advisor's role.

Purpose

  • Stop the default in which the oldest, wealthiest, most risk-averse member ends up holding the fastest-growing assets.
  • Move growth to the youngest members and the longest-term exempt trusts through documented, arm's-length intrafamily lending.
  • Give the family a lending institution that develops borrowers' human and intellectual capital and circulates knowledge across the family.
  • Keep the Advisor as designer, administrator, and reporter — never the lender of last resort or the judge of a member's worth.

Trigger

Any of: a new investment is proposed for the family; the family's mission statement commits to long-term growth of financial capital; a member asks the family for funding (a venture, an education, a home, a career change); trusts with broad investment discretion exist or are being drafted; the family council asks for a lending policy; a member is ready for a managed slice (SOP 42, T19).

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: AA (growth estimates, allocation memo, loan analysis, register), CSA (applications, minutes, loan register, calendar) · Consulted: counsel and the tax adviser (every loan and every allocation to a trust), trustees, the family council or principals, the family bank's board, [Trust Co.] where trusts lend or borrow, [ESOP Co.] where a member's venture or the family business is involved.

Timing

Item Timing
Investor-allocation policy adopted After the mission/values session (SOP 43) and before the next major investment
Allocation decision For every new investment above the family's stated threshold, before purchase
Family bank charter Within one quarter of the family's decision to lend
Loan applications On the bank's calendar (quarterly), emergencies excepted
Borrower reports Quarterly for investment loans; annually for enhancement loans
Bank review and report to the council Annually at the family meeting

Inputs

  • The family mission and values statement (SOP 43) with its commitment, if any, to long-term growth.
  • The family map and entity/trust map (T14): generations, ages, exempt long-term trusts, trustees and their discretion.
  • The investment plan and IPS for each household and trust (SOP 13).
  • Counsel's and the tax adviser's guidance on intrafamily loans, gifting capacity, and trust investment authority.
  • The family bank charter and forms (T20).

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Every family investment vehicle listed with its owner, horizon, and tax position.
  • [ ] Trust instruments checked with counsel for the breadth of investment discretion.
  • [ ] Each adult member asked whether they elect to participate in investor allocation.
  • [ ] The family's own investment-policy conversation held (step 3), recorded as prompts, not prescriptions.
  • [ ] Bank charter drafted from T20 with counsel's review of loan documentation and tax treatment.
  • [ ] Conflicts disclosed: the Advisor's fees on assets moved; sister companies' roles; [Firm Compliance] consulted.

Procedure

A. Investor allocation

  1. Confirm the preconditions. (a) The mission statement commits to long-term growth of financial capital; (b) each member elects to participate after weighing their own goals; (c) trustees, foundation directors, and managers of family vehicles agree to take part in the same spirit as the overall asset allocation; (d) the trusts grant, or can be given, broad investment discretion — trustees cannot surrender ultimate discretion, so the allocator respects it. If (a) or (b) is missing, stop; run the mission session first.
  2. Name the investor allocator. A family member, a family-office professional, or the Advisor. The role: for each proposed investment, estimate its long-term growth rate and recommend who should hold it.
  3. Hold the family investment-policy conversation. Prompts, not prescriptions — the firm's platform builds portfolios: how the family thinks about an operating business as a core holding; whether control of the business is ever for sale; whether illiquidity is a feature the family wants for some capital; where the family concentrates to build and diversifies to protect; how many major investment decisions a year the family wants to make. Record the answers in the family-level IPS (SOP 13).

  4. Map holders to horizons.

    Holder Horizon Takes
    Oldest generation ~20 years Lowest-growth, income-producing assets; current cash flow they actually want
    Middle generation ~50 years Intermediate growth
    Youngest members and the longest-term exempt trusts ~100 years Highest-growth, highest-risk assets

  5. Solve the funding problem with loans, not gifts. The youngest members and exempt trusts usually have the least money; gifts are capped. The primary mechanism is a loan from the oldest generation to the younger members (and, with careful legal advice, to exempt long-term trusts) to buy the growth asset. Rules: arm's-length terms; documented; counsel and the tax adviser confirm the loan will not be recharacterized as a gift; collateral and repayment liquidity planned in advance; the lender's own portfolio analyzed for how much should go into the program. The senior generation receives the interest income it wanted while the growth of that slice of its estate is capped.

    Caution

    Nothing in this section is tax or legal advice. Every allocation to a trust and every intrafamily loan is designed with counsel and the tax adviser before it is executed.

  6. Decide and document each allocation. The allocator's memo: the investment, its estimated growth, the recommended holder, the funding route, and the trustee's or member's decision. File with the investment plan; report annually to the council.

  7. Coordinate the trustees. Trustees hold the family's longest-horizon capital; their investment programs must be aligned with the family's allocation for the program to work. Where the family has a private trust company or common trust funds, every member can participate in every sector regardless of individual wealth.

B. The family bank

  1. Write the bank's mission statement (T20). Why it exists — a deliberately high-risk, low-interest lender whose return is measured in members' independence and the family's growth in human, intellectual, social, and spiritual capital — with a values section that incorporates the family's mission statement. Every participant, lender or borrower, concurs in writing.
  2. Keep it informal but ruled. Not a chartered institution (privacy; freedom to evolve), but with formal meeting rules, officers, a board (with advisers as needed), and written procedures for receiving and deciding applications. Rules vary with who funds the loans — members, trusts, or both.
  3. Define the two loan types.
    • Investment loans — to grow financial and intellectual capital by backing a member's business or an investor-allocation purchase. Process: the borrower prepares a business plan and an application equal to what a commercial lender would require; discusses feasibility with the board and its advisers; once granted, files proper business reports; repays.
    • Enhancement loans — to grow human, intellectual, social, and spiritual capital by increasing a member's independence (education, a career change, a start in life). The application states how the loan will increase the borrower's independence and add to the family's capitals; the borrower must be able to explain that to peers and advisers on the board. Repayment is measured in independence and capital as much as money.
  4. Set the terms as policy choices, in advance. Options the family may adopt: below-market interest; interest-free but repayable in full; grants for defined purposes; a no-bailout rule (the bank funds starts, education, homes, health, ventures — never the consequences of a member's own imprudence); collateral or none. Some families also use the bank to replace commercial mortgages, car loans, and certain insurance, lowering the family's total cost of living. Record the choices in the charter.
  5. Apply the transparency rule. Every participating member receives every loan application's qualitative portions — purpose, how it enhances, what it adds to the family; personal financial detail may be redacted. This circulation of intellectual capital is the bank's real return.
  6. Include the trusts. Trusts are potential lenders and borrowers; trustees must understand and agree to participate, and their instruments must permit it — counsel confirms.
  7. Decide and record. The board meets on the calendar; hears the applicant; decides; records the decision, terms, and reporting duties (T20); the CSA maintains the loan register; the AA reviews reports.
  8. Add the managed slice. Where a member is ready (T19), the bank or a household allocates a small sum — roughly half to one percent of family financial capital, or a fixed amount — for the member to manage with coaching. Mistakes are the curriculum; size it so they are affordable.
  9. Report annually. To the council or principals at the family meeting: loans made, repaid, outstanding; what borrowers reported learning; allocations made and their outcomes; policy changes proposed.

Follow-up

  • Within one week of a board meeting: decisions recorded; loan documents to counsel; register updated; applicants informed with reasons.
  • Quarterly: investment-loan reports received and reviewed; allocation memos filed with the investment plan.
  • Annually: bank and allocation report to the family meeting; charter and policies reviewed; every participant's concurrence renewed.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Investor-allocation policy and each allocation memo Family-level IPS (SOP 13); [Document vault] LA / AA
Intrafamily loan documents Counsel's file; copies in the [Document vault] Counsel
Family bank charter and mission statement (T20) Family's records; [Document vault] Family; CSA
Applications, decision records, loan register (T20) Bank's records kept by the CSA CSA
Borrower reports [Document vault]; summarized annually AA
Managed-slice records (T19) [CRM]; [Document vault] LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Treat the application process as the education — a real business plan, a real hearing.
  • Circulate every application's qualitative portions to everyone who participates.
  • Get counsel's and the tax adviser's sign-off before any loan or allocation to a trust.
  • Start with one small loan that succeeds.

Don't

  • Don't let the bank become a remittance channel; dependence on distributions is the liability the bank exists to prevent.
  • Don't let the Advisor or the board judge a member's worth; judge the application.
  • Don't allocate high-growth assets to trusts whose trustees have not agreed and whose instruments do not permit it.
  • Don't present Bonner's investment posture as the firm's advice; it is a conversation menu.

Metrics

  • Share of new family investments with an allocation memo before purchase.
  • Loans outstanding, repaid on schedule, and borrowers' reports filed on time.
  • Members holding a managed slice or a bank role as a share of adult members.

  • Extension — the Advisor's operating role and the sequencing are ours.

48 Trust system design and review

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — expert network; the private-client attorney as the most important member; bring the expert into the room · Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 17–21 and App. 3–6 — transitions, modification routes, succession, termination, the comprehensive model (DC, OTB, protector), private trust companies, Family Trust Review, perpetual trusts; Family Wealth Ch. 8, 11, 14, 15, 21 — protector, trustee reaffirmation, peer review, private trust company assessment, perpetual trusts; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 8 — the humane trustscape · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes — transfer techniques as agenda items for counsel; insurance objections as a devil's-advocate list (paraphrased); Extension — the trigger table, sequencing and the conflicts register are ours

48 — Trust system design and review

The ongoing trustee–beneficiary relationship (SOP 46) is continuous; the family's trust system changes at events — a new trust, a trustee's death, a beneficiary coming of age, a decanting, a termination, the decision to form a private trust company. This procedure handles those events: designing the roles around a trust so the trustee's highest duty can actually be met, reviewing the whole system on a ten-year horizon, commissioning a Family Trust Review when a transition calls for one, and closing trusts well.

Purpose

  • Design trust structures whose roles — trustee, Distribution Committee, Office of the Beneficiary, protector — are oriented to growing capable beneficiaries.
  • Review the family's trust system periodically for fit, cost, succession, and looming problems.
  • Handle modifications, successions, and terminations with every stakeholder involved.
  • Keep the Advisor as coordinator and translator; counsel drafts, the trustee decides, the family owns.

Trigger

Trigger Response in this procedure
A new trust or gift is being planned Section A (design) and the perpetual-trust counterweight (step 12)
A generational transition; a trustee or family leader stepping back Section B (ten-year review) and Section C (Family Trust Review)
A trust will terminate or make a large principal distribution within ten years Section C, then Section E (termination)
The family is considering decanting, reformation, or a private trust company Sections C and D
A trustee dies, resigns, or is to be replaced Section D (succession)
Beneficiaries and trustee are in persistent conflict Section D (protector) and SOP 46
Every three to five years, regardless Peer review (step 20); ten-year review refreshed

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: AA (trust inventory, cost tally, review worksheets T24), CSA (document collection, records, calendar) · Consulted: counsel (every drafting item), [Trust Co.] and any individual trustees, the protector, the family council or principals, a Family Trust Review consultant from the EEN, tax adviser, [Firm Compliance] for conflicts and fee disclosure.

Timing

Item Timing
Design conversation for a new trust Before counsel drafts; allow two to three meetings over 4–8 weeks
Ten-year trustscape review Every three years, and at every trigger above
Family Trust Review engagement 3–6 months from commissioning
Peer review of a trust or foundation Every three to five years; one day on site
Trustee reaffirmation Every five years
Termination protocol Begins at least two years before a scheduled termination
Conflicts register Reviewed annually with [Firm Compliance]

Inputs

  • Trust inventory: every instrument, purpose statement, letter of wishes, IPS, latest accounting, fee schedule, trustee and protector roster (T14 trust map).
  • The family map, decision rights, and transitions inventory (T14, SOP 44).
  • Trustee–beneficiary relationship notes and mutual assessments (SOP 46, T22).
  • The family's history, values, and executive summary (SOP 41).

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Every active trust listed with trustee, protector, beneficiaries, funding status, distribution activity, and fees (T24 Part 2).
  • [ ] Purpose language located for each trust — or its absence noted.
  • [ ] Succession position known for each trustee and for each beneficiary class.
  • [ ] Conflicts of interest across the trustscape listed (drafting attorney as trustee; institutional trustee with in-house investment; the firm's own sister companies; the Advisor's fees) and disclosed to creator, trustees, protector, and adult beneficiaries.
  • [ ] Counsel identified for the matter; where the family has counsel, they lead; the Advisor's EEN attorney fills gaps only.

Procedure

A. Design the roles around a new trust

  1. Start with the creator's exercise, not the document. Before any drafting, ask the creator to spend several days on one question: who can be counted on to advocate for this trust's highest purpose — the beneficiary's growth and eventual freedom — especially when the beneficiary is not in the room. Write the names down. Then the twist: those people may be better placed as protector or committee members than as trustee.
  2. Choose the protector first. The person with judgment and practical wisdom from step 1 becomes the protector — a narrow, largely dormant role: get to know trustee and beneficiary; ask each separately once a year how it is going; act only when asked; in conflict, ask each party what they contributed, then mediate; at impasse, remove and replace the trustee, or leave things as they are. The protector never decides a distribution. Because the role is not fiduciary in most places, people who would refuse trusteeship may accept it. Counsel confirms the design.
  3. Use an institutional trustee for administration and process. [Trust Co.] or another institution does what it does best — administration, investment process, continuity — and is informed on distributions by a Distribution Committee and on the beneficiary's development by an Office of the Beneficiary.
  4. Design the Distribution Committee (DC) for counsel. Its sole job: get to know each beneficiary before any request, understand the context when one is brewing, and advise the trustee. It never approves or declines. Drafting points: authorize it in the instrument, tied to the purpose statement; costs paid by the trust; members appointed by the creator, trustee, or an independent party in consultation with the primary beneficiaries; beneficiaries cannot add or remove members; five-year terms, two-term cap, age-out; each member nominates a successor; formal review of the DC every three years by trustee, protector, and beneficiaries. Members are chosen for the wisdom to ask broadening questions, the skill to listen before responding, and self-awareness — not technical trust knowledge. Where an existing trust lacks a DC, the trustee may convene one on its own initiative, or counsel may add it by settlement, reformation, decanting, or protector action. Do not combine the DC and the protector.
  5. Offer the Office of the Beneficiary (OTB). The beneficiary's own, transitory, beneficiary-funded team for becoming ready to receive: an accountant who teaches, an investment expert, later a mentor for the personal side. The trustee acknowledges it and supplies documents. It may draw on family-office and [Firm] resources; it must not be housed in the family office. Escalation logic: if a trustee consistently ignores DC advice, that is the moment to switch on the protector.
  6. Size the model. The full model suits trusts above roughly $10M; below that, a DC of one and an informal OTB. As family wealth approaches $100M, consider whether a private trust company should house these functions (step 22).
  7. Sequence the drafting agenda for counsel (this is a menu, not advice): purpose language and letters of wishes (SOP 46); fund growth assets into long-term trusts before they appreciate; leveraged sales to trusts, grantor-trust techniques, valuation discounts, trust situs and state tax — each as an item counsel evaluates; insurance-funded plans tested against a devil's-advocate list (compounding costs, counterparty lock-in, the fate of a lump-sum payout in the hands of an unprepared heir); addiction and behavioral provisions (SOP 46 step 34).
  8. Write the one-page summary and communication plan (T21) for every structure before it is signed — who will be told what, in what tone, by whom, when — and run the advance-notice rule (SOP 42).

B. Ten-year trustscape review

  1. Run the review worksheet (T24 Part 2) for the whole system: who serves as trustee and protector, and who the primary beneficiaries are; which trusts are active and funded; what each pays out now and is projected to pay over ten years; which will terminate within ten years; total fees to trustees, investment advisers, and other parties; what succession looks like if a trustee dies or steps down; what happens if a beneficiary or a whole class dies; where the foreseeable problem spots are.
  2. Tally the cost of the system across trustee, adviser, custody, tax, and legal fees. A quarter or half a point of trustee fee stacked on management fees compounds over generations; say so in numbers.
  3. Report to the principals and the council with recommendations: keep, simplify, modify, or commission a Family Trust Review.

C. Family Trust Review

  1. Commission it on a trigger: a generational transition; educating trustees, beneficiaries, or family-office and trust-company managers; a coming change in family or trust leadership; a termination or large principal distribution ahead; a decanting or reformation of a complex, costly system; the creation of new trusts or a private trust company. The perpetual-trust counterweight conversation belongs here too: before any dynasty structure, the family hears the unintended consequences (a class of beneficiaries who never own anything), society's likely view, and the certainty that nothing lasts forever.
  2. Engage the reviewer. Usually an EEN consultant experienced in multigenerational family enterprise; the Advisor coordinates and supplies data. Scope, timeline, interviewees, and fee on T24 Part 1.
  3. Three research activities: interview family leaders (and, where wise, adult beneficiaries and trustees); study written and oral accounts of the family's and the enterprise's history; review existing structures and documents.
  4. Five deliverables: a summary of family history with short biographies of leaders past and present; a history of the family enterprise and its philanthropy; a summary of the family's prominent values; a description of the existing trust system — architecture, how the trusts interact, and their costs; recommendations for trust-system design and for family education.
  5. Present to the family at a family meeting (SOP 43); feed recommendations into the advanced-planning tracker (T10), the governance work (SOP 45), and the learning plans (T19).

D. Modify, succeed, and guard

  1. Modification routes — involve every stakeholder. Options counsel will weigh: a non-judicial or judicial settlement agreement (least burdensome; can shift income terms or settle an interpretation; generally cannot create or destroy beneficial interests); judicial modification or reformation (long, costly, no guarantee); decanting (a new trust and usually a new situs; can add a protector, change administration, divide trustee duties; generally not beneficial interests). Whatever the route, someone left out of even a beneficial change may be aggrieved years later.
  2. Trustee succession is a duty from day one. Every trustee: keeps records a successor could pick up quickly; documents the reasoning behind major administration, investment, and distribution decisions; treats the beneficiary as a partner so skills outlive any one trustee; keeps candidates in mind and makes sure the beneficiary knows who holds the appointment power and has met the likely successors; and, where possible, serves side by side with the successor before stepping back. Where the beneficiary holds the power, the trustee guides them through interviewing and selecting.
  3. Trustee reaffirmation every five years. Beneficiaries confirm, in good faith, that they wish the trustee to continue; a trustee not endorsed resigns. Where an instrument cannot be amended, sitting trustees may agree voluntarily; make acceptance of reaffirmation a condition for successor trustees.
  4. Peer review every three to five years of each significant trust and foundation: reviewers of proven experience, independent of the family and its advisers, serving once, paid, one day on site; scope — fidelity to purpose, the empowerment of beneficiaries, beneficiary literacy and the mechanisms sustaining it, the trustee's awareness of each beneficiary's chosen path, and the policies and providers for investment, tax, and legal matters; conduct constructive; serious deficiencies stop the review and go to the selector; reviewers raise issues and never implement them; implementation is never assigned to a reviewer. The family council schedules it.
  5. Keep the conflicts register. Acknowledge every structural conflict (drafting attorney as trustee; institutional trustee with in-house investment management; a [Firm] sister company serving as trustee while the Advisor advises the beneficiary; the Advisor's own fees), document it, disclose it to creator, trustees, protector, and adult beneficiaries, and record how it is managed. Review annually with [Firm Compliance].
  6. Assess a private trust company (PTC) when wealth approaches the threshold. Factors: personnel turnover at commercial trustees; confidentiality; financial standing and investment competence; situs tax; insurance and bonding costs; the need for successors to individuals; chartering and operating cost; outside-trustee fees; the cost of managing in-house staff versus an outside relationship — and the subjective test: does a PTC fit the family's governance intentions? If yes, six practices: an annual or biennial meeting of beneficiaries, managers, and the owner-trustee; the family's values and history captured in a usable form for the independent managers; attention to the owner-trustee role; family engagement in the PTC's mission at least once a generation; the PTC as the locus of family education; the OTB available to every beneficiary. A protector remains necessary even with a family PTC.

E. Close a trust well

  1. Start two years out. Treat a scheduled termination or large principal distribution as the moment the trustee's highest duty stops being hypothetical: commission a review (Section C) and an OTB for each receiving beneficiary.
  2. Recognize a new gift. If terminating assets flow into new trusts — by will, by the beneficiaries' own plans, or by choice — a new gift is being made: run the creator's questions (purpose, hopes, recipients, integration, joy) and write a new purpose statement.
  3. Terminate with care. Full final accounting to present beneficiaries; a release after review; a closing gathering where beneficiaries reflect on the trust's effect, thank the creator and the trustees past and present, and discuss where they go from here; optionally a short written history of the trust for the family archive.
  4. Mark departures. When a trustee, protector, or adviser leaves the trustscape: a dinner, a letter of appreciation, a passing of the torch — step back, reflect and give thanks, return carrying the learning.

Follow-up

  • Within one week of any design meeting: counsel briefed in writing; T21 summary drafted; decisions logged.
  • Within 30 days of a ten-year review: report delivered; tracker (T10) updated with actions coded as completed / in progress / future.
  • Family Trust Review: recommendations tracked to closure at each annual family meeting.
  • Annually: conflicts register reviewed; succession answers refreshed; reaffirmation and peer-review dates checked on the calendar (T15).

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Role design memo for counsel (protector, DC, OTB, trustee) [Document vault] trust folder; counsel's file LA
DC charter checklist and roster (T24 Part 4) Trustee's records; copy in the [Document vault] Trustee
Ten-year trustscape review (T24 Part 2) [Document vault]; summary in the family profile AA
Family Trust Review engagement outline and report (T24 Part 1) Family's records; copy in the [Document vault] Reviewer; LA
Conflicts register [CRM] family record; [Firm Compliance] file LA
Reaffirmation and peer-review records Trustee's records; calendar (T15) Trustee; CSA
Termination file: final accounting, release, closing notes, trust history Trustee's records; family archive Trustee; CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Choose the protector before the trustee.
  • Put every conflict on paper and in front of every adult party.
  • Start termination work two years early.
  • Ask what harm a structure could do before asking what good.

Don't

  • Don't let the DC or the protector decide a distribution.
  • Don't fold the Office of the Beneficiary into the family office.
  • Don't sell perpetuity as a tax product; put the counterweight in front of the client.
  • Don't leave any beneficiary class out of a modification, however beneficial.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The Advisor coordinates the whole system with the family's counsel and trustees; the trust map on T14 is the master inventory.
  • The family council receives the ten-year review and schedules peer reviews and reaffirmations.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • The family's trust system is theirs; the Advisor contributes to reviews and designs only when invited by the FCT or a trustee.
  • For his own individuals, he prepares them for terminations and successions, helps them convene an OTB, and advises on requests (SOP 46) within the mandate on T05.
  • Where [Trust Co.] is the family's trustee, the confidentiality wall inside [Firm] applies to everything the Advisor learns from his individual.

Metrics

  • Trusts with a named protector and a functioning distribution-advice mechanism as a share of significant trusts.
  • Ten-year review refreshed within the last three years (yes/no per family).
  • Conflicts register reviewed and disclosed in the last twelve months (yes/no).

50 Asks inside service meetings — held-away assets and introductions

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 5 — the five-step asset-capture process; the twelve-step referral process; when to ask; common mistakes; Ch. 4 — ask points at the Mutual Commitment Meeting, the 45-Day Follow-up and every Regular Progress Meeting · Hughes: Compact — the family council as the family's voice to outside professionals; elders as intermediaries · Other: Extension — the Mode A routing through trustees and elders and the Mode B etiquette are ours

50 — Asks inside service meetings

Business development is handled elsewhere. What remains inside the service relationship are two asks that belong to the client experience itself: the invitation to bring held-away assets under one plan, and the invitation to introduce the practice to people the client cares about. Both are made at fixed moments in the sequence, in the same words every time, and both are followed through and thanked whatever the answer.

Purpose

  • Complete the client's financial picture by bringing assets held elsewhere into the plan — most families at this level have several advisors, and the Discovery profile shows exactly what sits where.
  • Grow the practice through people the client already trusts, without a marketing effort that would take time away from serving them.
  • Do both in a way that deepens the relationship rather than straining it.

Trigger

  • Part A (held-away assets): every Regular Progress Meeting; immediately after an advanced-planning win; when the profile or reporting shows assets outside the plan.
  • Part B (introductions): the Mutual Commitment Meeting (SOP 14), the 45-Day Follow-up (SOP 16), and every Regular Progress Meeting (SOP 20).
  • Both only where T05 permits; never in a Discovery meeting.

Roles

Owner: LA (makes every ask; nobody else) · Does: CSA (thank-you notes, contact records, prospect letters, report-back to the client), AA (held-away asset map from the profile and reporting) · Consulted: [Firm Compliance] for gifts and any referral arrangement.

Timing

When What
Before each RPM AA lists held-away assets and their managers from SOP 11 and SOP 24; CSA confirms on T05 that asks are permitted
In the meeting Asks come after the plan discussion and remaining questions, before scheduling the next meeting
Same day Handwritten thank-you for any introduction; [CRM] record of each ask and outcome
Within one week Each introduced prospect contacted; the client told what happened
After any outcome Thank the client again; gift within the limits set by [Firm Compliance]

Inputs

  • The Total Client Profile (assets and advisors areas) and the quarterly reporting package.
  • T05: asks permitted, and in what form.
  • The annual satisfaction survey results (SOP 25) — asks land best when satisfaction is high and are deferred when a service issue is open.
  • The practice's one-paragraph description of the families it serves best (from SOP 01), used verbatim in every introductions ask.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Held-away asset map current: what, where, who manages it, approximate size, any known dissatisfaction.
  • [ ] No open service failure with this client (SOP 23); if there is, defer both asks.
  • [ ] T05 permits the asks; Mode B limits noted.
  • [ ] Ideal-family description ready; handwritten note cards and stamps on hand.
  • [ ] [CRM] opportunity records ready to open.

Procedure

Part A — held-away assets

  1. Set expectations at every RPM. Remind the client that the practice cares about the whole picture — total allocation, total cost, total risk — including assets held elsewhere.

    Say something like

    "Part of my job is to keep the whole picture in view, including the accounts we don't manage; may we look at how those fit with the plan?"

  2. Review the relationship. Ask what the client likes and does not like about working with the practice; use the annual survey (SOP 25) as the formal version. A strong relationship, not performance, is what earns additional assets.

  3. Identify the opportunity from the profile. Name the specific held-away asset and why bringing it in serves the plan (allocation, cost, tax, simplicity, a single view for the family).
  4. Ask. Offer a second opinion on how the asset is managed, or ask directly whether the client would like the practice to manage it going forward. Ask when satisfaction is highest — at a progress meeting, or just after an advanced-planning solution has landed.
  5. Thank the client, whatever the answer, for the trust already placed in the practice.

Part B — introductions

  1. Set the stage. Explain, once, that introductions let the practice spend its time serving families rather than marketing, and that the practice would welcome serving people the client cares about.

  2. Ask, using the ideal-family description.

    Say something like

    "We work best with families like yours — several generations, real complexity, and a wish to keep the family together. Who else comes to mind who might value what we do for you?"

  3. Keep asking — "who else comes to mind?" — until the names stop. Expect two to five.

  4. Gather background and contact details only after the names stop, never interrupting the flow.
  5. Ask for a personal introduction — a call or note from the client so the prospect expects to hear from the practice. At this level a personal introduction is expected; a cold call is not made.
  6. Commit to follow up on every name, and say how.
  7. Wrap up by thanking the client and restating that their help lets the practice focus on them.
  8. Same day: handwritten thank-you note (print if handwriting is poor; email only as a last resort).
  9. Call each prospect within a week. Goal: a Discovery meeting.
    • No (usually "I already have an advisor") → offer a complimentary second opinion on their current plan.
    • Maybe (usually cost) → there is no cost for Discovery, and the practice only proceeds where it can add real value.
    • Yes → schedule; send the pre-meeting letter (T01) listing what to bring.
  10. Report back to the client — a short note, mindful of the prospect's confidentiality; silence devalues their effort.
  11. Thank again with a gift within [Firm Compliance] limits; a dinner for the couple beats dinner with the Advisor.

Follow-up

  • Every ask, outcome, and follow-through is logged in [CRM] the same day.
  • Second-opinion and held-away reviews are scheduled as a defined project with an expert where needed.
  • The client hears the result of every introduction, whether or not it becomes a relationship.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Held-away asset map and ask outcomes [CRM] opportunity records AA / CSA
Introductions: names, background, introduction method, outcome [CRM] CSA
Thank-you notes and gifts (with compliance limit check) [CRM] activity CSA
Report-back to the client [CRM]; note sent LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Ask in the same words every time; the consistency is the professionalism.
  • Ask when satisfaction is high; defer when a service issue is open.
  • Follow through on every name — the client will mention you to them.
  • Thank regardless of outcome.

Don't

  • Don't appear too busy to take on another family; the client will not add to your burden.
  • Don't chase introductions that do not fit the practice; judgment, not volume.
  • Don't interrupt the flow of names to take contact details.
  • Don't ask a prospect for anything; offer them a Discovery meeting or a second opinion.

Common mistakes: not asking; asking once and never again; making yourself seem too busy; failing to follow through; abandoning the ideal-family profile for a large but wrong-fit prospect.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Consolidation of assets held in trusts goes through the trustee relationship (SOP 46); the ask is made to the trustee and the beneficiaries together, never around the trustee.
  • Introductions are framed as other members or branches the family would like the practice to serve, routed through the elders or council where they exist (SOP 45); a new member enters through SOP 42.
  • The capacity framing, if used, is about serving the family well, not about scarcity.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Held-away assets: only those within the individual's own discretion and outside the family's central management, and only after confirming on T05 that the mandate welcomes it. Nothing is solicited that the FCT or a sister company of [Firm] manages.
  • Introductions: other members through the individual, with the FCT informed as agreed on T05; plus the ask to be introduced into the family team (CFO, CIO, trustee, counsel) so coordination starts.
  • The scarcity or capacity framing is dropped entirely.

Metrics

  • Share of RPMs where both asks were made when permitted (target 100%).
  • Held-away assets identified versus brought under the plan, per year.
  • Introductions received and Discovery meetings held from them, per year.

60 SOP maintenance and blueprinting

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 6 — blueprint every client-experience and business system; precisely define, perfect and write it down; staff have access and improve it; the founder does not blueprint alone; Ch. 6 — service failures resolved same day and used to improve the system · Other: Palaveev — the service-process definition checklist; hiring before the recipes exist as the named failure mode (paraphrased)

60 — SOP maintenance and blueprinting

This library is the practice's blueprint. It is only worth what it says today, so it is reviewed on a calendar, corrected whenever a service failure or a new hire exposes a gap, validated by the build tooling, and published in one shareable page. This procedure is how that happens and who does it.

Purpose

  • Keep every procedure precise, current and actually followed — the difference between a documented system and a good intention.
  • Turn service failures and new-hire questions into SOP improvements within the month.
  • Make the library the training curriculum and the proof, for the firm and for clients, that the practice runs on a system.

Trigger

Quarterly (SOP 74) and annually (T15, Q1 slot); and on any event: a service failure traced to a procedure (SOP 23), a new hire's question during onboarding (SOP 73), a regulatory or firm-policy change, a new service or template, or a document's updated date passing twelve months.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA as librarian (status tracking, build runs, change log, publishing), each document's owner for its review · Consulted: SA/AA as peer reviewers of changes; [Firm Compliance] for anything touching disclosures, consent or recording.

Timing

Cadence Action
Continuous Change requests logged as they arise
Monthly Service-failure log mapped to SOP steps (SOP 74)
Quarterly SOP review in the quarterly meeting: changed, failed, missing
Annually (Q1) Every document read by its owner; coverage audit; rebuild and republish; version tag
On hire The new hire's questions reviewed at the 90-day review and fixed

Inputs

  • Service-failure log (SOP 23); onboarding questions (SOP 73); quarterly-review notes (SOP 74).
  • The build tooling: python3 build/build.py --check, --write-index, --write-sources, and the build itself.
  • build/_skeletons.md — the conventions every document follows.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Change log current in the team folder (date, document, what changed, why, who reviewed).
  • [ ] For the annual review: each owner has the list of documents they own with updated dates.
  • [ ] --check passes on the current library before edits begin.

Procedure

  1. Own the library. The LA is accountable for the content; the CSA is the librarian who tracks status, runs the tooling and publishes. Every document has an owner in its front matter.
  2. Keep the status lifecycle. draft → in use (after the LA has run it once with a client) → reviewed with a new updated date at each annual review. A document with an updated date older than twelve months is flagged in the quarterly review.
  3. Change control. Anyone may propose a change; the document's owner drafts it; a second professional peer-reviews it (for a one-professional practice, the LA reviews the CSA's drafts and a sister-company colleague reviews the LA's when the change is material); the LA approves. Changes that alter what a client experiences — a meeting's structure, a report, a contact rule — are communicated to affected clients in the next confirmation letter or progress meeting (SOP 21), never discovered by them.
  4. Map every service failure to a step. In the monthly review, each entry in the failure log is traced to a procedure step that was missing, unclear or skipped. Missing or unclear → change request; skipped → coaching, and a check on whether the step is realistic.
  5. Run the quarterly SOP review (SOP 74 item): documents changed this quarter; documents implicated in failures; gaps noticed in client work; templates that were worked around rather than used — a workaround is a template defect.
  6. Run the annual review (Q1). Every owner reads every document they own with a client from the last quarter in mind and either confirms it or changes it. Then the coverage audit below. Then the rebuild: --check must pass; --write-index and --write-sources regenerate the README index and SOURCES; the build produces the shareable page; the repository is tagged with the year.
  7. Treat the library as the curriculum. New hires read it in the order set in SOP 73 and log every question; the 90-day review turns those questions into changes. A question a new hire had to ask is a sentence the document is missing.
  8. Invite improvement from the people who run the steps. The CSA and SA carry out most of the procedures daily and see the friction first; their suggestions are reviewed within the quarter and credited in the change log. The founder does not blueprint alone.
  9. Publish and share. After each annual review and after any material change, republish the page and tell the team where the current version is. Old versions are kept for reference, never used.

Beyond Bowen

Service-process coverage audit — once a year, confirm the library answers each of these for the practice; every "no" or "unclear" becomes a change request.

  • What information do we collect from a prospective and current client, where is it stored, and how is it secured?
  • How are services proposed, with what documents, and who signs off?
  • How is the fee determined for each segment and scope (T05; SOP 14)?
  • Which legal documents and disclosures does each engagement require, and who checks them?
  • What is the scope of planning we deliver, with which tool, and what exceptions are permitted?
  • What is the investment philosophy, how is it implemented, and which decisions belong to the firm's platform rather than to us?
  • When is a portfolio or a report customized, and how is that customization priced?
  • Which reports go to which clients, on what cadence?
  • Who is each client's point of contact, for what, and in which situations does that change?
  • How often does each segment meet us, and what is the standard preparation?
  • How are plans, portfolios and client data reviewed and updated, and how are changes decided, implemented and recorded?
  • Who trades and how (platform), and what do we verify?
  • How does the investment committee (firm) communicate decisions to us, and how do we pass them to clients?
  • What is the quality-control process that prevents errors in plans, portfolios and documents?
  • Which steps in the library are performed by borrowed specialists or vendors, and what would happen if each disappeared tomorrow?

Follow-up

  • Within the week: change requests from failures and new-hire questions logged.
  • Within the quarter: changes drafted, peer-reviewed, approved, and clients told where the experience changes.
  • Annually: rebuild, republish, tag; the coverage audit's open items carried into the next quarter's list.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Change log Team folder CSA
Updated documents with new updated dates and status Library Document owner
--check result, README index, SOURCES Library (generated) CSA
Published page and version tag dist/ and the shared link; repository tag CSA
Coverage-audit results and open items Team folder; quarterly review LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Change the document, not just the behavior; a fix that lives in one person's head is not a fix.
  • Keep the tooling green — a broken link or a missing section is a symptom of a document nobody is using.
  • Credit the people who improve the blueprints.

Don't

  • Don't hire before the recipes are written; the first professional's productivity depends on this library existing.
  • Don't let documents drift into "everyone knows we don't really do that" — remove or fix the step.
  • Don't change a client-facing procedure without telling the affected clients.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Family-layer documents (40–48) are reviewed with the last family meeting and trustee cycle in mind; T14 and T16 usage is part of the audit.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • SOP 33 and T05 are reviewed against every current FCT protocol; any protocol a family's central team imposed in writing is reflected in the library, not held only in email.

Metrics

  • Documents with an updated date within twelve months (target 100%).
  • Service failures mapped to an SOP step within the month (target 100%).
  • New-hire questions converted to changes by the 90-day review (count; trend down over successive hires).
