Team building

70 Team roadmap — from solo with borrowed expertise to an ensemble

referenceOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 6 — blueprint every system before delegating it; Ch. 7 — drop / defer / delegate / do · Hughes: Compact — 'who is your successor?' asked of every leader · Other: Palaveev, The Ensemble Practice — ensemble definition, stages, capacity and economics triggers, leverage arithmetic, readiness tests, delivery unit, ratios, compensation and ownership principles, failure modes (paraphrased)

70 — Team roadmap

The practice is a solo profit center inside a federated firm, with specialists borrowed from sister companies. This reference is the map from that starting point to an ensemble: what each stage looks like, the numbers that say when to hire, what the Advisor stops doing at each step, and the principles that keep compensation and ownership sane. Procedures 71–74 execute it.

Purpose

  • Give the Advisor and the firm a shared picture of where the practice is, what the next stage requires, and which trigger fires the next hire.
  • Fix the sequence: borrow first, hire when the numbers say so, delegate in a set order — so the client experience never depends on who happens to be free.
  • Keep compensation and equity decisions principled before there is anyone to negotiate with.

The stages of a practice

Stage Revenue marker (profit center) What it looks like Management priority This practice
Practice growth ~$0.5–1M The owner is the business; clients accepted opportunistically; value proposition = the owner's attention Reach critical mass of relationships so referral sources treat the practice as established Entry point today
Team service ~$1–3M Staff hired for named functions (CSA, then SA); delivery becomes a team but the value proposition still rests on the owner; training and management become daily work Define the service and how it is delivered — decisions made here persist for a decade Target for the next 24 months
Partnership ~$3–10M Non-owner professionals serve clients independently; written service standards are followed; explicit client selection; a management team Institutionalize the reputation — stop being one person's practice Later
Past the owners > $10M The value proposition is the firm's, not a person's; departments; ownership and management separate Combine necessary structure with surviving entrepreneurship Not in scope

The size self-test. The day there is a client the Advisor has never met, the practice is a true ensemble. The day there is an employee he has never met, it is a large one. The day there is a partner he has never met, it may be too large.

Ensemble or silo?

The test is economic, not organizational: what share of a principal's income comes from a shared bottom line? Roughly 40–50% shared is an ensemble; 5–10% shared is a silo that happens to share an address. Inside a federated firm the same test applies twice — to the Advisor's own future team, and to his profit center's relationship with the firm: if borrowed specialists are paid only per transaction and nothing flows into a shared pool, cooperation will stay transactional (see SOP 71 for the credit rules that keep it from becoming so).

The borrow-then-build sequence

Step Configuration What the Advisor stops doing Trigger to move on
0 — Now LA + [Firm shared services] for administration + ISB and EEN per matter (SOP 71) Nothing yet; but every activity is written down (this library) Recipes written; capacity strain visible
1 — First hire: CSA LA + CSA + borrowed specialists Scheduling, correspondence, paperwork, transfers, notebook, [CRM], reporting assembly Recurring administrative errors, or the LA spends > 25% of client-facing hours on CSA work
2 — Second hire: Service Advisor LA + SA + CSA (the canonical delivery unit) Plan and portfolio production; periodic reviews; routine progress meetings (co-attended → independent) ~$500–700K revenue and ~40 relationships, or the Discovery pipeline exceeds what the LA can prepare for
3 — Third: Associate / Analyst LA + SA + AA + CSA Drafting, analysis, packets, tracker upkeep, case briefs ~$1M revenue with two professionals; relationship size justifies a third level
4 — Depth A second SA, or an operations lead grown from the CSA seat Relationship management of a defined book Revenue per professional back above ~$500K after step 3; a single-point-of-failure risk in either track

Triggers — the numbers

Trigger Threshold Action
Affordability of the first professional ~$500K revenue. Overhead in a lean profit center runs ~$120–150K (one administrative salary plus space and systems); what is left after tax, minus the founder's bogey (the pre-tax income the household needs), is the hiring budget Compute the bogey on T28; if the surplus covers a Service Advisor's total cost with margin for a market decline, hire
Optimal economics ~$700K revenue with professional compensation (owner's market salary plus the hire) at ~40% of revenue Treat as the comfortable point; hiring earlier is a deliberate investment, not a mistake
Revenue per professional (owner included) ~$500K is the working norm; add the third professional when two of them pass ~$1M Review semiannually in SOP 74
Revenue per head (owners and staff) < ~$200K suggests too many hires too early; > ~$250K says it is time to hire Review semiannually
Relationships per professional ~40 in a practice serving $30M+ families (more in an affluent practice) Count relationships, not accounts; a family is one relationship
Time per relationship ~20 hours a year of professional time; ~1,600 client-facing hours per advisor per year Capacity = hours ÷ hours per relationship; log borrowed and delegated hours on T28
Hire ahead of capacity A new professional takes up to a year to be fully productive Start the search when the trigger is approaching, not after it is breached

The leverage arithmetic. Delegating half of the professional time in each relationship to a Service Advisor roughly doubles the practice's capacity at a fraction of the owner's cost. With 40 relationships at an average annual fee F, revenue is 40F; if the owner's market salary is S and the SA's total cost is C, professional compensation moves from S ÷ 40F to (S + C) ÷ 80F once the second forty relationships are in place — and the owner's time shifts toward the largest relationships, quality control, and the asks. The arithmetic only works if the SA is productive from the first month, which is why the recipes come first.

Readiness — five self-tests before the first professional hire

  1. Can the role be given specific, consistent responsibilities on day one? Hiring someone to watch the Advisor work is a cost and a demoralizer.
  2. Is there a written service process another person can follow? "I listen and respond to what they need" is not a process. This library is the answer to this test.
  3. Can the practice offer a career path and tolerate a second professional — including, eventually, giving that person relationships of their own?
  4. Will the Advisor hold himself accountable to the process and to the person?
  5. Can the practice afford it after the bogey, with room for a bad year?

The delivery unit

One lead advisor, one service professional, and operations support is the unit that serves a family. It balances capacity, economics, and mentoring, and it remains the building block even inside a large firm. Every SOP in this library names those three roles for that reason.

The founder's role and the delegation order

Stage The Advisor's client-facing time goes to Delegated in this order
0 Everything — (borrowed specialists take defined deliverables only)
1 Meetings, plans, asks, coordination 1. Routine execution → CSA
2 Discovery, plan presentations, asks, drop/defer/do, network and family facilitation, the largest relationships 2. Plan and portfolio production, periodic reviews → SA · 3. Routine progress meetings: co-attended, then SA-led with the LA present, then independent
3 Quality control, largest relationships, business-development handoffs, team management 4. Relationship management (the client calls the SA first) · 5. Relationship ownership (all meetings including strategy), each gated by the tests in SOP 73
4 Strategy, the firm relationship, the next generation of the team 6. Business development — last; it requires a decade of experience and is outside this library

Two Bowen habits govern every step: apply drop / defer / delegate / do to each task in that order, and never delegate a step that has not been written down.

Dashboard and the common-sized P&L

Ratio Reads Cadence
Earnings before owner compensation (EBOC) Basic profitability; ~50–60% of revenue is typical for a $1–5M practice, higher for a very small one Monthly
Overhead % of revenue Spending on "stuff"; ~35% is the guideline Monthly
Revenue per staff head Staffing pace (the < $200K / > $250K bands above) Semiannual, in budgeting
Revenue per professional When to hire professionals rather than operations (~$500K) Semiannual
Revenue per relationship Relationship size and scope; drives minimums and service design Trend

The common-sized guideline: revenue 100 → professional compensation (owner at a market salary plus employee professionals) ~40 → gross profit ~60 → overhead ~35 → operating profit ~25. CSA and administrative staff sit in overhead; anyone titled advisor, associate, analyst or planner sits in professional compensation. Vote the owner a market salary for this analysis so that profit is real, not residual.

Compensation and ownership — principles only

  • Pay the position, not the person's history. Salary ranges sit roughly ±20% around a credible survey midpoint; movement within the range follows responsibility, experience and relevant credentials, not tenure.
  • Labor and equity are different payments. An owner earns a market salary for the job done and a return on equity for the capital owned; confusing the two is what makes "equal partners" unequal.
  • Install a compensation system by the second employee professional. Individual deals stop working past two or three people.
  • Incentives are 5–25% of salary, funded above a revenue threshold so that a bad year pays zero rather than draining the practice.
  • Partnership, when it comes, follows revenue: roughly one partner per $750K–1M of revenue; criteria published in advance; equity is bought, never granted — loyalty is expressed in financing terms.
  • Hold an equity conversation once a year even before there is anyone to admit, so the trajectory is deliberate. Ask of every leader, including the Advisor: who is your successor?

Failure modes by stage

Stage Failure mode Guard
Solo Hiring the first known candidate; hiring before the recipes exist; hiring beyond the bogey; salary-plus-payout hybrids; a veiled partnership promise SOP 72; this library; T28; SOP 72's offer rules and equity scripts
First team Keeping the new professional out of client meetings; giving them only the small clients; expecting business development from someone a decade short of it; a single junior with no depth; the first hire plateauing and blocking growth SOP 73; SOP 73's promotion tests; hire ahead of capacity
Partnership Silo economics; agreeing to disagree; cancelled partner meetings; owner salaries anchored to prior-employer income; payouts so high nothing is left to own SOP 74; the principles above

Revenue (profit center) ______ ______ ______
Professional hours available / used __ / ____

71 Engaging borrowed expertise — the internal bench and shared services

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the expert network: the client is yours; fees disclosed; four vetting traits · Hughes: Compact — the personne de confiance intermediates outward to raise the quality of what other professionals deliver · Other: Palaveev — profit-center and shared-resource rules, internal cross-referral norms, vendor questions, anti-captivity principle, 'whoever has the ball is the quarterback' (paraphrased)

71 — Engaging borrowed expertise

The practice serves $30M+ families with one professional today. It can do so because the firm's sister companies — [Trust Co.], [ESOP Co.], sister RIAs, tax, insurance and lending specialists — and [Firm shared services] can be borrowed per matter. This procedure makes that borrowing systematic: scoped in writing, walled where it must be, credited fairly, delivered through the Lead Advisor, and logged so it feeds the capacity model. It covers outsourced paraplanning and back-office vendors the same way.

Purpose

  • Put the right expertise in front of a family within days, without the client ever feeling handed off.
  • Keep the relationship, the decisions and the accountability with the LA while the work is done by someone else.
  • Protect confidentiality inside a firm whose sister companies may already serve the same family in another capacity.
  • Make every engagement improve the bench roster in SOP 31.

Trigger

Any of: a Total Client Profile gap, a tracker item (T07/T10), an expert-network meeting output (SOP 32), or a client request that needs expertise the LA does not hold or hours the LA does not have — or a routine function (paraplanning, reporting, transfers) that the practice has chosen to outsource.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (request logistics, memo circulation, hours log, roster update), AA (data pack for the specialist) · Consulted: ISB or vendor specialist; [Firm Compliance] on disclosure, fee sharing and walls.

Timing

Step When
Request and resource choice Within 2 business days of the trigger
Scope memo agreed (T25) Within 5 business days
Client introduction Before the specialist sees any client data beyond what the memo allows
Delivery and LA sign-off Per the memo; never later than the next scheduled client meeting it feeds
Debrief and scorecard Within one week of delivery
Standing-vendor review Annually, with the external-relationship review in SOP 31

Inputs

  • The item that triggered the need, with the client's TCP context (SOP 11) and T05 (mode, scope, consent).
  • The bench roster and scorecards (SOP 31); the firm's policy on internal referrals, credit and fee sharing.
  • Any existing relationship the sister company has with this family (checked in [CRM] and with the sister company).

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Need stated in one sentence: what question must be answered, for whom, by when.
  • [ ] T05 consulted: is this matter in scope, and who may receive the client's information?
  • [ ] Conflict and wall check: does any sister company already serve this family or its central team?
  • [ ] Resource chosen (internal bench / external network / the client's own advisor) using the rule below.
  • [ ] T25 drafted.

Procedure

  1. State the need and choose the resource. Write the one-sentence need. Apply the rule: use the internal bench when the expertise exists in the firm and independence is not compromised; use the external network when independence matters (for example insurance, or a second opinion on a sister company's own product), when the expertise is missing internally, or when the client prefers it; use the client's existing advisor when they already have a competent one — coordinate under SOP 33 rather than duplicate.
  2. Clear conflicts and declare the wall. Ask the sister company whether it serves this family in any capacity. If it does — especially if it sits on a Mode B family's central team — record the confidentiality wall on T25: which people may see which information, and that nothing learned for this engagement flows to the sister company's other relationship with the family. Confirm with [Firm Compliance] where a wall is needed.
  3. Write the scope memo (T25). Deliverable, timeline, data the specialist will receive, whether the specialist is client-facing, who signs off, and the credit or fee basis. A memo of five lines is enough for a small matter; no matter proceeds without one.
  4. Agree credit and compensation, then disclose. Follow [Firm] policy. Where internal credit is paid for a referral it is a modest share of first-year revenue (norms in the industry cluster around 5–15%) and always below what an external referral source would receive; legal fees are never shared. Disclose to the client in writing what is being paid to whom, through [Firm Compliance]. Investment-management fees for the Advisor's own work are priced as the premium for coordinating everything else, not padded by the specialist's charge.

  5. Introduce the specialist to the client — by name, role, and what they will do for this family, in the meeting or in the confirmation letter (T01). State plainly that the LA remains the client's point of contact.

    Say something like

    "For the succession question I've asked our firm's ESOP team to model the options; you'll meet Dana at our next meeting, and everything still comes back through me."

  6. Supply the data pack. The AA or CSA sends only the information the memo allows, in the format the specialist needs, with the client's consent noted on T05.

  7. Deliver through the LA. The specialist works to the LA unless the memo names them client-facing for a defined part. Questions from the client go to the LA; the LA answers or brings the specialist in. Whoever receives a question owns it to completion — nobody is "put through to someone."
  8. Quality check and sign-off. The LA reviews the deliverable for fit with the family's profile and the plan before anything reaches the client. Complex items are presented with the specialist in the room (SOP 20).
  9. Debrief and score. Within a week: what was delivered, on time or not, how the client responded, what would be done differently. Score expertise, integrity, professionalism, chemistry, timeliness and client feedback on T25; update the bench roster in SOP 31.
  10. Log the hours. Record borrowed hours against the relationship in [CRM] and on T28 so that capacity planning in SOP 70 counts what the bench is carrying — that number is part of the case for the next hire.
  11. Review standing arrangements annually. For any vendor or sister-company service used routinely, ask the six questions: is their strategy a fit with ours; exclusive or one of several, and what does exclusivity buy; how concentrated is our dependence and does it buy better service; how durable are they (ownership, exit risk); how much will they customize; how will clients perceive them if they look them up.

Anti-captivity

Own the process even when the platform or a sister company does the work. Keep the data, the templates and the client relationship in the practice's own systems so that the service survives a change of vendor or a reorganization inside the firm.

Beyond Bowen

Bowen's expert network assumes external free agents. The internal-bench protocol, the confidentiality wall inside a federated firm, the credit norms and the capacity log are our own, informed by Palaveev's profit-center and vendor rules.

Follow-up

  • Within 24 hours of delivery: the client receives the LA's summary and knows the next step.
  • Within one week: debrief held, scorecard filed, roster updated, hours logged.
  • Annually: standing vendors and bench members reviewed together with the external network (SOP 31).

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Scope memo and wall declaration (T25) [CRM] activity; client's [Document vault] CSA
Disclosure of credit or fees Client file; [Firm Compliance] record LA
Deliverable and LA sign-off [Document vault]; tracker updated (T07/T10) LA
Debrief and scorecard Bench roster (SOP 31) CSA
Hours logged [CRM]; T28 capacity worksheet CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Use the internal bench generously — it is the practice's competitive edge — but scope every engagement in writing.
  • Tell the client who is being paid what, before the work starts.
  • Keep one thread: the LA is the voice to the client; the specialist speaks in the room with the LA present.

Don't

  • Don't let a sister company become the family's primary contact through the back door.
  • Don't share a client's information with a sister company that serves the family elsewhere without the wall declared and the client's consent.
  • Don't accept a deliverable you cannot explain to the client yourself.
  • Don't build the practice's process inside a vendor's system.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The bench and the external network are coordinated by the LA as the family's personal CFO; the family's incumbent advisors are brought in under SOP 33, not replaced by the bench.
  • Where the family has a council, the LA tells the council which specialists are engaged on family-level matters.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Check first whether the sister company already serves the family's central team; if so the wall on T25 is mandatory and [Firm Compliance] signs it.
  • The family's counsel and trust company are the default experts for family-level matters; the bench fills gaps for the individual's own affairs only, with the FCT aware as agreed on T05.
  • Credit and fees are disclosed to the individual and, where the FCT gatekeeps professional relationships, to the FCT.

Metrics

  • Share of borrowed engagements with a scope memo before work started (target 100%).
  • Borrowed hours per quarter, by relationship (feeds SOP 70 triggers).
  • Average scorecard rating of bench members; number of members below threshold acted on within a quarter.

72 Hiring a team member

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 6 — hire for genuine emotional warmth; service failures are relationship failures · Other: Palaveev — hiring protocol, job description contents, candidate archetypes, offer rules, equity-question scripts, first-hire sequencing (paraphrased)

72 — Hiring a team member

The practice hires in a fixed order — a Client Service Associate first, a Service Advisor second, an Associate/Analyst third — and only when the triggers in SOP 70 say so. This procedure runs each hire the same way: the role is defined before the advertisement, the search produces real choice, the process is never shortened for a candidate in a hurry, and the offer pays the position rather than the person's history.

Purpose

  • Fill each seat in SOP 03 with someone who is productive within the first quarter and on a path the practice can sustain.
  • Prevent the classic first-hire mistakes: the one-horse race, the custom deal, the veiled partnership promise, the relative nobody will manage.
  • Keep the client experience stable through the hire — the procedures do not change; who performs them does.

Trigger

A trigger in SOP 70 is reached or clearly approaching, the five readiness tests pass, and the bogey worksheet on T28 shows the hire is affordable through a bad year.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (postings, scheduling, candidate correspondence, reference logistics — for the first hire, [Firm shared services]), [Firm] human resources where it exists (background checks, offer paperwork, compensation bands) · Consulted: a sister-company leader or the firm's head of advice as a second interviewer; [Firm Compliance] on licensing and non-solicitation language.

Timing

Step Elapsed
Role defined and description written (T26) Week 0–1
Search open; ten qualified résumés Weeks 1–5 (longer for a Service Advisor — they are scarce)
Screens and first interviews Weeks 4–7
Work sample, checks, second interviews Weeks 6–9
Offer and acceptance Week 9–10
Start Notice period + 2 weeks to prepare onboarding (SOP 73)

Start the search when the trigger is approaching: a professional takes up to a year to reach full productivity.

Inputs

  • SOP 03 role definition; SOP 70 trigger reading and readiness tests; T28 bogey and capacity worksheet.
  • [Firm] compensation bands and, where available, industry salary surveys for the role.
  • The library itself — the new person's curriculum and the proof that the recipes exist.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] The role's responsibilities, reporting line, measures of success, required and desirable qualifications written on T26.
  • [ ] Internal compensation range set (survey midpoint ±20%, reconciled with [Firm] bands) and the factors that move a person within it.
  • [ ] Scorecard weights set for the three dimensions (technical; client relationship; business development) — for a CSA, technical and relationship only.
  • [ ] Interview panel named (the LA plus one other; never the LA alone for a professional hire).
  • [ ] Sourcing plan: inside [Firm] first, then external channels.
  • [ ] Non-solicitation and offer templates reviewed by counsel / [Firm Compliance].

Procedure

  1. Confirm the trigger and the affordability. Record the SOP 70 reading, the readiness tests and the bogey result in the hiring file. If the surplus does not cover a bad year, borrow more (SOP 71) and revisit next quarter.
  2. Define the role before the advertisement. Complete T26: responsibilities; place in the practice and reporting line; key measures of success; required skills and knowledge; required experience; desirable extras. Keep the compensation range internal.
  3. Build the scorecard. Three dimensions — technical and theoretical knowledge; client-relationship skill; business-development capacity — weighted for the role. A Service Advisor is scored heavily on the first two and lightly on the third; nobody is hired for sales.
  4. Source widely; inside the firm first. Post inside [Firm] and ask sister-company leaders for candidates; then professional associations, job boards, professional networks, and referrals from colleagues and centers of influence. Do not begin interviewing until there are at least ten qualified résumés; if there are fewer, widen the search. Referred candidates submit a résumé and go through the identical process.
  5. Screen résumés against the description, not against a feeling. Reject early and courteously.
  6. First interview. Past experience; career goals; proficiency in the professional topics the role needs; communication style. Note the candidate's questions — a candidate who asks about the service process and the career path is signaling seriousness.
  7. Work sample or short case. For a Service Advisor: a small planning or portfolio case using the practice's own templates (T06/T10) and a five-minute presentation of it. For a CSA: an implementation-tracker exercise and a client-correspondence draft (T01). Score it against the scorecard.
  8. Background check and references. The background check is mandatory and precedes the second interview. Ask each reference for the name of someone else who worked with the candidate and call them too; unselected references speak more freely.
  9. Optional matching test for communication and thinking style, used to shape the second interview's questions rather than to decide.
  10. Second interview. Probe the concerns raised by the sample and the checks; test the ability to work inside a team and to hold a client's confidence; discuss the career path honestly. Answer the equity question with the scripts below and nothing more.
  11. Decide with the scorecard, not with the calendar. If no candidate clears the bar, reopen the search — a wrong first hire costs more than a late one. If the strongest candidate is a relative or friend, hire only if the practice will manage them exactly as anyone else and they have already built a career elsewhere.
  12. Make the offer in writing. Title and reporting line; start date; salary within the range; how the incentive works, honestly; benefits and time off as they actually are; non-solicitation language drafted by counsel; the probationary review at 90 days. Do not haggle — listen to a well-argued objection and, if valid, reissue a revised offer once. Pay the position, not the candidate's blended memory of their best year. Never shorten the process because a candidate must decide by Monday.
  13. Complete the start-date checklist. Accounts and licenses; [CRM] and [Custodian] access at the right level; a desk and the reading order; the first-month meeting calendar with named roles; the onboarding plan (T27). Hand over to SOP 73.

Candidate archetypes — what each brings and what to check

Archetype Strength Check before hiring
Entry-level professional Theory, energy, affordability A decade from business development; needs the full curriculum and second-chair time
Technician (planner, analyst wanting to advise) Technical depth; slots into many roles Client skill untested; compensation expectations may exceed the role
Existing service professional The ideal Service Advisor Rare; ask why they are available; good firms keep them
Career changer Client skill, maturity, sometimes networks Technical gaps; salary history that will not fit the range
Experienced broker or advisor with a book Capability Product habits; difficulty sharing clients; this is a merger conversation, not a hire

The equity question — how to answer

Say something like

"Ownership is possible in this practice for someone who becomes a lead advisor and contributes to growth; the criteria will be written and applied the same way for everyone, and I make no promise today."

Never imply a promise you do not intend to keep, and never dodge the question; a clean "not now, and here is what would have to be true" keeps trust.

Hiring sequence for this practice

  1. CSA — support track; sits in overhead; removes routine execution from the LA.
  2. Service Advisor — the first professional; must be able to serve existing relationships independently from the first quarter. Prefer this over a paraplanner if only one professional hire is affordable: the leverage is far greater.
  3. Associate / Analyst — when relationship size justifies a third professional level and there is enough substantive work for it.

Follow-up

  • Same day as acceptance: welcome note; onboarding plan (T27) started; team and, where relevant, [Firm] leadership informed before any client hears of it.
  • Before day one: the first 30 days of client meetings scheduled with the new person's named role in each (SOP 73).
  • Unsuccessful candidates told promptly and courteously — some will be colleagues or referral sources later.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Role definition, scorecard, compensation range (T26) Hiring file (LA only for the range) LA
Candidate pipeline and scores Hiring file CSA
Background and reference results [Firm] HR file [Firm] HR / LA
Signed offer and non-solicitation [Firm] HR file LA
Start-date checklist Onboarding file → SOP 73 CSA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Write the role first; advertise second; interview third.
  • Insist on real choice — ten qualified résumés — even when a good candidate appears early.
  • Give the work sample real weight; it predicts better than the interview.
  • Hire for genuine warmth as well as competence; clients assume competence and leave over relationships.

Don't

  • Don't hire someone to watch you work; the role must be productive from the first month.
  • Don't custom-compensate; don't blend salary with a payout.
  • Don't hire a professional expecting them to bring business.
  • Don't skip the background check, ever.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • Families are told about a new team member before they meet them, in the confirmation letter (T01), with the person's role stated.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Where the family's central team must know who has access to the individual's information, the FCT is informed of the new hire per the protocol on T05 before access is granted.

Metrics

  • Qualified résumés per search (target ≥ 10) and weeks to offer.
  • New-hire productivity: weeks until the first independently owned deliverable (CSA) or independently run progress meeting (SA).
  • Retention at 12 and 24 months.

Related

73 Onboarding a team member and transitioning relationships

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — honor the client's stated process preference for the life of the relationship; Ch. 6 — tell clients about personnel changes before they hear it elsewhere · Hughes: Family Wealth — welcome ritual for new advisers joining a family's circle · Other: Palaveev — named role in every meeting, mixed-book rule, second chair, promotion tests, business-development apprenticeship, stalled-first-hire failure mode (paraphrased)

73 — Onboarding a team member and transitioning relationships

A new hire earns the client's trust the same way the Advisor did: by doing visible, competent work in the room. This procedure runs the first ninety days on a plan, puts the new person in every client meeting with a named role, gives them a real mix of relationships rather than the leftovers, and defines the two tests that decide when a relationship moves from the Lead Advisor to the Service Advisor — without the client ever feeling handed down.

Purpose

  • Reach productivity fast: a CSA owning execution within a month, a Service Advisor leading routine meetings within six.
  • Make the team, not a person, the client's experience — while honoring every client's stated contact preference.
  • Grow the first professional into a relationship owner, so the practice is not permanently capped at the Advisor's hours.

Trigger

An accepted offer under SOP 72; or an existing team member changing seat (for example CSA to operations lead); or a borrowed specialist becoming a standing part of the team.

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: the new hire (the plan is theirs to execute), CSA (accounts, calendar, introductions in correspondence), SA (buddy for an AA) · Consulted: [Firm] HR and [Firm Compliance] for access and licensing.

Timing

Window Focus
Before day one Access, reading order, first-month meeting calendar with named roles
Days 1–30 Curriculum; shadow with a role in every meeting; owns notes and follow-through
Days 31–60 Presents one defined analysis per meeting; owns a project; CSA owns the tracker
Days 61–90 Second chair on large relationships; SA owns a first set of smaller relationships; 90-day review
Months 4–12 Progression against the two tests; rotation meeting; business-development apprenticeship begins
Month 12 Full productivity expected; relationship-manager test on the target number of relationships

Inputs

  • The signed role definition and scorecard (T26); the start-date checklist from SOP 72.
  • This library (the curriculum) and the reading order below.
  • The relationship list with size, complexity and the client's process preference and personality note ([CRM]).
  • T27 onboarding grid.

Prep checklist

  • [ ] [CRM], [Custodian], [Planning software] and [Document vault] access at the level the role needs; licensing confirmed with [Firm Compliance].
  • [ ] Reading order issued: 03, 05, 01, 02, 04 first; then 10, 11, 20, 21, 22, 23; then the section the role performs; then the family layer and 70–74.
  • [ ] First 30 days of client meetings scheduled, each with the new person's named role written on the agenda (T02).
  • [ ] The mix chosen for a Service Advisor: three to five smaller relationships to own by day 90, plus second chair on three large ones.
  • [ ] Clients due to meet the new person told in the confirmation letter (T01) who they are and what they will do.

Procedure

  1. Before day one — set the stage. Send the welcome note and the reading order. Book the first-month meetings with a named role in each. Tell the team, and any family that will meet the new person in month one, before they arrive.
  2. Day one — the welcome. Introduce the new person to every team member and to the borrowed-bench contacts they will work with. Walk the library's map (README) and the role's SOPs. Explain the two promotion tests and the 90-day review so the path is visible from the first day.

  3. Days 1–30 — learn by doing in the room. The new professional attends every client meeting with a named role from the menu: owns the notes and the follow-through on decisions; or presents one defined analysis; or is introduced as the named specialist for one topic; or owns one project (for example collecting cost basis for a transfer). Introduce them each time by name, role, and what they will do today — and promote their skills without hedging. A CSA shadows the LA on correspondence and paperwork, then takes the tracker (T07) and confirmations by week three.

    Say something like

    "Sam trained in planning and will be tracking every decision we make today and making sure each one happens; from now on you'll hear from Sam on the follow-through."

  4. Days 31–60 — visible ownership. The SA presents one analysis per meeting and owns a project with a client-facing deliverable; the AA owns packets and case briefs; the CSA owns the meeting cycle end to end (SOP 05) with the LA reviewing. Weekly one-on-one with the LA; corrections given in private, credit given in front of the client.

  5. Days 61–90 — the mix. Give the SA a genuine mix: a few smaller relationships to own outright and second chair on the largest, most complex ones — never only the small clients. Record second-chair status in [CRM]. Update each affected client's contact plan (SOP 21) and confirmation letters: who to call for what, with the LA still the first name for anything strategic.
  6. The 90-day review. Score against T26's measures; confirm probation; set the next-quarter targets; ask the new person what in the library was unclear — and fix the SOP (SOP 60).
  7. Months 4–12 — progression. Move routine progress meetings from co-attended to SA-led with the LA present to SA-led alone, relationship by relationship, gated by the relationship-manager test: the SA runs most scheduled meetings independently; the client calls the SA first; the client brings new plans and life changes to the SA; the client gives the SA both praise and complaints; the client asks the SA for more resources. When all five hold, record the SA as relationship manager and the LA moves to quality control on that relationship.
  8. Start the business-development apprenticeship in year one even though results are years away: teach opportunity recognition with existing clients first (held-away assets, planning openings — SOP 50); bring the SA to the LA's development conversations to observe; introduce them to referral sources; push them into professional and community bodies early.
  9. The relationship-owner test (later). The SA conducts all meetings including strategy and portfolio decisions; the client seeks no other senior professional's advice; the SA has brought new assets or services into the relationship; the SA can delegate parts of the work to others with the client's acceptance. When all four hold, the relationship is recorded as owned by the SA — owned meaning lead responsibility; every relationship belongs to the practice.
  10. Quality control throughout. The LA reviews every plan and proposal before it is presented (SOP 74); one meeting a year on each SA-led relationship is attended by the LA or another professional; random reviews of documents and portfolios continue.
  11. Guard against the stall. If by month 12 the first professional shows no movement toward the relationship-manager test, decide deliberately: more coaching with a dated target, or a change. A stalled first hire blocks the practice's growth and every later hire.

The process preference still governs

A client who asked in Discovery to hear only from the Advisor keeps that until they say otherwise. Team introductions are offered, not imposed; a few reluctant clients are not grounds for abandoning the model.

Follow-up

  • Weekly for the first quarter: one-on-one with the LA; the onboarding grid (T27) updated.
  • After each client meeting in the first quarter: two-minute debrief on what the new person did well and what to change.
  • Month 6 and month 12: progression reviewed against the two tests; contact plans updated; [CRM] second-chair and relationship-manager fields current.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Onboarding grid and 90-day review (T27) HR file; onboarding folder LA
Named role per meeting Agenda (T02); [CRM] activity CSA
Second-chair register; relationship-manager / owner status [CRM] relationship fields CSA
Updated contact plans and confirmation-letter wording [CRM]; T01 CSA
SOP corrections raised by the new hire SOP 60 change log LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Put the new professional in every meeting from week one, with something real to do.
  • Promote their skills to the client; uncertainty on the Advisor's face becomes the client's avoidance.
  • Give large, complex relationships as second chair — they carry the budget and the lessons.
  • Tell clients about personnel changes before they hear it from a competitor or a returned call.

Don't

  • Don't let them merely observe; observation teaches little and signals less.
  • Don't hand over only the small clients.
  • Don't expect business development from a professional a decade short of it.
  • Don't transfer a relationship because the calendar says so; the tests decide.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • New attendees at family meetings are cleared against the family's confidentiality matrix (T14) and introduced to the council or principals first; consider a welcome ritual when a new adviser joins a family's circle for the long term.

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Access to the individual's information for a new team member is granted only within the consent on T05; the FCT is told of the change per the agreed protocol before the new person appears on correspondence.

Metrics

  • Weeks to the CSA's first independently run meeting cycle; months to the SA's first independently led progress meeting (target ≤ 6).
  • Relationships passing the relationship-manager test at 12 and 24 months.
  • 90-day review completed on time; SOP corrections raised by new hires (a healthy number is not zero).

  • SOP 60 — SOP maintenance

74 Team operating rhythm — meetings, reviews, quality control and culture

procedureOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 6 — blueprint systems; staff improve them; the WOW service standard; red-flag methodology · Hughes: Compact — bring the critics inside; small joint successes first · Other: Palaveev — meeting and review cadences, ratio dashboard, productivity measures, quality-control tools, culture rules, decision hygiene, the porch of indecision (paraphrased)

74 — Team operating rhythm

Once there is a team — even a team of one plus borrowed specialists — the practice runs on a calendar of short, disciplined internal meetings and reviews. This procedure fixes that rhythm: what happens weekly, monthly, quarterly, semiannually and annually; the numbers reviewed at each; the quality-control tools that let the Lead Advisor delegate without exposing clients; and the culture rules the team holds itself to.

Purpose

  • Keep every client meeting, open item and red flag visible to the whole team every week.
  • Read the practice's economics on the cadence at which each ratio actually changes.
  • Institutionalize quality control so that delegation never lowers the standard.
  • Make decisions rather than discussing them, and revisit the ones that have stalled.

Trigger

Standing calendar. From the first hire onward (and, for the monthly and quarterly reviews, from today with [Firm shared services] in the room where useful).

Roles

Owner: LA · Does: CSA (agendas from T28, minutes, dashboards, the service-failure log), SA/AA (their sections; peer reviews) · Consulted: [Firm] finance for the P&L; sister-company leaders for the borrowed-expertise pipeline.

Timing

Cadence Meeting Length
Weekly Team meeting 30 minutes
Weekly One-on-one, LA with each team member 20 minutes (first year), then biweekly
Monthly Principal review 45 minutes
Quarterly Quarterly review and state-of-the-team 2 hours; never cancelled, never rescheduled twice
Semiannual Staffing check inside the quarterly review
Annual Planning, budget, reviews, compensation, equity conversation half a day, in the Q4 slot of T15

Inputs

  • [CRM] pipeline of scheduled CCM, progress, family and trustee meetings; trackers (T07, T10); red-flag list (SOP 22); service-failure log (SOP 23).
  • Monthly P&L for the profit center from [Firm] finance; hours logs (T28).
  • Borrowed-expertise engagements in progress (T25).

Prep checklist

  • [ ] Agendas from T28 circulated the day before; anyone may add an item.
  • [ ] Dashboard figures updated for the monthly and quarterly meetings.
  • [ ] Peer-review queue current: every plan or proposal due in the next two weeks has a reviewer named.

Procedure

  1. Weekly team meeting. Walk the next two weeks of client meetings — who attends with what named role, packet status, anything the client must be told beforehand. Then open service items and who has the ball; red flags since last week; implementation tracker exceptions; borrowed engagements due. Decisions recorded with owner and date; nothing is "discussed" twice without a decision.
  2. Weekly one-on-ones. Progress against the onboarding grid or the quarter's targets; one correction, one thing to do more of; blockers the LA must remove.
  3. Monthly principal review. EBOC and overhead percentage against the bands in SOP 70; the service-failure log — every entry traced to a step in an SOP that was missing, unclear or skipped; the pipeline of borrowed-expertise engagements and their scorecards; hours by professional. Fifteen minutes on the numbers, thirty on what to change.
  4. Quarterly review. Common-sized P&L against the 40/35/25 guideline; capacity check on T28 against the SOP 70 triggers; the SOP review with SOP 60 (which procedures changed, which failed); client review for fit, risk and unpriced customization; and the state-of-the-team conversation — honest, no agenda item skipped: what is working, what is not, what each person needs.
  5. Semiannual staffing check. Revenue per staff head and per professional; relationships per professional; the roadmap block in SOP 70 updated; a hiring decision made or explicitly deferred with a date.
  6. Annual cycle (Q4). Budget built by cost owner — each person drafts the lines they spend — and loaded so budget-versus-actual can be reviewed monthly; performance reviews against stated standards before compensation decisions; bonus frequency matched to review frequency; the equity conversation held even if there is nothing to decide; the porch-of-indecision list reviewed (hiring, succession, compensation structure, pricing, the firm relationship) and each item given a decision or a date.
  7. Quality-control tools, always on. Peer review and sign-off on every investment plan and wealth management plan before presentation; LA sign-off on proposals and client documents; one meeting per year on every relationship attended by a second professional (rotation) so another set of eyes sees the work and the client; random review of a sample of portfolios and files each quarter.
  8. Productivity measures kept per professional in [CRM]: relationships owned; second-chair relationships; revenue managed; growth of managed relationships; organic growth from existing clients; new relationships served. Reviewed quarterly; they feed the promotion tests (SOP 73) and, later, incentives.
  9. Decision hygiene. Written agendas; decide rather than defer; a materiality threshold below which each person acts alone (SOP 03) and above which the item comes to the meeting; disagreements resolved in the room, not agreed-to-disagree; hard decisions supported by a one-page analysis.
  10. Culture rules, enforced by example. The team owns the client experience; "our" clients, never "my"; no puck-passing; no exceptions for brilliance; leaders arrive prepared and on time; critics are brought inside and given real roles; small joint successes are engineered before hard problems are attempted.

Beyond Bowen

Bowen supplies the standard (WOW service, red flags, blueprints improved by staff). The cadences, ratios, quality-control tools and culture rules are drawn from Palaveev and Hughes, adapted to a one-professional practice that is growing.

Follow-up

  • Minutes with decisions and owners sent the same day; the dashboard (T28) updated before the next meeting.
  • Service-failure lessons that point to an SOP are logged to SOP 60 within the week.
  • Quarterly review actions checked at the next monthly review.

Outputs and records

Output Where it lives Owner
Agendas, minutes, decisions Team folder; [CRM] tasks CSA
Dashboard and capacity worksheet (T28) Team folder CSA
Peer-review and sign-off records Client file; plan cover sheet Reviewer
Productivity measures [CRM] CSA
Porch-of-indecision list with dates Team folder; SOP 70 roadmap block LA

Do / Don't

Do

  • Keep the meetings short and the agendas written; decide.
  • Review the numbers on their natural cadence — EBOC monthly, staffing semiannually.
  • Treat every service failure as evidence about a procedure.
  • Hold the state-of-the-team review even when things seem fine — especially then.

Don't

  • Don't cancel the quarterly review; "we talk all the time" is not a substitute.
  • Don't judge different people by different standards (effort for the familiar, results for the new).
  • Don't let one person's excellence excuse behavior the team would not accept from anyone else.
  • Don't leave decisions on the porch for years; a non-decision is a decision.

Mode A / Mode B

Mode A — whole family

  • The weekly walk includes family meetings and trustee meetings with the attendee list checked against the family's confidentiality matrix (T14).

Mode B — individual within a larger team

  • Items concerning a Mode B client are discussed only among team members inside the consent on T05; the borrowed-expertise pipeline shows the wall status for any sister company that also serves the family.

Metrics

  • Quarterly reviews held as scheduled (target 4 of 4).
  • Plans and proposals with a recorded peer review before presentation (target 100%).
  • Service failures traced to an SOP change within the month (target 100%).

Templates

01 T01 — Client correspondence

templateOwner: CSAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — pre-meeting letter listing what to bring; written confirmation after every meeting; Ch. 5 — same-day handwritten thank-you; report results back to the referrer · Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 11 — an introductory letter that states hopes, walks the agenda, and invites questions · Other: Extension — courtesy notice to a family central team is ours

T01 — Client correspondence

Purpose

The standard letters and notes the practice sends around every meeting, so that a client hears the same voice whoever writes. Each block is fill-in; keep the tone warm, brief, and specific.

How to use

  • CSA drafts from the block; LA signs anything that carries advice or a commitment. Send by the channel the client chose under Process (SOP 11).
  • Replace <span class="ph">[Client]</span>, <span class="ph">[Advisor]</span>, <span class="ph">[Firm]</span> and the blanks. Delete lines that don't apply. Never paste a block unedited.
  • File every sent item in [CRM] against the meeting.

1. Pre-meeting letter (T−7 days)

Dear [Client],

Thank you for agreeing to meet on __ at _ (time) at (place / video link). The purpose of our meeting is ___ (one sentence — e.g., "to understand what matters most to you and your family, and to decide together whether we are the right firm to help").

I've attached a short agenda. Please add anything you'd like us to cover — the meeting is yours.

It would help if you could bring, or send ahead: recent statements for all investment and bank accounts; your last two years' tax returns; trust, partnership, and company documents; insurance schedules; any current investment policy or plan. Don't worry about completeness — bring what is easy and we'll work from there.

Joining me will be __ (name, role, what they will do in the meeting). We have set aside _ minutes. Parking / arrival: ___.

I'm looking forward to it.

[Advisor], [Firm]

2. Next-meeting confirmation (≤ 24 hours after any meeting)

Dear [Client],

Thank you for today. As agreed, our next meeting is on __ at _ (place / link). Its purpose is ___.

Before then: we will __ (what the practice will do); you agreed to _ (what the client will bring or decide). Please call ___ with any questions before then.

[Advisor]

3. Post-meeting recap (≤ 24 hours)

Dear [Client],

A short record of what we decided today so we stay aligned.

Decisions: __ · _ · ___

Actions: __ (owner, by date) · ____ (owner, by date)

Documents outstanding: ______

Next meeting: __ at _ — purpose: ___.

If I've missed or misstated anything, tell me and I'll correct it.

[Advisor]

4. Handwritten notes

Occasion Send within Content
After an introduction or referral is offered Same day (next day at the latest) Thanks; what it means to the practice; you will follow up personally
After the commitment meeting Same day Congratulations on taking an important step; you are glad to be part of it
After a family event (birth, wedding, graduation, loss) Within a week Acknowledgement only — no business
After a family meeting Within two days Thanks for the trust and the candour

Conventions: fountain pen or good ballpoint; print if handwriting is hard to read; the firm's plain card, no logo larger than a thumbnail; never a marketing enclosure. Gifts follow [Firm Compliance] limits.

5. Courtesy notice to a family central team (Mode B, only with the client's consent on T05)

Dear ______,

[Client] has asked me to let you know that [Firm] has begun working with them on __ (scope in one line). I understand that your team is responsible for _, and I'll make sure our work fits within it. Would a short call in the next two weeks suit you to agree how best to coordinate? My direct line is ___.

[Advisor]

6. Thank-you after an introduction, and report-back to the referrer

Thank-you (same day): see the handwritten note above.

Report-back (within a week of first contact, then at each milestone):

Dear ______,

A quick note to say that I reached __ as you kindly suggested. We have ____ (met / scheduled a first meeting / agreed to speak next month). I won't share anything about their circumstances, but I wanted you to know your introduction was welcome and is being handled with care. Thank you again.

[Advisor]

Never disclose what the introduced person said, decided, or holds. If they declined, say only that you were grateful for the introduction and left the door open.

02 T02 — Meeting agendas

templateOwner: CSAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the step lists for each of the five consultative meetings · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 16 — family-meeting design; three tracks; stories; gratitude close; Family Trusts Ch. 13 — open with the success question; annual review block

T02 — Meeting agendas

Purpose

Ready-to-adapt agendas for every standard meeting. An agenda goes out with the pre-meeting letter (T01), is walked at the opening, and is invited to change.

How to use

  • Copy the block, fill the blanks, cut items that don't apply, keep the standing items (marked ★) from SOP 05: state purpose and ask what would make the meeting successful; ask what has changed; schedule the next meeting in the room.
  • Timings are for a ninety-minute meeting; scale.
  • Materials column lists what the CSA puts in the packet.

CCM1 — Discovery (≤ 90 min)

Purpose: to understand what matters most to you and decide together whether we are the right firm.

Min Item Leads Materials

03 T03 — Discovery interview guide

templateOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — the seven areas and the second-order question; the nine HNW personalities (Ch. 3) as cues · Hughes: Family Wealth Ch. 17 — passion and mentor questions; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 1 — budget comparison; Ch. 4 — rising-generation topics; Compact — essential-question topics and generational position · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes — the pitfalls probe (paraphrased); Extension — Mode B mandate prompts and the closing sequence are ours

T03 — Discovery interview guide

Purpose

The interviewer's guide for CCM1 and Rediscovery. It keeps the seven areas in order, supplies prompt questions in the practice's own words, and adds the overlays for large families and for Mode B mandates. It is a guide, not a script — follow the client.

How to use

  • Read it before the meeting; do not read from it in the meeting. Keep the mind-map sheet (T04) in front of you, not this guide.
  • Use one open prompt per area, then go one level deeper on every general answer: what specifically… · what would that look like… · why does that matter to you…
  • Assets are fourth. If the client starts with money, listen, note it, and return to values.
  • Mark the personality cues you hear. Tick the overlay prompts you used so the AA knows what was covered.

The seven areas

1. Values

  • When you think about your money and your life, what matters most?
  • What would you never want the wealth to do to your family?
  • What did you learn about money growing up that still guides you?
  • If we are working well together in five years, what will be true that isn't today?
  • Deeper: what specifically about that matters most? What would it look like in practice?

2. Goals

  • What do you want to achieve over the long run — for yourself, your family, your enterprise, the world?
  • What has to happen in the next two years? The next ten?
  • What would you do if you never had to think about work or money again?
  • Which goals are shared across the family, and which are yours alone?
  • Deeper: when, for whom, and what does "done" look like?

3. Relationships

  • Who counts in your life? Tell me about each of them.
  • Who depends on you, and on whom do you depend?
  • Who in the family is easy to talk to about money, and who isn't?
  • Anyone outside the family — or any pets — you'd want us to keep in mind?

4. Assets (fourth)

  • Walk me through what you own and where it sits — accounts, entities, trusts, property, businesses. Documents to the CSA as we go.
  • What is held elsewhere, and with whom? How is it going?
  • Which positions are large relative to the whole? Any restrictions?
  • What income arrives each year and from where? What debt?
  • What events could change the picture — a sale, a vesting, an inheritance, a distribution?

5. Advisors

  • Who do you rely on today — accountants, attorneys, trustees, other managers, insurance, a family office?
  • What has worked with each, and what hasn't?
  • Who among them do you trust most? Who would you change if it were easy?
  • Have your advisors ever met one another?

6. Process

  • How do you like to work with an advisor — how often, by what channel, in how much detail?
  • Who should be in the room when we meet? Who should never be?
  • How do you prefer to make decisions — quickly, after reflection, together with someone?
  • What has annoyed you about advisors' communication in the past?

7. Interests

  • What do you do that has nothing to do with money?
  • What are you involved in — boards, causes, faith, sport, collecting?
  • Where do you go to relax, and with whom?

UHNW overlay prompts

  • Entities and trusts: for each: why it exists, who is trustee or manager, who benefits, who protects it, where it sits, how the people touched by it feel about it. Do you receive and read the statements?
  • Concentrated positions and businesses: what share of the whole; restrictions; succession intentions; has anyone raised an employee-ownership route or a sale?
  • Liquidity events: anything pending or possible in the next three years; what would you do with the proceeds?
  • Philanthropy: how you give today; what vehicles; who in the family takes part; appetite.
  • Family office / central team: does one exist; who leads it; what does it do for you; how do you experience it?
  • Governance: family meetings, a council, a constitution, a mission statement, a family bank; rituals the family keeps.
  • Rising generation: each person's stage and work; how much they know; who is looking out for them.
  • Transitions: what is changing in the family, the ownership, the board, the management; health.

Family prompts

Beyond Bowen

Use with a household that belongs to a larger family, or where wealth spans generations. Choose; do not run them all.

  • Calling and mentor: what are you passionate about? Who do you learn from?
  • Budget comparison: roughly what does the family spend each year to protect and grow its money — fees, advisors, lawyers, accountants? And what, deliberately, on developing its people — education beyond tuition, gatherings, coaching, learning to give? What does that ratio say?
  • Generational position: are we talking with the founding generation, siblings, or cousins? What has moved from one generation to the next already, and how did it go?
  • Essential-question topics (in your words): what the family stands for; whether the family sees itself as bound by choice, not only by blood; how decisions are made together and whether that works; whether each generation is finding its own dreams rather than living the founder's; who the family's elders are and what they do; how the family thinks about the seventh generation.
  • Pitfall probes: do the heirs know what is coming — the money and the responsibility? Does every heir have a role they consider important? Are there mixed messages between the parents about the wealth? Has the founder waited too long to pass real responsibility? Is succession a shared vision or a decree?
  • Institutionalisation: has any asset been formally set aside as the family's rather than someone's personal money? Who decided that, and how?

Mode B mandate prompts

  • What does your family's team already do for you, and how well?
  • What do you want from us that you are not getting?
  • Who else will need to know that we are working together, and how would you like that handled?
  • What information about your own affairs can you not get access to today?
  • Is there anyone — a trustee, the family office, a sibling — whose approval matters for what you're asking us to do?
  • Are there sister companies of ours already working with your family? (Check conflicts with [Firm Compliance].)

Personality cues

Personality Listen for Adjust
Family steward Everything framed around the family's security; cautious; little interest in investing Lead with family outcomes; simplify the mechanics
Independent Freedom, options, exit; investing is a means Emphasise what the plan makes possible
Phobic Discomfort with money talk; chooses on trust Slow down; fewer numbers; more reassurance
Anonymous Privacy first; concentrates assets with whoever protects them Confidentiality explicitly; discretion in everything
Mogul Control; decisiveness; power Options with a clear recommendation; respect the decision
VIP Prestige; affiliation with leading names Credentials of the network; quality of materials
Accumulator Portfolio size; performance; frugality Be candid; a demanding client — check fit
Gambler Excitement; high risk tolerance; very involved Usually a poor fit for this practice
Innovator Complex products; technically savvy Usually a poor fit; if taken, narrow mandate

Closing and precommitment

  • "Let me tell you what I heard…" — one-minute summary in their words; ask what was missed.
  • "Here is what happens next…" — the plan meeting in two weeks, commitment a week later, follow-up at forty-five days, then your cadence.
  • "Does it make sense to take the next step together?"
  • If the fit is poor: "I don't think we're the right firm for what you need — here's who I'd suggest, and I'd be glad to introduce you."
  • Schedule in the room. Thank them for their candour.

T04 — Total Client Profile outline

Purpose

The typed counterpart of the mind map: a nested outline the AA fills within 24 hours of Discovery and maintains in [CRM]. Level 1 is the family (Mode A only); level 2 is one outline per household. Every node carries a confidentiality flag: S shared at family level · H household only · P private to the individual.

How to use

  • Transcribe from the mind-map scan in the client's own words; put interpretation in the notes column, not the node.
  • Date every node when confirmed; blank means "not yet discussed" — record that explicitly.
  • Set flags from T05 (Mode B) or T14 (Mode A) before sharing any extract with a specialist.

T07 — Implementation tracker

Purpose

One row per account, entity, or trust that is opening, moving, retitling, or changing designations. It is the CSA's daily control sheet during the window between the Mutual Commitment Meeting and the 45-Day Follow-up, and again whenever a progress-meeting decision creates new accounts or structures.

How to use

  • Open it in [CRM] (or the firm's tracking sheet) on the day documents are executed; one tracker per client, one row per account.
  • Review every open row each morning; anything past its expected date moves to the exceptions log the same day.
  • Close a row only when positions, cash, cost basis, registration, and beneficiary designations reconcile to the plan.
  • Print or export the completed tracker into the notebook (T08) under Implementation.

T08 — Client notebook index

Purpose

The table of contents for the client's notebook — the [Document vault] structure (and the physical binder where a client wants one) that holds every plan, policy, statement, and communication for the life of the relationship. It is built at the 45-Day Follow-up and maintained by the CSA thereafter.

How to use

  • Create the folder structure below in the [Document vault] the day of CCM3; populate during implementation; walk it with the client at CCM4.
  • Every document filed gets a row in the register. Every progress meeting adds its report and recap.
  • Access permissions mirror the consent on T05 (Mode B) or the confidentiality matrix on T14 (Mode A); review permissions whenever consent changes.
  • Retain at least five years of material in the live notebook; archive older years per [Firm] policy without deleting.

T10 — Advanced-planning tracker

Purpose

The single page that shows the whole advanced-planning picture — every recommended action in the four areas, its priority, the client's decision, its status, and the next step — so each Regular Progress Meeting starts from the same place and nothing is lost between meetings. It is Part 3 of the wealth management plan (SOP 30) in working form.

How to use

  • AA maintains it; LA reviews it before every RPM; CSA files each dated version to the [Document vault].
  • Update within 48 hours of every RPM and every expert-network meeting. Never delete a row — move it to dropped with the date and reason.
  • Priority is the impact on the client's life, not the size of the fee or the ease of execution. Keep no more than three items per area marked high.
  • Status codes: C completed · P in progress · F future · X dropped. Decisions: do · defer (with a revisit date) · drop · refer (Mode B: to family team).
  • Mode B: fill the scope tag on every row from T05 — in (Advisor owns) · FT (family team owns) · co (coordination only).

Bowen: Ch. 6 — the three-tier hierarchy of client needs (relationship, service, wealth management) and the seven satisfaction factors; lost-client interviews; mystery shopper; Ch. 5 — annual client survey · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 9 — the three service questions and the fee conversation as evidence of an adviser's quality · Other: Extension — every item below is original; Bowen's checklist and survey are not reproduced

T12 — Service quality instruments

Purpose

Five instruments used by SOPs 21, 23 and 25: (a) the practice's own service self-audit in three tiers; (b) the annual client satisfaction survey; (c) the service-failure log; (d) the lost-client interview guide; (e) the Mode B coordination check. All items are original to this practice.

How to use

  • (a) is scored by the LA with the team each May before the survey goes out, and again in November as a mid-year check. Score every item met / partly / not; every "partly" or "not" gets an owner and a date.
  • (b) goes to every client household in late May per SOP 25; both spouses may answer separately.
  • (c) is a running log in [CRM]; every failure is entered within an hour of discovery.
  • (d) is used by the LA within two weeks of any client giving notice.
  • (e) is sent, with the client's knowledge, to the FCT contact of each Mode B relationship alongside the survey.

(a) Service self-audit

Tier 1 — Relationship: does the family feel known and cared for?

# Standard Met Partly Not Owner / date
R1 Every client's stated process preference is written in a contact plan and followed for the life of the relationship
R2 Each client hears from us about their life and interests more often than about their portfolio
R3 The LA can name, for every client, the three things that matter most to them beyond money
R4 Both spouses have a first-hand relationship with the Advisor, not a relayed one
R5 Every family member we serve knows exactly who on our team to call for what
R6 We ask what has changed in the client's life at every meeting and act on the answer
R7 The client is invited to raise any concern at any time and knows we want the criticism
R8 Nobody on the team uses possessive language about clients or speaks of one family in front of another
R9 Difficult news reaches the client from the LA before the meeting, never in it
R10 Every meeting has a written agenda sent in advance, including the "quick" ones
R11 Personal details recorded after each contact are used at the next one
R12 We introduce clients to the experts and people who can help them, by name and with a reason
R13 Team members and borrowed specialists are introduced with a role, and the client never feels passed down
R14 Rising-generation members are advocated for, not merely accommodated
R15 The client relationship survives the absence of any one team member (vacation, illness) without a gap the client notices

Tier 2 — Service: is the administration flawless and the communication timely?

# Standard Met Partly Not Owner / date
S1 Every client message is acknowledged the same business day with a time for the answer
S2 Every promise made in a meeting has an owner and a date before the day ends
S3 Whoever receives a request owns it to completion; no client is transferred to "someone who can help"
S4 Transfers, titling and beneficiary designations are tracked to closure with no administrative errors reaching the client
S5 The quarterly reporting package ships on the same business day every quarter
S6 Every fee the client pays, to anyone, is shown in the package
S7 Service failures are logged within the hour and resolved the same day where possible
S8 Problems are told to the client together with the solution, before they discover them
S9 The red-flag review runs monthly and every flag is resolved within three business days
S10 A market shock triggers same-day outreach to top relationships with one consistent message
S11 Clients learn of firm and staff changes from the LA before anyone else
S12 Client information is accessible to the team members who serve the family and to no one else
S13 Confidentiality is absolute: no acknowledgment of a relationship outside the consent on T05
S14 The secure client portal ([Document vault]) holds the current notebook, and clients can find what they need in it
S15 Customizations are priced or declined, never absorbed silently
S16 A lost-client interview is held for every departure
S17 An outsider has tested our responsiveness in the last twelve months

Tier 3 — Wealth management: is the advice specific, complete and understood?

# Standard Met Partly Not Owner / date
W1 Every client has a current Total Client Profile refreshed within the last twelve months
W2 The investment plan and IPS state the client's own objectives and were reviewed within the last year
W3 Every client with an advanced-planning mandate has a tracker with statuses and next steps, presented at every progress meeting
W4 Each recommendation was coached to drop, defer or do — never pushed — and the choice is recorded
W5 Recommendations are presented with real alternatives and their trade-offs
W6 Anything touching a long-term structure passed a "do no harm" consequences check before execution
W7 Every new trust, gift or plan came with a one-page plain-language summary and a communication plan
W8 Performance is reported against the client's objectives over the plan's horizon, with short-term results framed
W9 The expert network covered every planning area the client needs; no advanced planning was promised before the network could deliver it
W10 The client's other advisors were coordinated, with no contradictory advice reaching the family
W11 Family-level matters (Mode A) have a family-level plan and a meeting rhythm
W12 Trustee–beneficiary relationships we support have an annual meeting and a written distribution process
W13 The fee conversation was held in the last twelve months, in writing and in context
W14 Held-away assets were reviewed with the client at least annually where the mandate allows
W15 The client can explain, in their own words, what their plan is trying to achieve

(b) Annual client satisfaction survey

Cover note: why we ask; every answer read by the LA; criticism welcome; ten minutes; attributed unless you prefer anonymity (tick here ☐).

Scale: 1 = strongly disagree · 2 · 3 · 4 · 5 = strongly agree · N/A

# Statement Factor Score
1 When the team promises something by a date, it arrives by that date reliability
2 Details are handled correctly; I do not find errors reliability
3 When something goes wrong, I hear about it from the team before I notice it myself, along with what they are doing about it no surprises
4 I feel free to complain, and the team wants to hear it no surprises
5 I learn about things that affect my affairs — markets, the firm, my own plan — from the team first timely information
6 The quarterly package tells me what I need to know without my having to ask timely information
7 The people I deal with are genuinely warm, not merely polite warmth
8 My family members who deal with the team are treated with the same care I am warmth
9 The team listens more than it talks; I feel heard listening
10 Explanations are patient and pitched to me, not to a specialist listening
11 The team understands what matters to me and my family beyond the money understanding needs
12 The plan reflects my situation, not a standard product understanding needs
13 When the team recommends something, I see the alternatives and the trade-offs providing alternatives
14 I know what I pay, to whom, and what I receive for it providing alternatives
15 I would describe the team to a friend as excellent (rather than fair) overall

Open questions:

  • What is one thing the team should start doing, stop doing, or do differently?
  • Was there a moment this year when the team exceeded, or fell short of, what you expected? What happened?
  • Whom on the team, or which service, do you value most — and is there anyone or anything you would want to see more of?

(c) Service-failure log

Date found Client What happened How found (client / us / red flag) Promised date Resolved date LA call made (date) Root cause (SOP step) SOP change made Repeat? (Y/N)

(d) Lost-client interview guide

Thirty minutes, by the LA, within two weeks of notice. Open by thanking them and saying the purpose is to learn, not to persuade.

  1. When did you begin to think about making a change — was there a moment, or did it build?
  2. What did we miss, or what did we do, that mattered most in the decision?
  3. What did you need from us that you were not getting?
  4. How did the team's communication feel over the last year — too much, too little, wrong kind?
  5. What will the new arrangement give you that we did not?
  6. What would you tell a friend about working with us?
  7. Is there anything that would make you reconsider, now or later?
  8. Is there anything we should do differently for other families?

Close: thank them; confirm how the transition will be handled; leave the door open. Record answers the same day; bring to the next results session (SOP 25).

(e) Mode B coordination check

Sent to the family central team's designated contact with the client's knowledge; three questions, a 1–5 scale and a comment box.

  1. When our team needs something from yours, or you from ours, is it handled promptly and through the right person?
  2. Does the information you receive from us about the individual(s) we serve arrive in the form, and within the limits, you expect?
  3. In the last year, did anything reach the family from us that surprised you or contradicted your own communication? If so, what?
