templateOwner: LAMode AMode BUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 and 5 — the working scripts of the consultative sequence and the asks · Hughes: Family Wealth Ch. 10, 13, 17, 21 — the beneficiary question, the dream question, passion and mentor, the unintended-consequences questions; Compact — the children's-wealth question; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 9, 16 — the fee conversation, family-meeting openers and the gratitude close · Other: Extension — all wording is ours, adapted for $30M+ families

T13 — Scripts sheet

Purpose

A one-place convenience copy of the practice's working scripts. The canonical version of each script lives inline in its SOP; if the two ever differ, the SOP wins. Every script is two sentences or fewer, in the practice's own words, so it can be said naturally.

How to use

  • Read the script for the meeting you are about to run; say it in your own voice, not from the page.
  • The label on each script names the SOP it belongs to. Update this sheet when the SOP changes (SOP 60).
  • Scripts marked beyond Bowen come from the family layer and are used in Mode A, or in Mode B when the family invites the conversation.

Discovery (SOP 10)

Moment Script
Opening — qualify, don't sell "I'm glad you're here; our purpose today is to find out whether we are the right firm for your family. If it turns out we are not, I'll say so and point you to someone who is."
Second-order follow-up "You said financial security matters most — what specifically about it concerns you?"
Ask about assets fourth "Now that I understand what matters and who matters, let's map what you own and where it sits."
Process preference "How do you like to work with your advisors — how often, by what means, and with how much detail?"
Precommitment and next steps "Based on what you've told me I believe we can make a real difference; the next step is for us to prepare your investment plan and meet again in two weeks. Shall we fix the date now?"
Mode B mandate "Your family already has a central team — tell me what they do for you, what you want from me, and who else needs to know we are working together."

Investment plan meeting (SOP 12)

Moment Script
Commitment ask — no check today "If this plan makes sense to you, I'd like you to take it home and live with it for a week; then we meet again and, if you're ready, we put it to work together."
Set the stage for advanced planning "Investments are the foundation, not the whole house; once we're working together, my network of specialists will look at everything beyond the portfolio."

Mutual commitment meeting (SOP 14)

Moment Script
Congratulations "Congratulations — this is an important step toward everything you told me matters to your family."
Buyer's-remorse and media inoculation "It is normal to feel a flicker of doubt in the coming weeks, especially when the financial news gets loud; treat that noise as entertainment and let the plan do its work."
Concentrated gains, long view "Returns arrive unevenly and the best days are impossible to time; staying invested through the dull and the frightening stretches is how the plan achieves its goals."
Introductions ask #1 "We serve a small number of families like yours; who else comes to mind who might value what we're now doing for you?"
Mode B — into the family team "So that we coordinate well from the start, would you introduce me to the people on your family's team who should know we are working together?"

45-day follow-up (SOP 16)

Moment Script
Opening "What has happened since we last met?"
Returns reframe "What matters is achieving your goals over your lifetime, not the last forty-five days; in the short run nobody can predict the market, and in the long run prudent decisions are what tilt the odds in your favor."
Introductions ask #2 "As we talked about last time, who else comes to mind who might benefit from the way we work?"

Regular progress meeting (SOP 20)

Moment Script
Opener "What have you been doing since we last got together?"
Drill deeper "Has anything happened in your life or the family's that affects your finances and that I should know about?"
Drop / defer / do "For each item, tell me: do it, hold it for now, or take it off the list — and I'll record why."
Additional-assets ask "Part of my job is to keep the whole picture in view, including the accounts we don't manage; may we look at how those fit with the plan?"
Second-opinion offer "Would it help if we gave you a second opinion on how that account is being managed, at no cost and with no obligation?"
Introductions ask "We work best with families like yours; who else comes to mind who might value what we do for you?"
Keep asking "Who else comes to mind?"
Fee conversation (annual) "Once a year I put our fees in writing, in the context of everything we do for the family, and I'd like you to lead the questions."

Calling an introduced prospect (SOP 50)

Response Script
"No — I have an advisor" "That's exactly why families come to us: would a complimentary second opinion on your current plan be useful?"
"Maybe" "There's no cost for a Discovery meeting, and we only go further if we're sure we can add real value."
"Yes" "Let's set a date; I'll send a short note listing what to bring so the meeting is worth your time."

Family layer

Beyond Bowen

The scripts below come from the Hughes material and our own extensions; use them in Mode A, or in Mode B when the family invites the conversation.

Moment Script
Passion and mentor (SOP 10, 41) "Two questions I ask everyone in a family: what are you passionate about, and who is your mentor?"
The children's-wealth question (SOP 41, 43) "How wealthy do you want your children to be?"
The dream question (SOP 42, 43) "What is your dream — and how can the family invest in it?"
The beneficiary question (SOP 46) "May I ask the question nobody asks: are you an excellent beneficiary, and what would it take to become one?"
Family-meeting opener (SOP 43) "What needs to happen in the next few hours for each of you to say this was worth the trip?"
Gratitude close (SOP 43) "Before we close, each of us names one person we're grateful to this year and how we'll tell them."
Trustee–beneficiary success (SOP 46) "What must happen today for you to leave thinking this was a very good meeting?"
Distribution conversation (SOP 46) "Tell me what this would do to enhance your life — and if the trust didn't exist, how would you pursue the same goal?"
Consequences check before a perpetual structure (SOP 20, 30) "Before we build something meant to last generations: what could this do to the people it's meant to help, and what harm might we do before we do good?"
Advance notice to heirs (SOP 42) "Nobody should learn about a trust from a trustee's phone call; let's plan how and when each of your children hears about what is coming."

16 T16 — Family meeting pack

templateOwner: LAMode Abeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — every meeting has an agenda sent in advance · Hughes: Complete Family Wealth Ch. 16–18 — design frame, ground rules, exercises, story prompts, rituals, mission statement; Family Wealth Ch. 2 — the mission-statement session · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes Ch. 8 — timed first council meeting

T16 — Family meeting pack

Purpose

The fill-in forms for SOP 43: the design frame, the ground-rules sheet, pre-work forms, the mission/values run-sheet, the two agendas, the exercise menu, story prompts, the rituals calendar, the minutes template and the takeaway round.

How to use

Complete Part 1 with the family's leaders four weeks before any meeting; send Parts 3 and 8 with the invitation; bring Parts 2, 4–7 and 9–11 to the room. All wording is the practice's own; the family is encouraged to rewrite it in their voice.

Part 1 — Design frame

Question Answer
Why are we meeting? (the one thing this meeting must change)
What will we cover? (family's items first)
Who attends? (members · in-laws · rising gen · elders · experts for which portion · childcare / parallel program)
When? (dates · two half-days or one day · breaks every 75–90 minutes)
How? (formats for different learners · pre-reads · flip charts · time to react after disclosures)
Where? (not a parent's home; room for work and play; quiet; convenient; food and rest)
Chair and secretary for this meeting
Facilitator (yes / no; who)

Part 2 — Ground rules for signature

We meet to stay connected, to learn, and to decide together. To make that possible we agree to:

  1. Be here. Devices away, on time, pre-work done.
  2. One voice at a time. We let each other finish.
  3. Play it back before pushing back. We show we understood before we answer.
  4. Say "I." We speak for ourselves, not for "everyone."
  5. Hold our outcomes loosely. We come to decide, not to win.
  6. Drop the "but." We begin a reply with what we heard.
  7. Candor with care. We say the hard thing in a way that can be heard.
  8. Park, don't drop. What isn't settled today gets an owner and a date.
  9. What's said here stays here unless we agree otherwise.
  10. These rules bind all of us, whoever is oldest or pays.

Signed: ____ (every attendee) · Date: ______ · Reviewed at each meeting.

Part 3 — Pre-work forms (due two weeks before)

A. One-page profile (what a good friend would know) - What I'm working on right now: __ - What I care about most this year: _ - What I'm good at, in my own words: - Who I'm learning from at the moment, and about what: - Something the family may not know about me: ___

B. Ten-year statement - In ten years I would like to be __. - The family could help by _. - I could contribute to the family by ___.

Part 4 — Mission/values session run-sheet

Time Step Lead Materials
0:00 Rules read; chair and secretary confirmed Chair Part 2
0:10 Profile round — passions and mentors, one minute each Chair Part 3A
0:25 Values lists — each writes the handful of values the family's long-term success depends on; post; cluster into a shared list Facilitator / LA cards, wall
0:50 The long view — write what you'd want the family to remember mattered most, looking back from very old age; share in threes Facilitator paper
1:10 Break
1:25 Twenty years out — each describes the family in 2046; read aloud Chair paper
1:55 Family history — committee draft (crises, opportunities, memorable ancestors, decisions good and bad) reviewed and corrected History committee draft
2:50 Break
3:05 How we will decide — forms of family government in brief; the family chooses its decision method and representation LA, then family T14 Part 3
3:35 Drafting committee named (two or three, across generations); date for the first draft Chair
3:45 Takeaway round; close Chair Part 11

Part 5 — First meeting agenda (family standing up its office or council; about four hours)

Block Minutes Content Lead
1 15 Open; rules; celebrate the year's family accomplishments Chair
2 30 Roll call; each member's profile Chair
3 60 The family office idea; the family balance sheet (T18) — what the family holds beyond money; the qualitative-vs-financial budget LA
— 15 Break
4 45 Family-office budgets: support and allowances, property upkeep, travel to family events CSA / LA
5 30 Constituting the investment committee; the investor-allocation idea (SOP 47) LA
— 15 Break
6 30 How decisions get made: decision rights, confidentiality, communication (T14) LA / Chair
7 15 Takeaways; next meeting date Chair

Part 6 — Annual family meeting agenda

Day 1 — connect and learn 1. Open; rules; a rising-generation member reads the mission/values statement. 2. Individual track: each member's update (3 minutes each; no questions until all have spoken). 3. Learning session (chosen by the family: a trust explained; how the family's money is held; giving; a skill). 4. Generational track: each generation caucuses — what we want to share with the others, what we want to learn from them — then reports. 5. Story time (Part 8); grandparent–grandchild lunch (parents elsewhere).

Day 2 — the business of the family 6. The four health questions (SOP 43 Part C). 7. Capitals review — T18 year on year. 8. Family-level tracker (T10): drop / defer / do on open items. 9. Money and structures: the year in review; trusts and entities; family bank and investor allocation (SOP 47); giving. 10. Review of representatives and advisors; the fee conversation. 11. Decisions requested (proposer · options · recommendation · decision). 12. Rising generation: what is your dream, and how can we invest in it? (separate from money decisions) 13. Rituals for the year's passages (Part 9). 14. Next steps with owners and dates; next meeting fixed; gratitude round; close.

Part 7 — Exercise menu

  • What matters most to me, and why. A round the table; the secretary lists every answer; the list becomes raw material for the values statement.
  • Founding values vs present values. The whole family names the founders' values; each generation separately names today's; compare and discuss the gaps.
  • The long view. Each person writes what they would want remembered, looking back from very old age; read in small groups.
  • Twenty years out. Each person describes the family two decades from now — who is where, what the family does together, what it owns.
  • Which hats do I wear? Each member lists every role they hold in the family (parent, child, owner, trustee, beneficiary, employee, board member) and names the two that conflict most.
  • Across the generations. Each generation answers: what we'd like the others to know; what we'd like to learn from them.
  • A life well spent. Elders describe one as themselves; the rising generation as if looking back at fifty; compare.
  • Allies, neutrals, opponents. Before a contested decision, each person privately maps where others stand and tests whether their own position is best for the whole.

Part 8 — Story prompts (sent to the designated storyteller in advance)

  1. Tell us about a person who shaped you, and what of them lives on in how you act.
  2. Describe a time the family — or you — nearly lost something that mattered, and what saved it.
  3. What did you learn the hard way that you'd like the young ones to learn the easy way?
  4. What are you proudest of that nobody outside this room knows?
  5. If a great-grandchild asked what our family stood for, what would you want them to hear?

Formats: a story after dinner · the eldest retelling a story they heard as a child · a rising-generation member interviewing a grandparent with the prompts · stories generated in the across-the-generations exercise.

Part 9 — Rituals calendar

Passage Who is honored What the family does (three parts: a step away from the everyday; the new thing learned or received; the return, marked by a ceremony) Owner Next occasion
A birth
Coming of age / joining the family meeting
Marrying in
A new elder
A death
Welcoming a new advisor or trustee
Departure of a trustee, beneficiary or advisor

Part 10 — Minutes template

[Family] family meeting — date — venue — chair — secretary — present / apologies

Item Discussion (themes, not attribution) Decision Owner Date

Parked items (owner · date): __ · Next meeting: _ · Draft circulated on · Final on ___

Part 11 — Takeaway round

Each person, one sentence: the one thing I'm taking from today is ______. The secretary records them verbatim; they open the next meeting.

T17 — Family executive summary pack

Purpose

Everything the LA needs to run SOP 41: the kickoff record, the interviewee list, the interview guide, the confidential notes form, the report outline, the leader-review checklist and the sharing plan.

How to use

  • Parts 1–2 at kickoff; Part 3 in every interview; Part 4 typed within 48 hours; Part 5 drafted after the last interview; Parts 6–7 before and after the leader review. All parts live in the family's restricted folder in the [Document vault].
  • Prompts are conversation starters, not a script; choose no more than five overlays per interview.

Part 1 — Kickoff record

Item Entry
Family [Family]
Leaders present ______
Why the family is doing this (in their words) ______
Outputs promised executive summary · T18 results · family map · next steps at a family meeting
Dates: interviews from / to · draft · leader review · family meeting ______

  • [ ] Confidentiality statement approved by leaders
  • [ ] Invitation letter (T01) approved
  • [ ] T18 instrument attached to invitations

Part 2 — Interviewee list

# Name Household / generation Role in family (from T14) Family member / in-law / stakeholder Invitation sent T18 returned Interview date Notes filed
1
2

Stakeholders to consider: family counsel · CPA · family-office executive · long-serving trustee · business CFO · a trusted family friend the leaders name.

Part 3 — Interview guide (60–90 minutes)

Opening (5 min). Thank them; restate confidentiality (themes only, never attribution); ask permission to record or take notes; confirm the time available.

Two questions to begin (10 min). - What are you most absorbed by right now — in work, in life, in something you're building? - Who do you learn from at the moment, and how did you find them?

Topic A — What's working (10 min). - When this family is at its best, what is happening? - What would you protect at any cost? - Who in the family do others turn to, and for what?

Topic B — What's coming (15 min). - In the next two years, what will test the family? In the next twenty? - Which transition is underway — a generation stepping up, a business or property changing hands, leadership of the money or of the family? - What does the family avoid talking about?

Topic C — What you'd do (15 min). - If you were running this, what would you change first? - What would you need — information, a decision, a person — to play your part? - Which decisions do you think the family should make together, and which should stay with households?

Topic D — What you'd learn (5 min). - What do you hope to understand about yourself from this? About the family?

Topic E — What you'd give (5 min). - What do you want to come out of this process? What are you willing to put in — time, a role, money, patience?

Household areas (if this person has not had a Discovery — 15 min). Values · goals · relationships · assets and where held · advisors · how they want to be worked with · interests (see T03).

Overlays (choose up to five — 10 min).

Overlay Prompts in our words
Deciding together How does this family make a decision that affects everyone? Who is heard last?
Growing each member Is every member becoming more capable, or only more comfortable?
Each generation's own dream Is the rising generation living its own ambitions or someone else's?
Calling before stewardship Do members find their work first, and their duties to the family second — or the reverse?
Attract or obligate Do people stay in this family's enterprise because they want to, or because they can't leave?
Elders Who mediates, who remembers, who holds the rituals? Is anyone being prepared for that?
The long view Whose grandchildren do we think about when we decide?
Generational position Are you one household, a set of siblings, several clans, or a tribe?
Three circles Family, ownership, management — which gets the least attention?
Budget comparison Roughly what does the family spend a year on managing money, and what on developing people?
Family money vs personal money Has any asset ever been set aside as the family's rather than someone's own?
Pitfalls Do heirs know what is coming? Does every heir have a real role? Is ownership passing while the senior generation can still teach?
Culture inventory Which of these does the family actually share — a business, a place, a giving tradition, a set of hobbies, a story of origin, an education path, a reputation?
Three Ds Where is the family divided, dissatisfied, or drifting apart?

Close (5 min). What should I have asked you? Who else should I be talking to? Thank them; say when they will hear the outcome.

Part 4 — Interview notes (confidential; one per interview)

Field Entry
Interviewee · date · interviewer · duration
Recording reference

B. Pressures named (near / long)

D. What they hope to learn

Household areas (if taken) link to T04
Overlay findings
Three Ds temperature (low / medium / high, with a phrase)
Quotes usable without attribution (mark each)

Part 5 — Report outline

Family executive summary — [Family] — date — confidential

  1. Purpose and process. Why the family did this; who was interviewed (by role, not name); the instrument; dates.
  2. Overarching themes. Five to eight, each one paragraph; state where generations or branches differ.
  3. Areas of strength. What to protect; what to build on.
  4. Key challenges and opportunities. Grouped: relationships · decisions and governance · money and structures · the rising generation · transitions underway. Each with the evidence (how many raised it, without attribution).
  5. Recommendations and next steps. Three to six, each with a proposed owner, a first step, and a date. Typical: hold a family meeting on the summary; a learning session on the trusts; a values/mission session; a decision the family needs to make.
  6. Appendices. T18 results (per capital and family averages, with range); draft family map and trustscape (T14 Parts 1–2); transitions inventory (T14 Part 6); glossary.

T18 — Family balance sheet and income statement

Purpose

The practice's own instrument for SOP 44: the balance-sheet statements every adult rates, the scoring sheet, the liabilities page, the income-statement forms, the budget-comparison worksheet and the transitions inventory.

How to use

  • CSA sends Part 1 to every adult with the invitation to family discovery (SOP 41) and with the annual-meeting pre-work; returns go to the AA only.
  • AA scores in Part 2; LA writes Parts 3–6 narratives. The family sees averages and ranges, never individual scores.
  • Rate honestly and quickly — first reactions are the useful ones. There are no right answers; the point is where we differ.

Part 1 — The balance sheet statements (rate 1 = strongly disagree … 5 = strongly agree)

Human capital — our people. The health, self-knowledge and freedom of each member to build a life that fits them.

# Statement 1–5
H1 Each adult in our family is in a position to do work that fits them, whether or not it pays.
H2 A member struggling with health, addiction or a setback gets the best help available, promptly.
H3 I feel free to choose where I live, what I do and whom I love without financial pressure from the family.
H4 Our children are growing up with a sense of who they are apart from the family's money.
H5 Members know how they could leave the family enterprise, and no one stays only because they cannot leave.
H6 Physical and emotional health are treated as family priorities, not private matters to hide.
H7 Each member has at least one relationship in the family in which they feel fully accepted.
H8 I can name what I am good at and what I want to build over the next ten years.

Intellectual capital — what we know and can do. Knowledge suited to each member's role, and the habit of passing it on.

# Statement 1–5
I1 Every adult understands, at a level suited to them, how the family's wealth is held and governed.
I2 Members can read a financial statement or a trust report well enough to ask a useful question.
I3 What one member learns — in business, investing or life — reaches the others in a usable form.
I4 Rising-generation members are given real responsibility with real money, sized so mistakes are survivable.
I5 Each member has a mentor, inside or outside the family, for the thing they are trying to become good at.
I6 The family funds members' learning — courses, travel, apprenticeships — as readily as it funds portfolios.
I7 Members who work outside the family enterprise are valued for what they bring back.
I8 We know how each member learns best and present information to them accordingly.

Social capital — our relationships. With each other, with newcomers, and with the communities we belong to.

# Statement 1–5
S1 Family members choose to spend time together when nothing requires it.
S2 Disagreements are aired and settled rather than avoided or fought through others.
S3 In-laws and newcomers are welcomed into the family's life and information, not kept at the edge.
S4 Members of different generations and branches know each other's lives, not just their names.
S5 The family makes decisions together in a way people accept even when they lose the argument.
S6 Members give time and money to their communities, and the family talks about it.
S7 When a member has a crisis, others show up.
S8 The cousins of the rising generation have relationships of their own with each other.

Spiritual capital — our shared purpose. A reason for the family beyond preserving money; humility, gratitude and a long view.

# Statement 1–5
P1 The family can say, in its own words, what it is for beyond preserving money.
P2 Members tell the family's stories — including the failures — and the young know them.
P3 We recognize that our wealth came partly from luck and others' help, and act with that humility.
P4 Major decisions are weighed for their effect on grandchildren not yet born.
P5 Members express gratitude to those who came before and to those who serve the family now.
P6 The family's values are visible in how it gives, invests and treats the people who work for it.
P7 Our rituals mark the passages — births, comings of age, marriages, new elders, deaths.
P8 I feel part of something larger than my own household.

19 T19 — Rising-generation learning map

T19 — Rising-generation learning map

Purpose

A one-page map of what a family teaches about money and stewardship at each stage of a member's life, who teaches it, and how the practice supports it — plus a per-member learning plan reviewed at the annual family meeting. It turns "we should educate the kids" into named activities with owners and dates.

How to use

  • The LA fills the map with the family during the family discovery (SOP 41) or a family meeting (SOP 43); parents and grandparents own most rows; the practice owns the rows marked practice.
  • One learning-plan form per member aged roughly 13 and up, or any adult new to financial responsibility (SOP 42). Reviewed annually; the member keeps a copy.
  • Nothing on this map is graded. Progress is described, not scored; the point is competence and confidence, not a career in finance.

Part 1 — The age-staged map

Stage Core message Activities the family runs Who teaches Practice support Milestone
5–8 "We have more than enough — and we share." Money as a physical thing: coins, a purchase counted out, a small gift chosen and given; the first grant in the grandchild philanthropy Parents; grandparents None beyond coaching the parents on the "are we rich?" answer (below) Has handled cash and made a gift
9–12 Industry and choices Allowance in three parts (spend / save / give); a saving goal reached; a site visit to a charity before proposing a grant; first look at a simple statement Parents; grandparents; an aunt or uncle Sample statement for the family's use Has proposed and presented a grant
13–18 Skills and values A small account in their own name, statements read monthly; the story of how the wealth was made, with the work and risk in it; a real case made for a large purchase (cost, alternatives, reasons); a share of expensive wants funded by the teen Parents; aunts/uncles for the first specific conversation about the family's wealth Practice: one session on reading a statement; the "are we rich?" frame coached Reads a statement; has made and lost an argument for a purchase
18–21 Managing independence A budget that lasts; a first mistake with real money treated as a lesson, not a stigma; notice of any trust the member is a beneficiary of, with the mechanics explained; first attendance at a family meeting as a listener Parents; trustee (introductory meeting, SOP 46) Practice: member Discovery on the compressed path (SOP 42); notebook set up (T08) Has attended a family meeting; knows the structures that name them
21–25 Structures and purposes Introduced to the entities, trusts, and their purposes; a beneficiary's responsibilities explained; a managed slice to run with coaching; a seat on the investment or grants committee; work outside the family enterprise; possibly a period abroad Trustee; the family's investment lead; the practice Practice: investment-plan meeting; managed-slice coaching; committee prep Has managed money with real consequences for a year
25+ Interdependence Full participation in governance; a role in one engagement channel (business, philanthropy, investment committee, property, family-office function, funded venture); mentoring the next stage; a personal mission statement and résumé updated annually (T18) The council; elders; mentors Practice: full consultative sequence; learning plan reviewed annually Holds a role with real responsibility

Part 2 — Principles the family agrees (tick the ones adopted)

  • [ ] Allowances are for learning, not reward or punishment; never withdrawn as discipline; never topped up when spent — running out is the lesson.
  • [ ] Wealth reduces the number of natural money lessons; the family creates them deliberately (cash purchases, price comparisons, a budget for a trip).
  • [ ] The wealth story is told with the work, the risks, and the failures in it — not to instil guilt, to explain what success costs.
  • [ ] Expensive requests get a hearing and a decision with reasons; "no" is a legitimate, explained answer.
  • [ ] A first financial mistake in early adulthood is normal and is met with a plan, not a stigma.
  • [ ] Each member works outside the family enterprise before joining it (suggested: three to five years).
  • [ ] Competence takes time: roughly a thousand hours of real involvement to be competent with family money; several thousand to be good. Plan for it.
  • [ ] Every member may hold a managed slice of family capital to learn on, sized so nothing important is at risk.

Part 3 — The "are we rich?" frame (for parents)

  1. Hear the question as one about security, not the balance sheet. Ask gently what prompted it — never as an interrogation.
  2. Do not deny it and do not deflect to richer families; both are discovered later as evasions.
  3. Use three categories — not enough, enough, more than enough — place the family in the third, and pair it with what the family does for those who do not have enough.
  4. Stop there unless the child asks more. Note the conversation on the member's learning plan.

20 T20 — Family bank charter and loan application

templateOwner: LAMode Abeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Hughes: Family Wealth Ch. 7 — family bank purpose, loan types, process, governance; Complete Family Wealth Ch. 20 — mission statement, meeting rules, transparency, trustees as participants · Other: Bonner, Family Fortunes — loan terms and no-bailout policy options (paraphrased); Extension — the forms are ours

T20 — Family bank charter and loan application

Purpose

The working documents for a family bank under SOP 47: a charter outline the family completes in its own words (counsel reviews), the two application forms, a decision record, and the loan register.

How to use

  • The LA drafts the charter with the principals or the council; every participant — lender or borrower, including trustees — signs concurrence. Counsel reviews loan documentation and tax treatment before the first loan.
  • Applicants complete the relevant form and present it to the board in person. The CSA files everything and keeps the register; the AA reviews borrower reports.
  • Qualitative portions of every application are circulated to all participants; personal financial detail may be redacted.

Part 1 — Charter outline

Section What the family writes
1. Mission Why the bank exists: a lender whose return is measured in members' independence and the growth of the family's human, intellectual, social, and spiritual capital, and in circulating what members learn
2. Values The family's mission and values statement, and how the bank advances them
3. Participants Who may lend (members, households, trusts with trustee agreement), who may borrow (adult members; conditions for others), and the concurrence each signs
4. Funding Sources and initial capital; how new capital is added; whether repayments recirculate
5. Officers and board Chair, secretary, treasurer; board composition across generations and branches; advisers (the Advisor, counsel, tax) with voice but no vote; terms; the investment-committee liaison
6. Meeting rules Cadence (quarterly); agenda circulated in advance; applicants heard in person; minutes; decision rule (consensus sought; majority with reasons recorded); conflicts — a member abstains on their own or their household's application
7. Loan types Investment loans (business plan and application to a commercial standard; feasibility discussion; business reports; repayment) · Enhancement loans (how the loan increases independence and adds to the family's capitals; repaid in independence and capital) · Grants, if any, and for what purposes
8. Terms (policy choices) Interest: below market / interest-free but repayable / other · Term and repayment schedule · Collateral: none / stated · Purposes funded: ventures, education, homes, health, career starts · No-bailout rule: adopted / not adopted · Emergency provision
9. Application and decision procedure Forms (Parts 2–3); calendar; who reviews; how the decision and reasons are communicated; appeal or resubmission
10. Reporting Investment-loan reports quarterly; enhancement-loan reflections annually; the bank's annual report to the family meeting
11. Transparency rule Every participant receives the qualitative portions of every application; financial detail may be redacted
12. Managed slices Whether the bank funds training allocations (T19), size, coaching, reporting
13. Review and amendment Annual review at the family meeting; amendment rule; dissolution
14. Concurrence Signatures of all participants; date; renewed annually

T21 — Structure summary and communication plan

Purpose

One page, in plain language, for every new trust, entity, gift program, insurance arrangement, or plan the practice helps create. The first half explains what was made and why; the second half plans how the family will hear about it. Planning usually ends in a flurry of documents nobody can later explain — this page is the antidote.

How to use

  • AA drafts within ten days of execution; LA reviews; counsel confirms the accuracy of any summarized legal terms.
  • One page per structure; two at most. Write for a rising-generation member with no financial training.
  • File with the structure's documents in the [Document vault] and in the notebook (T08); review with the client at the 45-Day Follow-up or the next progress meeting.
  • The communication plan is the client's decision; the practice drafts it, the client owns it.

22 T22 — Trustee–beneficiary meeting pack

templateOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 4 — agenda for every meeting; schedule the next one in the room · Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 11, 12, 13, 21 — introductory letters, mindset, premeeting checklists, standing agenda, appreciative reflection, protector check-in; Family Wealth Ch. 10 — the redesigned annual trust meeting · Other: Extension — the pack layout and the assessment items are ours

T22 — Trustee–beneficiary meeting pack

Purpose

Everything needed to prepare, run, and follow up a trustee–beneficiary meeting under SOP 46: the two introductory letters for a new relationship, the two premeeting checklists, the standing agenda with timings, the annual mutual-assessment form, the appreciative reflection, and the protector's check-in note.

How to use

  • The AA assembles the pack; the LA reviews; the CSA sends the accounting and proposed agenda two weeks before the meeting and collects the beneficiary's additions one week before.
  • Use Part 1 only for a new relationship. Parts 2–4 every meeting; Part 5 once a year; Part 6 after an unusually engaged meeting; Part 7 for the protector's annual round.
  • Letters are outlines to be written in each party's own voice. Never send a form letter.

Part 1 — Introductory letters (new relationship)

Trustee → beneficiary — outline

  1. Who I am and how I came to this role (two or three sentences).
  2. Proposed time, place, and length (suggest two hours with an optional meal afterward); practical logistics; a question about any needs or preferences.
  3. What the creator intended, in one sentence, and my hope for how we will work together.
  4. What must happen for you to leave this meeting thinking it was worthwhile? — asked, not assumed.
  5. What I plan to cover: getting to know each other (your questions about me included); your questions about trusts and about this trust — please read the instrument first; your goals, hopes, and concerns; my role and yours, and the roles of anyone else in the picture (protector, investment adviser, committee); how requests for funds work and how I analyze them; investments to whatever depth you want, with a sample statement; open questions.
  6. Please add anything to the agenda; there are no obvious questions.
  7. A follow-up call one week after the meeting for what surfaces on reflection.

Beneficiary → trustee — outline

  1. Who I am: what is going on in my life, what matters to me, my plans, how I see the trust fitting in; gratitude where I feel it.
  2. What I would like on the agenda (co-designing it).
  3. Advance notice of any distribution request, with documents to follow.
  4. A request for the agenda and any preparation materials.

Part 2 — Premeeting checklists

Trustee (and the Advisor supporting the trustee)

  • [ ] Instrument, correspondence, latest statement, and prior notes reviewed.
  • [ ] The highest purpose of this meeting written in one line; what an excellent outcome would look and sound like.
  • [ ] My narratives about this beneficiary, the creator, and the meeting examined; anything that does not serve both parties set aside.
  • [ ] Any pending request read with the enhancement standard in mind; one question prepared that would open a deeper conversation.
  • [ ] Good news: how will I respond with real interest?
  • [ ] The big questions considered as appropriate — is this person self-aware; have they sought their calling; do they have a mentor; can they express gratitude and joy; are they active in the wider world; do they evaluate advisers well — and am I equipped to help where growth is needed?
  • [ ] Mindset chosen: caution where warranted, advancement where possible.

Beneficiary (coached by the Advisor where asked)

  • [ ] Instrument, correspondence, and notes reviewed; the running master list of questions updated and brought.
  • [ ] Agenda reviewed; items added; would this agenda allow a great outcome?
  • [ ] Any request: how would it enhance my life, and what difference would that make?
  • [ ] My narratives about the trustee, the creator, and the meeting — where they came from and whether they help.
  • [ ] My strengths, and how I will bring them into the room.

Part 3 — Standing agenda (business meeting, private, social afterward)

Block Items Suggested time
Opening What do we each hope to accomplish; what must happen for this to be a success · agenda confirmed, additions and deletions · significant life changes since last time and their implications · status of prior to-dos and what we learn from it 15 min
Annual review (once a year) Beneficiary's hopes, challenges, opportunities for the year · trustee's, in role · what is working and what could improve · beneficiary's assessment of the trustee (Part 5) · trustee's assessment of the beneficiary (Part 5) · disputes: resolvable today, or next steps 30–45 min
Technical Statement, tax returns, quantitative items; a sample statement walked through for a new beneficiary 20 min
Distributions New requests · pending requests · anticipated requests (T23) 20–30 min
Close Anything else · to-dos with owners and dates · did we accomplish what we hoped; what worked; what to change next time · next meeting scheduled 10 min

Part 6 — Appreciative reflection (after an unusually good meeting; one week)

  1. Recall a meeting between us that was genuinely collaborative: what made it work — the setting, the preparation, what each of us did, and how that let each of us contribute fully?
  2. Rate our most recent meeting from one to five for engagement. What earned it that number, even if low? What, specifically, would have made it one point higher — who would have done what, with what effect?
  3. What practices bring out the best in our meetings? What do I do well and should do more of? What does the other party do well and should do more of?

23 T23 — Distribution request and decision memo

templateOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Hughes: Family Trusts Ch. 14 — the written request, supporting documents, the enhancement essay, the four-stage analysis, communication of the decision, documentation; Family Trusts Ch. 20 and App. 3 — Distribution Committee questions · Other: Extension — the form layout, the request calendar and the precedent notes are ours

T23 — Distribution request and decision memo

Purpose

A single pack that carries a discretionary distribution request from first conversation to documented decision: the beneficiary's written request, the supporting documents, the analysis worksheet the trustee (with any Distribution Committee and the Advisor) works through, the decision memo, and the request calendar. It makes the distributive function transparent, repeatable, and defensible.

How to use

  • The beneficiary completes Part 1 (with the Advisor's coaching if asked) and attaches Part 2. Much of it is assembled together in conversation — the form is a thinking aid, not a hurdle, and the trustee will not demand every item every time.
  • The trustee, advised by any Distribution Committee and by the Advisor, works Part 3 in order. The trustee decides; advisers advise.
  • Part 4 is written for every discretionary decision, approved or declined. Part 5 sets expectations at onboarding.
  • Emergencies bypass the calendar, not the analysis.

Part 1 — Request (beneficiary)

Field Entry
Beneficiary · trust · date ______
Purpose — what the funds are for, and the larger aim underneath it ______
Amount ______
The trust language I understand permits this request ______ (quote or reference the section)
Timing — when funds are needed; one-time or recurring ______
Related follow-on requests this will lead to (amounts, timing) ______
Other requests I anticipate in the next twelve months ______
My own resources going into this (financial or otherwise) ______
Routes I considered other than trust funds ______

Enhancement essay (where the request is significant or new in kind; half a page) How would approval enhance my life — my growth, my aims, my independence — rather than simply support it? What would be different in a year, and in ten?

Part 2 — Supporting documents (attach what applies)

  • [ ] Invoices, quotes, or receipts
  • [ ] Budget: major expense categories and projected annual spend
  • [ ] Business plan, scaled to my experience and the size of the request
  • [ ] Statement of outside resources (income, assets, other support)
  • [ ] For education: program, duration, cost, what comes after
  • [ ] For a residence: purchase details and a note on loan vs distribution
  • [ ] Anything else the trustee asked for: ______

Part 3 — Analysis worksheet (trustee, committee, Advisor)

Stage 1 — the conversation (before or after the written request)

Question explored Notes
What motivates the request; is there a larger purpose beneath it?
How does it square with the creator's intent (purpose statement, letters of wishes)?
How does it square with the trust's language?
Is there a better route to the goal than trust funds?
Will the beneficiary have their own stake in it?
If approved: best outcome, short term and long term?
If declined: what changes; what alternatives exist; what would a good outcome after a "no" look like?
Growth question inserted (e.g., what does having the trust pay for this cost you in independence?)

Stage 2 — the enhancement standard

Is making — or not making — this distribution more likely to enhance the beneficiary's life (maturation, pursuit of their own aims) than to subsidize it? Consider life stage explicitly. Assessment: ______

Stage 3 — the document

Would approval be a reasonable exercise of discretion under the trust's terms? __ If the language is narrower than the purpose: note for the structural review (SOP 48) — ____

Stage 4 — prudence checks

Check Finding
Size relative to the trust; effect on prudent capital
Request history — consistent with past decisions?
One-off or part of a plan; cumulative impact
Requests anticipated this year and beyond; constraint on future decisions
Effect on other beneficiaries (current and remainder)
Outside resources — must they be considered; what are they?
Loan, or part-loan / part-distribution, better than a distribution?
Committee advice received (if a Distribution Committee exists)

Part 4 — Decision memo (every discretionary decision)

Field Entry
Decision approved / approved in part / declined / deferred to ______
Amount and form (distribution / loan / mixed) and timing ______
Reasoning, stage by stage (conversation → enhancement → document → prudence) ______
Alternatives offered or brainstormed if declined ______
Conditions or follow-up (reports, milestones, next conversation) ______
How and when the decision was communicated; questions answered ______
Precedent notes — what this decision implies for similar future requests ______
Prepared by · advised by · decided by (trustee) · date ______

Note

Three uses of the memo: a template for the next request, a record for successor trustees, and evidence if the decision is ever questioned in the family or in court.

Part 5 — Request calendar (set at onboarding)

Type of request Cadence Submission deadline Decision within
Routine (living-expense budget, recurring education costs) Quarterly ______ ______
Significant (business, residence, large one-time) Annually, at the annual review ______ ______
Emergency As needed none as fast as prudence allows

T24 — Family Trust Review outline, ten-year review worksheet, and fiduciary selection questionnaire

Purpose

Four working tools for SOP 48: the engagement outline for a Family Trust Review; the ten-year trustscape review worksheet; a questionnaire for selecting (or briefing) a trustee or protector; and a Distribution Committee charter checklist.

How to use

  • Part 1 is completed with the reviewer and the principals at commissioning; the Advisor coordinates data and interviews.
  • Part 2 is the AA's worksheet every three years and at any trigger in SOP 48.
  • Part 3 is worked with any prospective trustee or protector — by the candidate for their own decision, by the creator as a selection instrument, and by the Advisor when briefing a named fiduciary at drafting time. Candidates who arrive asking these questions are a good sign.
  • Part 4 goes to counsel when a Distribution Committee is being authorized.

Part 1 — Family Trust Review engagement outline

Field Entry
Family · commissioning party (principal / council / trustee) ______
Trigger (tick) [ ] generational transition [ ] education of trustees, beneficiaries, or managers [ ] change in family or trust leadership [ ] termination or large principal distribution within ten years [ ] decanting or reformation of a complex or costly system [ ] new trusts or a private trust company
Reviewer (EEN) and the Advisor's coordinating role ______
Scope — trusts, entities, foundation, family office in scope ______
Research plan [ ] interviews with family leaders (and adult beneficiaries / trustees as agreed) [ ] study of written and oral family and enterprise history [ ] review of existing structures and documents
Interview list (name · role · consent to be interviewed · date) ______
Data the Advisor supplies trust inventory (Part 2), fee tally, IPS documents, purpose statements, governance documents, family executive summary (T17)
Deliverables 1 family history with short biographies of leaders past and present · 2 history of the enterprise and its philanthropy · 3 the family's prominent values · 4 the trust system: architecture, interactions, costs · 5 recommendations for design and for family education
Timeline commissioning __ · interviews complete _ · draft · presentation at family meeting ___
Fee and who pays ______ (placeholder; disclosed per [Firm Compliance])
Where recommendations are tracked T10 tracker; SOP 45 governance work; T19 learning plans

Part 2 — Ten-year trustscape review worksheet

Inventory (one row per trust or entity)

Trust / entity Purpose statement? Trustee(s) Protector Primary beneficiaries Funded / active? Distributions now (annual) Projected over 10 years Terminates within 10 years? Fees (trustee · investment · other)

System questions

Question Answer
Total annual cost of the system (all fees), and as a share of assets
What happens to each trust if its trustee dies or steps down this year? Who holds the appointment power; does the beneficiary know them?
What happens if a primary beneficiary — or an entire class — dies?
Which trusts have language narrower than their purpose (from decision memos, T23)?
Which trusts lack a protector, a distribution-advice mechanism, or purpose language?
Where are the foreseeable problem spots (relationships, liquidity, concentration, litigation risk, addiction)?
Conflicts of interest in the trustscape, and how each is disclosed and managed
Recommendation: keep / simplify / modify / commission a Family Trust Review
Reviewed by · date · next review

Part 3 — Trustee / protector selection questionnaire (our topics)

First response

  1. Who created the trust, who are the beneficiaries, and when would the role actually begin?
  2. Why were you chosen — and do you believe the reasoning?
  3. What is your first feeling about it, and what inclines you to decline or accept?

Document homework

  1. Having read the instrument closely, can you say what the trust is for?
  2. Who receives what, under what circumstances, and when does it end?
  3. Is there more than one trustee, and how are duties divided?

Self-inventory

  1. What story do you carry about trusts, beneficiaries, and family wealth?
  2. Are you yourself a beneficiary or a recipient of wealth, and how has that gone?
  3. How do you handle your own financial administration — willingly or as a chore?
  4. Have you made significant gifts or created trusts, and what did you learn?

Yellow flags (none disqualifying; each argues for slowing down)

  1. Are the beneficiaries known to you or strangers?
  2. Was the creator's relationship with them close or strained; is there a history of conflict, cut-offs, or litigation?
  3. Children of more than one marriage; multiple branches; multiple generations?
  4. Known addictions or behavioral issues among present or future beneficiaries?
  5. Assets needing special expertise; unusual directions to hold assets; a family business in the trust?

Deeper questions

  1. Are you humble about what you do not know, and willing to close the gaps?
  2. Are you comfortable overseeing a relative's spending, and will it change the relationship?
  3. In a disagreement with a beneficiary, what would you do, and whom would you consult informally?
  4. Have you already discussed goals and expectations with the beneficiary?
  5. Are you looking forward to it, and how will the beneficiary benefit?
  6. Will you be paid, how will that be set, and how do you feel about it?
  7. How significant is the liability, and are you comfortable with it?
  8. Is this a long-term commitment you can keep, and what is the exit if you cannot?
  9. Which "caps" do you wear with this beneficiary, and can the trustee cap sit on top whenever you act as trustee?
  10. For a protector: can you stay dormant, ask "how is it going?" once a year, and act only when asked?

Assessment (creator or Advisor)

Trait Evidence
Specific expertise, or willingness to buy it
Integrity
Professionalism (records, reliability)
Chemistry with the beneficiary
Capacity to mentor
Decision · date

Part 4 — Distribution Committee charter checklist (for counsel)

  • [ ] Authorized in the instrument (or added by settlement / reformation / decanting / protector action, or convened by the trustee on its own initiative)
  • [ ] Tied to the trust's purpose statement
  • [ ] Function: advises the trustee on distributions; never approves or declines
  • [ ] Composition: one or several members chosen for wisdom, listening, self-awareness; may be officers of a firm engaged for the purpose
  • [ ] Appointment by the creator, trustee, or an independent party, in consultation with primary beneficiaries; beneficiaries cannot add or remove members
  • [ ] Terms: five years; two-term cap; age-out; each member nominates a successor with existing members' approval, reverting to the trustee
  • [ ] Costs paid by the trust; compensation disclosed
  • [ ] Formal review every three years by trustee, protector, and primary beneficiaries
  • [ ] Not combined with the protector role
  • [ ] Information sharing between trustee and committee authorized

T26 — Job description, scorecard and interview guide

Purpose

The forms used in SOP 72: a job-description template, three ready-to-adapt role summaries, the three-dimension scorecard, interview topics for both rounds, work-sample briefs, reference-check topics, and the offer checklist.

How to use

  • Complete Part 1 before advertising. Keep Part 1's compensation block out of the posting.
  • Score every candidate on Part 3 after each stage; decide from the scores, not from the last conversation.
  • The role summaries in Part 2 are starting points — edit the measures to the practice's current numbers.

Part 1 — Job description template

Section Content
Title and track ______ · support / professional
Reports to ______
Purpose of the role (two sentences) ______
Responsibilities (owns / does / supports) ______ (reference the SOPs the role performs)
Key measures of success at 90 days and 12 months ______
Required skills and knowledge ______
Required experience ______
Desirable, not required ______
Career path from this seat ______
Internal only — compensation range and movement factors midpoint __ ; range _ to ___ ; moves with responsibility, experience, credentials

Part 2 — Role summaries to adapt

Client Service Associate (support track; overhead) Owns: scheduling and confirmations (SOP 05, T01); meeting logistics and packets; sign-here paperwork; the implementation tracker (SOP 15, T07); client notebook and [Document vault]; [CRM] hygiene; reporting assembly (SOP 24); service-failure intake (SOP 23); red-flag monitoring (SOP 22). Measures: confirmations within 24 hours (100%); zero administrative errors on transfers; tracker current weekly; every meeting ends with the next scheduled.

Service Advisor (professional track; direct expense) Owns: investment plan and IPS production (SOP 13, T06); periodic reviews and the quarterly package analysis; routine progress meetings — co-attended, then led with the LA present, then independent (SOP 20); the advanced-planning tracker (T10); watching for held-away assets and planning openings. Attends every client meeting with a named role. Measures: first independently led progress meeting by month 6; relationship-manager test (T27) passed on ≥ 5 relationships by month 12; plan drafts accepted with minor edits.

Associate Advisor / Analyst (professional track, entry) Owns: analysis for plans and reviews; meeting packets; tracker upkeep; expert-meeting case briefs (T09); executive-summary drafting support (T17). Second chair on large relationships. Measures: packets complete three days before meetings; case briefs accepted without rework; one defined analysis presented in a client meeting per month by month 3.

Part 3 — Scorecard

Dimension Weight (CSA / SA / AA) Evidence sought Score 1–5
Technical and theoretical 40 / 40 / 60 Work sample; credentials; how they explain a plan or a statement
Client relationship 60 / 45 / 25 Warmth; reliability; handling a hard question or a mistake; listening
Business development capacity 0 / 15 / 15 Recognizes opportunity with existing clients; comfort in professional communities
Team fit (pass/fail) — "Our" not "my"; takes feedback; no exceptions asked for

Weighted score: __ . Bar to proceed: ____ .

Part 4 — Interview topics

Round one (experience and proficiency) — walk through the last two roles and why each ended; the career the candidate wants in five years; explain a planning or portfolio concept to a non-expert; describe a client situation that went wrong and what they did; how they prefer to receive feedback; what they want to know about how this practice serves families.

Round two (concerns and fit) — the specific gaps the work sample and references raised; a scenario in which a client asks them something outside their remit (looking for "I'll own it and bring in the right person," not "I'll transfer you"); a scenario in which the LA is unavailable and a family calls with a problem; their view on sharing relationships across a team; the equity question, answered with the SOP 72 script; their questions for us.

Part 5 — Work-sample briefs

  • Service Advisor: a two-page family case (assets, entities, goals, one advanced-planning issue) → draft the executive summary of an investment plan on T06 and a one-page tracker on T10; present in five minutes; the panel asks two client-style questions.
  • Associate / Analyst: the same case → a case brief on T09 and the packet checklist for a first progress meeting.
  • Client Service Associate: a set of transfer instructions with one deliberate inconsistency → complete T07 and draft the client confirmation on T01; the panel looks for the inconsistency being caught and raised.

Part 6 — Reference-check topics

Confirm dates and role; the best work the person did; how they handled a mistake; how clients or colleagues spoke of them; whether they would hire them again and for what; who else worked closely with them — then call that person too.

Part 7 — Offer checklist

  • [ ] Title, track, reporting line, start date
  • [ ] Salary within range; incentive described as it really works, including that it can be zero
  • [ ] Benefits and time off as they actually are
  • [ ] Non-solicitation language drafted by counsel / [Firm Compliance]
  • [ ] 90-day review named
  • [ ] Written; one revision at most; no haggling
  • [ ] Acceptance recorded; team told before clients; onboarding plan (T27) opened

28 T28 — Team meeting agendas, dashboard, capacity check and bogey worksheet

templateOwner: LAMode AMode Bbeyond BowenUpdated 2026-09-01
Bowen: Ch. 6 — red-flag methodology; service failures as service opportunities · Other: Palaveev — ratio dashboard, capacity arithmetic, the founder's bogey, productivity measures, porch of indecision (paraphrased)

T28 — Team meeting agendas, dashboard, capacity check and bogey worksheet

Purpose

The forms behind SOP 74 and SOP 70: standing agendas for each internal meeting, the five-ratio dashboard with target bands, the capacity-check worksheet that reads the hiring triggers, the founder's bogey worksheet that sets the hiring budget, the per-professional productivity table, and the annual porch-of-indecision review.

How to use

  • CSA prepares the agendas the day before each meeting and the dashboard before each monthly and quarterly review.
  • LA completes the bogey worksheet privately once a year and whenever a hiring decision is on the table; only the resulting surplus figure enters the capacity check.
  • Fill the tables in place; keep prior quarters for trend.

Part 1 — Standing agendas

Weekly team meeting (30 min) 1. Next two weeks of client meetings — attendee, named role, packet status, anything the client must hear beforehand. 2. Open service items — who has the ball; anything older than a week. 3. Red flags raised since last week (SOP 22) and the contact made. 4. Implementation tracker exceptions (T07). 5. Borrowed engagements due this week (T25). 6. Decisions and owners.

Monthly principal review (45 min) 1. EBOC and overhead % vs bands. 2. Service-failure log — each entry mapped to an SOP step. 3. Borrowed-expertise pipeline and scorecards. 4. Hours by professional; borrowed hours. 5. Actions from last month.

Quarterly review (2 h) 1. Common-sized P&L vs 40 / 35 / 25. 2. Capacity check (Part 3) vs SOP 70 triggers. 3. SOP review (SOP 60): changed, failed, missing. 4. Client review: fit, risk, unpriced customization. 5. Productivity measures (Part 5). 6. State of the team — what is working, what is not, what each person needs. 7. Decisions and dates.

Annual (half day, Q4) 1. Budget by cost owner, loaded for monthly variance review. 2. Performance reviews (standards stated) → compensation decisions. 3. Equity and succession conversation. 4. Porch-of-indecision review (Part 6). 5. Roadmap block in SOP 70 updated.

Part 2 — Five-ratio dashboard

Ratio Definition Band Cadence This period Trend
EBOC Revenue − all expenses except owner compensation, ÷ revenue ~50–60% for a $1–5M practice; higher when very small Monthly
Overhead % Non-professional expenses ÷ revenue ~35% Monthly
Revenue per head Revenue ÷ (owners + staff) < $200K overstaffed · > $250K hire Semiannual
Revenue per professional Revenue ÷ professionals incl. owner ~$500K norm Semiannual
Revenue per relationship Revenue ÷ relationships trend; informs minimums Quarterly
